An Address to the Most Pious Emperor Theodosius, by the Same Holy Cyril, Archbishop of Alexandria. On the Right Faith in Our Lord Jesus Christ.

1. You, O Christ-loving emperors, hold the highest glory among human beings, raised and set above all others by distinctions beyond compare. This is an exceptional and fitting lot that God has given you, for you bear on earth an image of the supremacy that is his over all things. For every knee bows to him: Thrones and Principalities, Dominions and Powers bend their necks to him as slaves and honour him with the doxologies that are always his due, and they say that heaven and earth are full of his glory. In your Serenity too one may see the type of that glory, so conspicuous and highest of all, shining out clearly and vividly. For you are the sources of the dignities that are allotted [?], beyond all other supremacy, and the beginning and origin of human prosperity. Under the most gentle rule of your might, all that is subject to the thrones of the empire is steered into a lawful, admirable and celebrated life. Those who will not bear the yoke fall easily, overcome by your strength. If the emperor's shield merely flashes, their hopes vanish and are gone. At once they turn their minds away from the madness that possessed them [?], and falling down [?]

they beg for mercy. And so the most warlike, battle-hardened and ever-victorious host of your shield-bearers has prevailed over [?]. You are the song and the lyre of those who live toward the east and the west, the theme of all praise. Those toward the south, and indeed all who dwell further north, never cease to crown you with thank-offerings. And the unshaken support of your reign, so beloved of God and so pious, is our Lord Jesus Christ himself. "For through him kings reign, and the mighty decree justice," as it is written. His will is all-powerful, and by his mere nod comes the fullness of every good. Very readily he gives to those who love him the choicest of all things that are worth having and admired. What has been given to your might is enough to prove what I have said, and so is what will yet be given, as we believe. That the boast of piety toward God is an unshakeable foundation for the honours of kings, I shall try to show you convincingly from the holy and God-inspired Scripture itself, being as brief as I can.

2. Very many, over the course of time, have ruled the land of the Jews and administered the thrones of their kingdom. Those who impiously neglected reverence for God and counted as nothing the law that presides over righteousness plunged themselves, the wretches, into the depths of wickedness, and perished miserably, as wicked men do. For it is a most grievous thing to offend God, and to stray in any way at all from what is fitting, and so grieve him. But all who became guardians of piety toward him and genuine keepers of what pleases him conquered their enemies without toil and prevailed over their adversaries. Such was Josiah. He burned the priests of the idols together with their very shrines and altars, did away with every kind of sorcery and false divination, and abolished the playthings of demonic deceit. So he showed his kingdom to be worthy of all esteem, admirable to the peoples and admired even to this day by those who know how to honour whatever the divine mind approves. All these things, however, your ancestors and you yourselves have accomplished very well. It will also be useful to recall what was done in the times of Hezekiah, that wisest of kings, for the [?] of this account will profit your most pious head not a little.

3. There was a man from Babylon in Persia, Rabshakeh. He laid waste practically the whole land of the Jews, and when he had ravaged Samaria along with it, he advanced on Jerusalem itself, escorted by a host of countless men under his command. He had a cavalry phalanx that was not easily overcome, or rather was hard even to face, and foot soldiers as many as the sands. Then he set siege engines and all the apparatus of war around the wall. Swollen with no small barbarian arrogance, he declared that he would take the holy city itself by force along with the others. He was insolent toward the ineffable glory and uttered blasphemies, letting loose an unrestrained and unbridled tongue against God. For he said that even if God wished to save them, the favour of his help would be useless to those who trusted in him. When men came and reported to the king the outrages of that boor and his words full of Persian pride, then indeed the king was pained, it seems, by the blasphemies against God alone. He wisely judged that these would be the reason for the city's capture, so he tore his garments and went up to the house of God, plainly seeking to avert the divine wrath with supplications and to clear himself of the guilt of the blasphemies. And what came of it? He made the Lord of powers kindly and merciful toward him, and he conquered the Assyrian. He did not arm a well-bridled horse for battle. He did not rely on the aim of archers, or on the casting of spears, or on the tactical skill of those under his command. He relied instead on the decree of God, who appointed death for the Assyrian army in a single night. "For an angel of the Lord went out," it says, "and slew a hundred and eighty-five thousand in the camp of the Assyrians. And when they rose in the morning, they found all the bodies dead." These are the fruits of piety toward God, and of refusing to tolerate any word spoken against the divine glory itself.

4. I think it most necessary, then, that nothing blasphemous against God should be spoken in the pious ears of emperors, but rather whatever runs beyond all blame and slander and pays him the doxology that befits him. Since I know this very well, I felt compelled to write down in this book the tradition of the orthodox and apostolic faith, and to bring it as a kind of spiritual gift to your Might, and also to the truly most God-beloved empresses who shine together with your Serenity. The one takes pride in the offspring for which you so longed, and brings the scepters hope of their lasting for ever. The other, flourishing together with the virgin shoots [?],

makes the cares of your most glorious reign her own. Indian gems brighten your celebrated heads, but the ornament of soul and mind, perceived by the mind, would be right and unadulterated faith. Confident that you will keep it, I offer this discourse as a support for the mind, a glory for the soul and a crown for the heart. For it is written: "Wisdom is better than costly stones, and nothing precious is worthy of her." So I shall try to speak briefly about the Incarnation of the Only-begotten, and to set out as clearly as I can what the mystery concerning him is, so far as this is possible for those who see in a mirror and in a riddle and know in part, according to the measure of the gift supplied by the Spirit. As the inspired Paul writes: "For no one says 'Lord Jesus' except in the Holy Spirit; and no one says 'Jesus is accursed' except in Beelzebul."

5. Someone might say, I suppose: "Well then, since you have decided to enter the arena on this question and to take on so contentious and burdensome a labour, explain without hesitation the exact and unadulterated doctrine about Christ, free of every charge. For some are drunk on various opinions, and distort into ugliness what was prophesied of him in both the New and the Older Scripture." We are well aware that the senseless leave no absurdity untried. They fall very readily into the snare of Hades, as it is written, and into the trap of death, "understanding neither what they say nor the things about which they make assertions." What the babblings and solemn little fables of each of them are, I shall now set out.

6. Some have dared to think and to say that the Word from God the Father appeared as a man, but not that he also bore the flesh from the holy Virgin and Theotokos; they falsely ascribe to the mystery a mere appearance. Others again think it shameful to seem to worship a man, and refuse to crown flesh from the earth with the highest glories. Out of their great ignorance they suffer from a spurious and corrupted piety, and say that the Word, begotten of God the Father, was changed into the nature of bones and sinews and flesh. The wretches laugh openly at the birth of Emmanuel from a virgin and charge so excellent and God-befitting an economy with impropriety. Others have believed that God the Word, coeternal with the Father, came into being late, and was called into bare existence only when he received the beginning of his birth according to the flesh. And some have been carried to such a pitch of madness [?]

that they say the Word from God has no hypostasis of his own, and that a mere word, understood simply as something uttered, came to be in a man. These are Marcellus and Photinus. Still others hold that the Only-begotten truly became man, and believe that he came to be in flesh, but not that the flesh he assumed was perfectly ensouled with a rational soul possessing a mind like ours. Binding the Word from God and the temple from the holy Virgin into what they suppose is a complete unity, they say that the Word dwelt in it, made the assumed body his own, and himself filled the place of the rational and intellectual soul. Others again champion views opposed to these and resist their thinking. They affirm that Emmanuel is composed and woven together of God the Word and a rational soul and body, that is, simply of a perfect humanity. Yet they have not kept their doctrine about him entirely sound and blameless, for they divide the one Christ into two. Driving a thick cut between them, as it were, they present each as practically standing apart by himself. They insist that the one born of the Virgin is a perfect man, and that the Word from God the Father is someone else. They are not simply distinguishing what the nature of God is and what the nature of the flesh is, nor are they content to dwell only on the differences in that respect. If they were, they would not have missed the true understanding of the matter, since the nature of flesh and that of Godhead are indeed not the same. Instead they set the one apart, separately, as a man, and name the other God, by nature and truly, though they wish to be Christians. Indeed, in certain little treatises they have written on these matters, they have dared to say, in these very words: "For the one, the Word from God the Father, is Son by nature and truly; the other is Son homonymously with the Son." And again, further on: "The Word of God [did not become?] flesh, but assumed a man. For the Only-begotten is, primarily and in himself, Son of God the Creator of all. But the man whom he assumed, not being God by nature, is styled homonymously with him on account of the one who assumed him, who is truly Son of God. For the saying 'No one knows the Son except the Father' indicates the one who is perfect by nature and in truth Son from the Father. But what Gabriel said, 'Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favour with God; and behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus,' applies to the man." So much for their views. We, however, will not think this way. The argument of the heterodox will never persuade us to leave the straight track and run along another that misses the mark and is perverted.

7. If anyone chose to discuss each of these at length and to examine them thoroughly, he would spend an immeasurable amount of time, and only by enduring heavy and inescapable toil would he barely succeed. So let us set aside any thought of speaking at great length and with minute hair-splitting, and apply only a very brief examination to each. Come, then: first of all let us say to the Docetists: "You are wrong, because you know neither the Scriptures" nor the great mystery of godliness, that is, Christ, who "was manifested in the flesh, vindicated in the spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory." In my view our opponents must do one of two things. They may pass a still more shameful verdict on the men of old and call liars those who initiated the whole world into the mysteries, to whom Christ himself said, "Go and make disciples of all the nations." Or, if they shudder to do this, they must choose to think rightly about Christ. Bidding a firm farewell to their own ignorance, they must cling fast to the sacred writings, and walking the unerring path of the saints, make their way to the very

8. For the mystery of godliness would be, I think, nothing other than the Word from God the Father himself, who for our sake "was manifested in the flesh." For he was born through the holy Virgin and Theotokos, taking the form of a servant. He was also "seen by angels," who honoured him at his birth: "Glory to God in the highest," they say, "and on earth peace, good will among men." And indeed, pointing out to the shepherds God the Word, who for our sake was in the flesh, they say: "Behold, there is born to you today a Saviour, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David. And this will be the sign for you: you will find a baby wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger." If there was a birth of God through a virgin and a manifestation in the flesh, how is it not feeble, idle talk, how is it not madness and nonsense, to label so clear and evident an economy with the name of "appearance"? For if it was shadow and appearance, if there was no true incarnation and the Virgin did not give birth, then the Word from God the Father did not take hold of the seed of Abraham and was not made like his brothers. For our condition is no [shadow?], no type or appearance. We exist in bodies that can be touched and seen, we are clothed in this earthborn flesh, and we succumb to corruption and passions.

9. So if the Word did not become flesh, neither is he able, "in that he himself has suffered when tempted, to help those

who are tempted." For a shadow could suffer nothing, and so the whole thing would truly have come to nothing for us. What back did he then give for our sake? What cheek did he offer to those who struck him, enduring the blows from the Jews? How could anyone suppose that one who did not appear in the flesh had his hands and feet pierced with nails? Or what side, tell me, did Pilate's soldiers pierce to show the onlookers the precious blood gushing out with water? And if we must go further still: then Christ neither died for us nor was raised. If that were accepted as true, faith is emptied, the cross, the salvation and life of the world, is gone, and the hope of those who have fallen asleep in faith has utterly perished. So it seemed to the blessed Paul as well: "For I delivered to you first of all what I also received, that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, and that he was buried, and that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the Twelve. Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once, most of whom remain until now, though some have fallen asleep. Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles. Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me." And again, further on: "Now if Christ is proclaimed as raised from the dead, how can some of you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? If there is no resurrection of the dead, then Christ has not been raised; and if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is empty, and your faith is empty too. And we are found to be false witnesses about God, because we testified about God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise, if indeed the dead are not raised." Tell me, how could a shadow die? How then did the Father raise Christ, if he was a shadow and an appearance that the bonds of death could not seize? Away, then, with their vomit! We regard their teachings as nothing but fable and the products of an unholy design. For the Saviour's disciple warns us in advance about such people when he writes: "For many false prophets have gone out into the world. By this the Spirit of God is known: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God. This is the spirit of the Antichrist, which you have heard is coming, and now it is already in the world." For if he did not become man, and did not ascend in the flesh to the Father and God in heaven, neither would he return to us from heaven, plainly as man and in the flesh.

10. Others, out of immeasurable dullness, think and hold that the Word begotten of God refused birth from the holy Virgin and dishonoured our nature, and was rather changed into flesh from the earth. This is the view of men who blaspheme the economy and have chosen to find fault with the divine counsels. For the Creator of all, the Word of God, rich in mercy, emptied himself for our sake, becoming man, born of a woman, "so that, since the children share in blood and flesh" (that is, we), "he himself likewise partook of the same things, that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and set free those who through fear of death were subject to slavery all their lives." So the sacred Writ says. But these men judge so beautiful and excellent a counsel to be unfitting, and as though it were in their power to know better, they find fault with the counsels of Wisdom. They say we ought not to ascribe the pangs of labour and birth from a woman to the Only-begotten, but should rather think that the nature of the Word was transformed into this frail, earthborn body. So they imagine change in him who knows no change. For the nature of God is firmly fixed in its own goods, and has an unshakeable permanence in what it is. A created nature, brought into being in time, might undergo alteration, and that would not lie outside proper and true reason. For whatever has received any beginning of existence has, as it were, the necessity of being altered already sown into it from the start. But God, whose existence is exempt from and surpasses all mind, nature, generation and corruption, will be superior to change as well [?]. Just as by the principle of his own nature he rises above and transcends everything that tends toward coming into being, and does so by differences beyond compare, so too he will rise above suffering the things that commonly happen to what has come into being through him, for he does not know what by nature does harm. The Divine, then, abides unchangeably in its goods, while created things are subject to alteration and change and are liable to be carried astray. Knowing this very well, and reasoning most wisely, the prophet Jeremiah says to God: "You sit enthroned for ever, and we perish for ever." For the Divine will sit as on its own throne, ever reigning and ruling over all, tyrannized by none of the passions. But we, whose nature is most unstable and very easily swept toward alteration and change, "perish for ever," that is, at every season and time we are corruptible and changeable. So the Divine could never fall away from its own stability [?]

[?] …nor would the corruptible and changeable nature, that is, created nature, ever be enriched with immutability as a property of its own being, nor would creation boast of the goods of the divine nature as if they were its own; for it would rightly be told, "What do you have that you did not receive?" That the nature of the Word is wholly unchangeable and unalterable, while created nature is in every way subject to change, anyone may very easily see when blessed David sings in the Spirit: "The heavens will perish, but you remain; they will all grow old like a garment, and like a cloak you will roll them up, and they will be changed; but you are the same, and your years will not fail." Where, then, has the Word who is from God still remained the same, if it is true to say that he gave up his firm and unshaken state, came down into what he was not, and was transformed into the nature of flesh, into something by nature subject to corruption? Is this not plain nonsense and madness? How could anyone doubt it?

11. For it is time to answer their ignorance with something still more ignorant, and to say that it is not unlikely that flesh not from the earth might one day be able to rise up to the nature of the Godhead and become part of the constitution of the substance that is supreme above all. For if the very nature of the Godhead, according to their stupefied notion, has passed over into the nature of flesh, nothing, it seems, any longer prevents the flesh from soaring above its own lower nature and being refashioned into Godhead and into the supreme substance. But we shall not surrender sound sense to their folly. Rather, we shall follow the divine Scriptures: the Prophet says, "Behold, the virgin shall conceive in her womb and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel"; and blessed Gabriel seals this prophecy and explains the decree from on high to the virgin: "Do not be afraid, Mary," he said, "for behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus." We therefore believe that Emmanuel was truly born of a woman, and, thinking rightly, we shall not cast away the splendid and most precious boast of our own nature. For the Only-begotten took hold not of his own nature (otherwise our condition would be no better off), nor of the nature of angels, but "of the seed of Abraham," as it is written. For in this way, and in no other, was it possible to save the race that had slipped into corruption.

12. What then? Is not this too, besides, worthy of wonder? For we are all but [?] …

[?] …to the divinely inspired Scripture, and some, handing over their own minds to a spirit of error, have come to such folly and childish stupidity that they think the Creator of the ages, God the Word, coeternal with God the Father, had the beginning of his existence at the same time as the birth of the flesh. They imagine as born late him who is beyond every age and time, as though God became Father only in the last times, the times of the incarnation, and as though he through whom are all things, and in whom are all things, entered into being and subsistence together with the temple taken from the Virgin. Have they not, then, reached the very uttermost of evils, these people who so readily accepted so loathsome an old wives' tale and filled their minds with sheer dullness? "Truly their throat is an open grave; with their tongues they deceive; the poison of asps is under their lips; their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness." For he through whom are all things must of necessity be understood to exist before all things. And what can they do, when John writes: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things came into being through him, and without him nothing came into being that has come into being"? And again: "That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon and our hands have touched, concerning the Word of life: and the life was revealed, and we have seen it, and we testify and declare to you the eternal life, which was with the Father and was revealed to us." And Christ himself pointed out to the Jews the remote antiquity of his own existence. For when they said, "You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?", they heard him answer plainly: "Truly I tell you, before Abraham came to be, I am." Where "was" stands with nothing added to it, and where "I am" is clearly set down, what beginning of his generation could anyone see? Or how could he who was in the beginning, beyond all understanding, admit of being brought into existence in time? If anyone should choose to oppose these people more laboriously, it is not hard to bring forward the words of the inspired Scripture and beat back the darts of their stupefaction. But things so plainly diseased and open to refutation, and so very unsightly, I think it superfluous even to treat as worth any attention. Let us go on, then, to the error that is akin to the one already condemned.

13. For some debase the beauty of the truth, as one might counterfeit a coin, "lifting up their horn on high and speaking unrighteousness against God," as it is written.

(Variant readings: "as being without existence"; "should wish" or "should choose".)

…[as without existence] and not subsisting individually, they imagine the Only-begotten. They say that he does not exist in a hypostasis of his own, but is simply a saying, a word that came from God only as something uttered, which, the wretches say, also took up its dwelling in a man. Having put Jesus together in this way, they say that he is holier than the saints, but not also God. So, as the Savior's disciple writes: "Who is the liar but the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ? This is the Antichrist, the one who denies the Father and the Son. Everyone who denies the Son does not have the Father either; whoever confesses the Son has the Father also." For both, and through both, and each in the other, are recognized both by us and by the holy angels. No one could learn what a Father is unless he received in his mind a Son who subsists and has been begotten. Nor, again, could one learn what the Son is unless he clearly considered that the Father has begotten him. So I think it necessary, and safe, to say that if the Son has no existence, we would not truly understand the Father to be a father either. For where is a father, if he has not truly begotten? Or if what he has begotten does not subsist and does not exist at all, what is begotten will be nothing. For what does not subsist is equal to nothing, or rather is nothing at all; and then the Father will be the father of nothing…

14. But, my good sirs, I would say to the expounders of such ideas, what you say is idle twaddle. Tell me, since I ask you, in what way the love of God the Father for us is extraordinary. If he gave for us the Son who, according to you, does not subsist, then he has given nothing for us. Then the Word did not become flesh, nor did he endure the precious cross, nor did he abolish the power of death, nor did he come back to life. For if he is nothing and without existence, as you say, how could he be involved in any of these things? In that case the word of holy Scripture has deceived those who believed, and the firm foundation of the faith goes off into nothing. What then? Has the sacred Writing not shown us that the Son exists in the form of God, and does it not call him the image and the imprint of the one who begot him? How is this not evident to everyone? Images are like their archetypes; they must be so, and not otherwise. So unless the image is subsistent, and unless the imprint is understood to exist in an existence of its own, they will be forced by necessary reasoning to grant that he whose imprint it is also lacks subsistence, and the defect of the image will run back entirely to the archetype.

15. Then tell me: when Philip, a most devoted disciple of Christ, asked to see the Father, saying, "Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us," was he asking to see the Father who exists and subsists, or the one who does not exist and has no subsistence? Anyone, I think, would say without hesitation: the one who

exists and subsists. If, then, the Son is nothing, since he does not subsist, according to their unbridled audacity, how did he present himself to us as the image and exact knowledge of the Father, saying, "Have I been with you all this time, and you do not know me, Philip? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father. Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? I and the Father are one"? But no one, I think, would see the subsisting in what does not subsist, nor could what exists ever be conceived as wholly identical with what does not exist. How, then, will the Father be in the Son, and the Son in turn in the Father? Or is it not easy to say that if the Word does not exist in an existence of his own, the Father himself would be in danger, having nothing within himself and being thought to exist in nothing? For what does not exist at all [?] could then only be thought of as nothing. The argument is not without harshness, for it carries a very great absurdity within it; yet it does reduce the opponents' doctrine to something jarring. One might fairly ask how the Father made existing things in the Son, if the Son never obtained being. And if someone asked whether being is good for existing things, or rather non-being, anyone would say at once: being. For he who gave being to things that were not has shown himself, and is, supremely good: the Creator. That is how the matter stands by nature. So creation is better off than he through whom all things were brought into being; for he is said not to subsist, while they subsist and are understood to be. What absurd notions! Away with such blasphemy! "For the Word of God is living and active," as it is written. That is why he also said, "I am the life." But he could not be understood as life if he did not subsist; and he is life by nature, for he will never lie. To say, then, that the Word who came forth from God does not subsist is a rotten falsehood, the outflow of a stony mind. For he himself said to Moses, "I am he who is." How could that which truly is, preserved in its own hypostasis, ever be thought not to subsist? We shall therefore rightly define the view of those who hold such opinions as the height of ignorance.

16. Yet neither shall we praise—we who have been well taught to hunt eagerly after the truth—those who say that the flesh united to the Word lacked a rational soul. They clothe the Word in flesh that possessed only vital and sensitive movement and so bring him into the world, assigning the activity of mind and soul to the Only-begotten. For, I know not why, they shudder at confessing that the Word was united by nature with flesh ensouled by a rational soul, with hu-

(Notes: "most foolish"; "therefore".)

-man flesh. They regard the tradition of the faith, which comes from above and is most ancient, as worth very little, and in their ignorance they have decided that one must follow only their own will and human reasonings, truly thinking otherwise than one ought to think. And what their reasoning is for such a doctrine, I will explain. We say that the Mediator between God and men, according to the Scriptures, is composed of our humanity, complete according to its own definition, and of the Son who came forth from God by nature, that is, the Only-begotten. We affirm that a coming together, a concurrence beyond reason, has taken place into a union of unequal and unlike natures. Yet we acknowledge that he is called one Christ, and Lord Jesus, and Son, at once existing and understood as God and man together. We are accustomed to keep the union wholly undivided, believing the same one to be both Only-begotten and firstborn: Only-begotten as the Word of God the Father, come forth from his substance; firstborn, in turn, inasmuch as he became man and is among many brothers. For just as there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, so there is also one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things. For we acknowledge the Word through whom are all things to be God by nature, even though he became flesh, that is, man.

17. But their views on this do not agree closely with ours. They too admittedly accept one Jesus Christ, and they firmly reject, as utterly impious, dividing Emmanuel into two. Yet, separating the flesh from the human and rational soul and stripping it of it, they say that the Word from God was united to it; and they have found a reason for this which they think persuasive. Things, they say, that have come together by composition to constitute one complete whole are usually seen to be parts, and to be made from incomplete elements, since what is complete in itself, as in its own nature, does not need composition from parts. Therefore, they say, we must rightly refuse to grant that the temple united to the Word was a complete man, so that the union, whatever it may be conceived to be in Christ, may keep its definition exact and above reproach. And they might add this as well, I suppose. For if, they say, we say that Emmanuel is made of a complete man and of the Word who is from the Father, no small danger will appear—rather, one now inescapable: that we will be forced, against our will, to think and speak of two sons and two Christs. What, then, do we answer them? First, that the so

(Variants: "are parts"; "composition"; "I suppose"; "we compose Emmanuel".)

most ancient tradition of the faith, which has come down to us from the holy apostles themselves, ought not to be dissolved by excessive precision, nor should things beyond understanding be subjected to extreme investigation. Nor should anyone come forward as a kind of lawgiver who recklessly declares that this is right and that is otherwise. It was surely necessary, and truly better, rather to leave to the all-wise God the course of his own counsels, and not impiously to censure what he has approved as good. For we hear him say plainly: "For my counsels are not like your counsels, nor are my ways like your ways; but as far as heaven is from the earth, so far is my way from your ways, and your thoughts from my mind."

18. We shall not worship two sons, nor shall we speak of two Christs, even if we believe that the temple united to the Word was ensouled with a rational soul. Consider what seems right to them: even if he is said to be made of flesh alone and of the Word who came forth from God the Father, no argument will persuade them to set the flesh apart on one side and the Only-begotten himself apart on the other, and so confess a pair of Christs. In the same way, even if we say that the Word from God was, as it were, brought together and united, in ways ineffable and beyond understanding, with our humanity complete according to the definition of its own nature, we shall not conceive of a pair of sons. We shall conceive of one and the same: by nature God, come forth from the very substance of God the Father, who in the last times of the age became man, was born through the holy Virgin, the Mother of God, and is worshipped both by us and by the holy angels, according to the Scriptures.

19. Suppose they should say that our condition needed only the coming of the Only-begotten, and that because he wished to be seen by those on earth, to live among men, and to show us the way of the angelic life, he put on, by way of dispensation, flesh like ours (since the divine is not visible by its own nature). Then they will be caught not knowing the purpose of the incarnation, and not understanding at all the great mystery of godliness. For if the Only-begotten's taking of flesh, or rather his becoming man, had as its only motive that he might be seen by those on earth, and nothing else was added to human nature, would it not be better, and wiser, for us too to agree with the opinion of the Docetists, who strip the Word of flesh and an earthly body and invent the fable that he was seen on earth as a man? [?] Having strayed

from the truth, they would be refuted without much effort. But would they not have a better case, if the Word from God in no way benefits human nature even though he became flesh, in saying that he kept himself free of fleshly impurity, merely seemed for a time to make use of an earthly body, and so accomplished the purpose he had set himself? What, then, would be the reason for his coming, what the manner of his becoming man, and for whose sake was it done? If anyone should ask this, he will hear our answer: the divine Scripture will teach. Come, then, noble friend, inquire of the sacred writings, and fixing the eye of your mind firmly on the words of the holy apostles, consider carefully what is being sought. Our wise Paul, who had Christ speaking within him, said: "Since, then, the children share in blood and flesh, he himself likewise partook of the same things, so that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and free those who through fear of death were held in slavery all their lives." And elsewhere, explaining the manner of it to us, he says: "For what the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh, God did: sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin, he condemned sin in the flesh, so that the just requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit."

20. Is it not, then, perfectly evident, and unclear to no one at all, that the Only-begotten became as we are, that is, a complete man, so that he might free our earthly body from the corruption that had been brought in, by instilling his own life into it through the dispensation of the union; and so that, making the human soul his own, he might render it stronger than sin, dyeing it with the firmness and unchangeableness of his own nature, as wool is dyed with colour? For I think that discussion of these matters, which are very obscure, needs illustrations; for I see the divine mysteries that are beyond understanding only dimly, "in a mirror and in a riddle." The illustration would not, I think, be out of place, for it carries within it a probable, or rather a true, line of reasoning. Just as the flesh, since it became the flesh of the Word who gives life to all things, rises above the power of corruption and death, in the same way, I think, the soul, since it became the soul of him who knows no sin, now has a firmly fixed and unchangeable stance in all that is good, incomparably stronger than the sin that once tyrannized over us. For Christ is the first and only man on earth who "committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth." Set as root and firstfruits of those who are being refashioned in the Spirit into newness of life, he will pass on to the human race both the incorruptibility of the body and the firmly fixed security of the Godhead, by participation and by grace, and [?] now. And

knowing this, the divine Paul writes: "Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, let us also bear the image of the heavenly man." By the image of the man of dust he meant our proneness to slip into sin and the death that was cast upon us as a result; by the image of the heavenly man, that is, of Christ, he meant steadfastness in holiness, and the return from death and corruption and renewal into incorruption and life.

21. We say, then, that the Word from God was united to the whole of our humanity. For he would surely not have regarded the better part in us, that is, the soul, as unworthy of any consideration, and granted the labours of his coming to the flesh alone. The mystery of the dispensation was fittingly accomplished through both. He made use, as of an instrument, of his own flesh for the works of the flesh and its natural infirmities, such as are far from blame; and of his own soul, in turn, for the human and blameless passions. For he is said to have hungered, to have endured the weariness of long journeys, to have known alarm and fear, grief and agony, and death on the cross. With no one compelling him, he laid down his own life of his own accord for us, so that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living. He paid his own flesh in exchange for the flesh of all, a truly worthy gift, and he made his soul a ransom for the souls of all, even though he came back to life again, since as God he is by nature life. And so the divine Peter says: "Brothers, I may speak to you freely about the patriarch David: he both died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day. Being therefore a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn to him with an oath to set one from the fruit of his loins on his throne, he foresaw and spoke of the resurrection of the Christ, that his soul was not abandoned to Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption." For it is not permissible to say that the flesh united to the Word could ever be overcome by corruption, or that the divine soul was held fast by the gates of Hades; for it was not abandoned to Hades, as the divine Peter said. We shall surely not say that the nature which is wholly beyond grasp and cannot be captured by death, that is, the Godhead of the Only-begotten, was brought back up from the recesses beneath the earth. For the matter would not have been thought worthy of wonder if God the Word had not remained in Hades [?], by the activity and nature of the Godhead, marvellously and beyond reason, filling all things and present to all. For the divine is above all limitation, place and measurable size, and is itself contained by nothing.

22. It is extraordinary, and yet it should astonish no one, that the body, corruptible by nature, came back to life; for it was the own body of the incorruptible Word. And his soul in turn, which had been granted concurrence and union with him, went down into Hades; but, using a power and authority befitting God, it appeared also to the spirits there. That is why he said to those in bonds, "Come out," and to those in darkness, "Show yourselves." And it seems to me that the divine Peter too says something of this kind about the Word of God and about his soul, which came to be his in the economy according to union: "For it is better, if the will of God should so will, to suffer for doing good than for doing evil; for Christ also died once for sinners, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God, being put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit; in which," he says, "he also went and preached to the spirits in prison, who had once been disobedient." For they would not, I think, claim that the Godhead of the Only-begotten, naked and by itself, went down into Hades and preached to the spirits there while being utterly invisible; for the divine is always beyond being seen. Yet neither shall we grant that it was shaped into the form of a soul in mere seeming and outward appearance; for seeming must be rejected everywhere. Rather, just as he lived among those on earth with flesh, so too he preached to the souls in Hades, having as his own vesture the [soul] united to him [?]

23. Deep, perhaps, and truly ineffable, and beyond the grasp of our minds, is the manner of the incarnation. Yet this at least we ought to consider: to pry into what lies beyond us is not without harm, and it is utter folly to put to the torture of questioning things that surpass understanding, and to try to understand what cannot be understood. Or do you not know that this deep mystery, which surpasses the mind within us, has been honored by our unquestioning faith? Leaving to Nicodemus and those like him the senseless saying, "How can these things be?", let us accept without hesitation the oracles uttered through the divine Spirit, and let us believe Christ himself when he says: "Truly, truly, I say to you, we speak what we know, and we testify to what we have seen." [?] then all nonsense, feeble myth, false opinion and the trickery of polished words. Shall we by any means admit what is by nature harmful, even if our opponents should pound us with highly practiced and indeed bitter arguments? For our divine mystery does not rest on persuasive words of human wisdom, but on demonstration

24. Being God, then, and Lord of all, the Only-begotten appeared to us according to the Scriptures; for he was seen on earth and shone upon those in darkness, having become man. Not in seeming, God forbid! It is madness to think or say that. Nor did he pass over into flesh by change of state or by alteration; for the Word from God is always unchangeable, remaining the same and in the same way. Nor did his existence begin at the same time as the flesh; for he himself is the Maker of the ages. Nor, again, was he a word without subsistence, or a bare utterance that came to be in a man; for he who calls things that are not into existence and being must necessarily exist beforehand, since he himself is the Life, having shone forth from the life of God the Father, and he exists and is conceived in his own hypostasis. Nor did he clothe himself only with flesh devoid of a rational soul; for he was truly born of a woman and appeared as man, he who lives and exists and is coeternal with God, and [?] God the Word, taking the form of a servant. And just as he is perfect in Godhead, so also he is perfect in manhood. He is not compounded of Godhead and flesh alone into one Christ and Lord and Son, but of two perfect things, I mean manhood and Godhead, wondrously bound together into one and the same.

25. But someone will perhaps say: "Whom, then, did the holy Virgin bear? The man, or the Word from God?" We reply: this very question is the error, and the missing of what is fitting and true. Do not divide for me after the union, and do not, by separating him into a man individually and into God, portray Emmanuel to us as two persons. Otherwise someone might rightly fault us for choosing to think nothing correct, but rather what holy Scripture too has condemned. For one of Christ's disciples spoke thus: "But you, beloved, remember the words spoken beforehand by the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ, how they told you that in the last time scoffers will come with scoffing, walking according to their own ungodly desires. These are the ones who make divisions, worldly people, not having the Spirit." We must not divide, then, in any way, nor above all [?] show the two after the union and conceive of each separately. We must recognize, then, that the mind does perceive a certain difference of natures, for Godhead [?] and manhood are by no means the same; but together with its thoughts about these it will also admit the concurrence of both into unity. So he sprang from the Father as God, and from the Virgin as man. For the Word who, from God the Father as begetter [?],

shone forth in ways ineffable and beyond understanding is said to have been born of a woman. He came down into manhood and lowered himself into what he was not, not so that he might remain emptied, but so that he might be believed to be God even while appearing on earth in a form like ours: not as having dwelt in a man, but as having himself truly become man, while keeping his own glory safe. Indeed the divine Paul gathers into one, by way of the economy, things that stand far apart from consubstantiality with each other and are separated by an immeasurable difference, Godhead and manhood, and from both he designates the one Christ and Son and God, saying: "Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God, which he promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was born of the seed of David according to the flesh, who was declared Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness." See, he says plainly that he has been set apart for the gospel of God, although he writes openly: "For we do not preach ourselves, but Christ Jesus"; and again: "For I decided to know nothing among you except Christ Jesus, and him crucified."

26. Having named him Son of God, he says that he was born of the seed of David, and insists that he was declared Son of God. How, then, tell me, did God spring from the seed of David? And how was he who is Son before the ages and eternally, inasmuch as he appeared from God, declared Son of God, as though he were being brought to a beginning of existence? For he himself said about himself: "The Lord said to me, You are my Son; today I have begotten you." Yet the word "today" always signifies for us not past time but rather the present. The mystery is deep; and for those who set things apart and divide them it is truly hard to reach and baffling. But for those who bind Emmanuel tightly into unity, the unadulterated knowledge of the sacred doctrines is close at hand to grasp and very readily available. For he who is coeternal with the one who begot him, and Son before every age, since he came down into human nature without slipping from being God, but taking on what is human, may rightly be understood both to have been born of the seed of David and to have a very recent birth in manhood; so that what was assumed is not foreign to him but truly his own. It is therefore reckoned as one with him, just as one might also observe in human composition. For a human being is woven together from things unlike in nature, I mean soul and body; yet the two together are understood as one man, so that sometimes the whole living being is named from the flesh alone [?]

and again, when [the soul] alone is named, the two together are understood. [?] In the same way, then, we shall accept this in the case of Christ himself. For there is one Son and one Lord Jesus Christ, both before the flesh and when he appeared

27. And let us not deny the Master who bought us, even if he is sometimes signified to us through human things and through the measures of the self-emptying. Our Lord Jesus Christ, speaking to the Jews, said: "If you were children of Abraham, you would do the works of Abraham; but now you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth. This Abraham did not do." And Paul writes of him: "Who in the days of his flesh, having offered up prayers and supplications with loud cries and tears to him who was able to save him from death, and having been heard because of his reverence, although he was a Son, learned obedience from what he suffered." Shall we then reckon Christ to be a mere man, in no way raised above those like us? God forbid! Shall we grant that the Wisdom and Power of God came down to such weakness as to fear death and to beg the Father to be saved? And shall we banish Emmanuel from being life by nature? Or shall we not rather do something praiseworthy by referring to the manhood, and to the measure of our nature, whatever seems lowly in the words, while from the things that show him to be God we behold his glory above the world, understanding that the same one is equally God and man, or rather God made man? Let the most approved Paul come forward among us, then, crying out and saying: "Yet among the mature we speak wisdom, but not a wisdom of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are passing away. Rather, we speak God's wisdom in a mystery, the hidden wisdom, which none of men, or rather none of the rulers of this age, has known; for if they had known it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory." And in addition to this: "Who, being the radiance of his glory and the exact imprint of his hypostasis, and upholding all things by the word of his power, having made purification for our sins, sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high, having become as much superior to the angels as the name he has inherited is more excellent than theirs." Yet to be, and to be called, Lord of glory: how is that not exceedingly transcendent, beyond everything begotten and brought into being? I pass over human things, for they are very small indeed. But I will say this: even if one were to name Angels and count up Principalities and Thrones and Dominions, and even if he recalled the highest Seraphim, he would confess that they fall behind a glory so transcendent, if indeed he has a mind

that is well grounded and wise. For I say that this honor is set apart and must be reserved for the sovereign nature of all things alone. How then could the crucified one be Lord of glory? And the radiance of the Father, the imprint of his substance, who upholds all things by the word of his power, is said to have become superior to angels, having taken, perhaps, as I think, the lesser place when he appeared as man. For it is written: "We see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death." Shall we then thrust the Word who shone forth from God the Father out of the essential pre-eminence that befits him and out of his exact likeness to the Father, because we see him surpassed by the glory of the angels on account of the lowliness that is understood in the economy? Not at all. For I think that we must neither entirely strip the Word from God of human things after his union with flesh, nor deprive the human of the glory befitting God, if it is understood in Christ and

28. However, I know well that some will ask: "Who, then, truly is Jesus Christ? The man from the woman, or the Word from God?" It is utterly foolish to contend over superfluous things and to answer idle prattlers back in kind. But I will say this: it is perilous and not without harm to cut him in two and set man and Word apart, since the economy does not allow it and the God-inspired Scripture proclaims one Christ. For I say that neither the Word from God without manhood, nor the temple born from the woman as though not united to the Word, ought to be named Christ Jesus. For the Word from God, brought together ineffably with manhood in a union according to the economy, is understood as Christ. He is higher than manhood, as God and Son by nature; yet he does not disdain to seem to be in a lowered state too, because of what is human. Accordingly at one time he said: "He who has seen me has seen the Father. I and the Father are one"; and at another time: "My Father is greater than I." For although he is not less than the Father in identity of substance and in every respect of equal standing, he says that he is in a lesser state because of what is human.

29. And he is proclaimed through the sacred Writings sometimes as wholly man, his Godhead being passed over in silence by way of the economy, and at other times again as God, his manhood being passed over in silence. Yet he is in no way wronged, because of the coming together of both into unity. Indeed the divine Paul, the [?]

Hebrew of Hebrews, of the tribe of Benjamin, the called apostle, writes to those who have been justified through faith and have put to death the members of the flesh (I mean fornication and passion, evil desire and covetousness): "For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God." How then did he say about his disciples: "Holy Father, keep them in your name, those whom you have given me, that they may be one, as we are. While I was with them, I kept them in your name, those whom you have given me; I guarded them, and none of them was lost except the son of perdition, that the Scripture might be fulfilled. But now I am coming to you, and I speak these things in the world, so that they may have my joy fulfilled in them"? Do you see how in these words he seems to be signified, as it were, from his manhood alone? For I shall by no means suppose that he was hidden and departed from the world, although he says: "Truly, truly, I say to you, wherever two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in their midst." And again: "Behold, I am with you all the days, until the end of the age." And you would see the most holy Paul himself often neglecting to proclaim him also as man. "Paul," he says, "an apostle not from men nor through a man, but through Jesus Christ." And besides this: "I make known to you," he says, "the gospel that was preached by me, that it is not according to man. For I did not receive it from a man, nor was I taught it, but it came through a revelation of Jesus Christ." And elsewhere too he says: "Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer." Who, then, is Jesus the Christ, who flashed into him [?] so unerring and ineffable a divine revelation of his own mysteries? Is it not the Word who became flesh and who, for our sake, did not disdain birth from a woman? And how is what I said not true? For we remember Gabriel saying to the holy Virgin: "Do not be afraid, Mary; for behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus." I think this name was given to the Word by the Father as a new one, through the angel's voice. For a prophetic oracle had cried out beforehand thus: "And they shall call him by his new name, which the Lord will name." So when he who is coeternal with the Father, the only-begotten Son before every age, became man in the last times, was born of a woman, was declared Son of God, was also called firstborn and came to be among many brothers, then the Father by nature too determines the name, following, so to speak, the laws of fatherhood.

30. The same one, then, is both only-begotten and firstborn. For he who is only-begotten as God is firstborn among us by way of the economy, according to the union, and among many brothers as man; so that we, in him and through him, might be sons of God both by nature and by grace: by nature in him, and in him alone; by participation and by grace, we ourselves, through him, in the Spirit. Just as, then, being only-begotten became proper to the manhood in Christ, because it was united to the Word by a conjunction according to the economy, so being "among many brothers" and "firstborn" became proper to the Word, because he was united to flesh. Yet, having his being God firmly established and being above change, he always remained what he was, even when he became man, crowned with pre-eminence over all things and with the highest glory. That is why even the holy and all-blessed multitude of the spirits above has been commanded to worship him together with us. For it would surely have been quite natural for them to refuse worship and hesitate to give honor, seeing the lowliness of the manhood, and not to think him worthy of glorification who for our sake became like us, keeping as far away as possible from seeming to go astray. For the mystery in Christ was still hidden even from them, but the Spirit revealed it to them and did not allow the sanctified ones to act impiously. Accordingly the divine Paul says: "And when he brings the Firstborn into the world, he says: And let all the angels of God worship him." For he who by natural property is distinct from the whole world and is outside it, insofar as he is understood as God, entered into it, appearing as a part of the world, as man; yet not on that account did he slip away from the divine glory. For he is worshipped as the Only-begotten, even if he is called firstborn, which is clearly most fitting to the measures of the manhood.

31. Shall we then worship Emmanuel as man only? God forbid! That is nonsense, deceit and error. We would differ in nothing from those who have worshipped the creation rather than the Creator and Maker, who "exchanged the truth of God for a lie," as it is written. If we think as they do, we too shall certainly hear with them: "Claiming to be wise, they became fools, and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and of birds, and of four-footed beasts, and of creeping things." Or shall we not ourselves become fellow-workers and like-minded with those just mentioned, exchanging the glory of God for a lie, for the likeness of an image of corruptible man, if we offer worship to Emmanuel as to a mere man, one of those like us? And what then? Will not even the [?]

multitude above [?] be ranked with those who have reached this pitch of madness? And shall we still, I suppose, fasten on the herd of the Gentiles the charge of error as one they cannot escape, and say that the harm of their ancient faults is hard to wash away? For [?], I think, even now no less than of old, it has failed to know the road that runs straight ahead. And the blessed Paul, it seems, was wasting his words when he addressed them, saying: "But then, when you did not know God, you were slaves to beings that by nature are not gods. But now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God, how can you turn back again to the weak and beggarly elements, to which you want to be enslaved all over again?" For what God have they come to know, if Christ, in whom they have believed, is not God by nature? And if they have worshipped a man, are they not held in the snares of their ancient error? Is what I say not true? It is true indeed. Consider, then, O Christ-loving emperor, how by necessary reasoning we are all but compelled to worship wisely, as God by nature, the Word who sprang from God the Father, even when he appeared in a form like ours. The concurrence of both into unity is fully able to remove what may at times trouble us with the suspicion of mere manhood. For the nature of the Word, having assumed what is human, will not be mere manhood; rather, by overcoming what was assumed with its own glory, it is preserved in the unshaken permanence of its pre-eminence befitting God. Thinking thus, the disciples worshipped him, saying: "Truly you are the Son of God," even though they saw him walking along, and in flesh like ours; for he was running wondrously along the crest of the wave

32. But perhaps the one who fights against this teaching will say: "And who was it that said to the woman in Samaria, 'You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know'? How, then, will he be worshipped who is ranked among the worshippers?" I for my part would say that the question "Who was it?", when asked about Christ at all, is rash and ignorant; for he is in no way divided. He who spoke to the woman was the one and only Lord Jesus Christ, who, being from the worshipping manhood and from the worshipped Godhead, has it as true of himself that he both is and is called at once God and man. Just as one might also speak of him in another way: insofar as he is God, he would be understood to be himself the Lord of glory; but insofar as he became man, glorified by participation in what comes from God, he also had need of glory, saying: "Father, glorify your Son." But there is "one Lord, one faith, one baptism," as it is written. Just as, then, the faith in Christ is one, and baptism is truly one, even though we are baptized and believe into [?] into Christ,

…Father, and Son, and Holy Spirit; and in the same way and on the same principle, I think, there is one worship of the Father, of the Son made man, and of the Holy Spirit. For the Only-begotten will never be shut out from the worship owed him by us and by the holy angels, even though he became flesh and dwelt among us and was called firstborn among many brothers. Otherwise, what would be left of the meaning of faith in him? How then is it not fitting to see [?]… For they would not say, I think, if they chose to think rightly, “We have believed only in the Word born of God the Father,” stripping him of the flesh. Nor again shall we fail to say this, for it shall be said: faith is not directed to one of us, nor to a man, but to the one who is God by nature and truly, in the person of Christ. The wise Paul will support the argument when he writes: “For we do not proclaim ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord, and ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake. For it is God who said, ‘Let light shine out of darkness,’ who has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of his glory in the face of Jesus Christ.” See, then, clearly and plainly: the light of the knowledge of God the Father has shone forth in the face of Christ. That is why he also said, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father,” and “I and the Father are one.”

33. The divine stamp is not bodily, but lies in power and in the glory most fitting to God, and this was unmixed in Christ. He wished to be made known by these things too, and he wanted his hearers to rise, through the surpassing greatness of his deeds, to right conceptions about him, since the visible flesh made him seem somewhat small in the eyes of the undiscerning. “For if I am not doing the works of my Father,” he says, “do not believe me; but if I am doing them, even if you do not believe me, believe my works.” I think Christ said this at that time knowing that the matter would contribute to their benefit. Some supposed that the one who became man for our sake was not God by nature, but simply a mere man like us, and for this reason they refused to accept faith in him. So, of necessity, to cut away their fear and their hesitation over these things, he ascribed faith to the nature of the Godhead, as in the person of the Father, and did not assign it to our lowliness, and said: “Whoever believes in me believes not in me but in him who sent me; and whoever sees me sees him who sent me.” Is this not the same as saying: “You who hear my words, do not form small and earthbound opinions about me. Know that when you put your faith in me, whom you see in the flesh, you will not have believed simply in a man, but in the Father himself through me, the Son who is in every respect equal and indistinguishable. I was made flesh for your sake and took humanity as my own as a lowly covering, yet I am of the same nature and the same working, and in identity

of glory [?], in every way, with him”?

34. One could also learn in another way that he does not reject the [?] humanity, but has received it without any division or difference as in his own person, even though he became man. When he healed the man blind from birth and planted in him the sweet but unfamiliar light, he was rightly marveled at by all. The man freed from his affliction was put on trial by the Jews and confessed his healer. Then Christ met him and said, “Do you believe in the Son of God?” And when the man cried out, “Who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him?” he answered, “You have seen him, and it is he who is speaking with you.” And the man said, “I believe, Lord,” and worshipped him. Yet is it not plain to everyone that the divine and supreme nature is wholly invisible? For “no one has ever seen God,” as it is written. If, then, he separated the humanity from himself, as being just that [?], and the Word who came forth from God the Father wished to be believed in naked and alone, why did he not instead bid the man he had healed to reflect on the nature of God, whatever it may be? Instead he showed himself bodily, so that the man might behold him present even with bodily eyes. For he said, “You have seen him, and it is he who is speaking with you.” Or shall we not say that he pointed to the flesh? How then could the flesh be himself, unless it is understood by way of union, as being his very own? It would be just the same in our own case: one could point out a man like us, I mean one made of soul and body, not partially or incompletely, even from his flesh alone.

35. The wise John too has written somewhere for us: “Now Jesus did many other signs in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book; but these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name.” And one might admire no less the inspired Peter, who addressed the Jews clearly and openly: “Rulers of the people and elders, if we are being examined today about a good deed done to a sick man, and by what means he has been healed, let it be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel that by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead, by him this man stands before you healthy.” And again, after other things: “And there is salvation in no one else; for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved.” Who then is the one who [Notes: ibid. 57, 58. Variant readings: “to behold, being present”; “present.”]

On the Right Faith, to the Emperor Theodosius.

…submitted to death and was raised in glory, and is from Nazareth, if not Christ Jesus? That is, the one ineffably begotten of God the Father before every age, but in the last time, when the age had reached its end, born also bodily of a woman. Whoever, then, puts his faith in him will carry off a surpassing prize, for he will be called a son of God. “For to all who received him, who believe in his name, he gave power to become children of God; who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of a man, but of God.” For so that he himself might be first in all things, as it is written, he was born of

36. He is the firstfruits of the creation that is being refashioned toward God through sanctification, and he himself, before all others, was shown to be born of the Spirit. He did not wait for the union of man and woman, and he did not condemn nature to dishonor and blame, for marriage is honorable, and “he who made them from the beginning made them male and female.” Rather, he was already in a way assigning human things to what is greater and incomparably higher, for he wished us no longer to be called born of men, but born of the Spirit. Indeed he says, “Call no one on earth your father; for you have one Father, who is in heaven, and you are all brothers.” Believing in him, then, is wholly blameless; more than that, it is honored with the forgetting of our offenses. And again the chosen Paul writes thus: “Knowing that a man is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, we too have believed in Christ, so that we might be justified in him.” I shall not hesitate at all to repeat what I have already said: Christ Jesus is not the Word from God understood naked and by himself, but the Word once he had taken on humanity and been joined to flesh without confusion. It was as such, seen in this way and existing in a form like ours, that the Father showed him to the holy apostles, with a voice sent from above saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him.” Notice, then, that he does not say, “In this one is my Son,” so that he would not be understood as divided, as perhaps one in another, but as one and the same by the union of the economy. That to oppose this is a fault, and one of the most dangerous, John convinces us when he writes: “For this is the testimony of God, that he has testified concerning his Son. Whoever believes in the Son of God has the testimony of God in himself; whoever does not believe the Son has made him a liar, because he has not believed in the testimony that God has given concerning his Son.” And he has testified that this one, with the flesh and in the [Notes: variant readings: “in him”; “to the better”; “and he himself”; “was.”]

form of a servant, is uniquely and properly my true Son. We must also grant that the glorious grace of holy baptism, the life given in it, and our sharing in God through sanctification in the Spirit have been accomplished through Jesus Christ. For we remember John saying: “He who comes after me is mightier than I; I am not worthy to carry his sandals. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire.” Tell me, do we say that the power to baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire is the work of a humanity like ours? How could that be? Yet, while calling “a man” the one who was just about to appear and be seen, he said that this man baptizes with fire and the Holy Spirit. He does not, like a servant and subordinate, infuse into the baptized a Spirit foreign to himself, but as God by nature, with supreme authority, he gives the Spirit that is from himself and his own. Through that Spirit the divine stamp is also impressed on us. For we are refashioned into Christ Jesus as into the divine image. We do not undergo a bodily remolding, which it would be utterly silly to imagine. Rather, through sharing in the Holy Spirit, we are enriched with Christ himself within us, so that we already cry out with joy: “Let my soul rejoice in the Lord, for he has clothed me with the garment of salvation and the robe of gladness.” And: “For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.”

37. But suppose someone came and asked, “Have we then been baptized into a man?” and said that this is the truth [?]. He will hear in reply from us: “Speak reverently, man! What are you doing, sir, dragging our hope down to earth? For we have been baptized not simply into a man, but into God made man, who releases from punishment and from the ancient charges those who have accepted, or rather welcomed, faith in him.” Indeed, the inspired Peter said when speaking to the Jews: “Repent, therefore, and let each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.” For when he has freed from sins the one who clings to him, he then anoints him with his own Spirit. He himself infuses this Spirit as the Word from God the Father, and makes it well up for us from his own nature. Yet, making the gift common [?] to the economy in the flesh because of the union, he also breathed it out bodily, as a man; for he breathed on the holy apostles and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit.” And, in the words of John, “he does not give the Spirit by measure”; he himself infuses it from himself, just as the Father does. That is why the inspired Paul, removing all difference in this regard, can be seen sometimes attributing the Spirit to God the Father himself, and sometimes to the Son. For he writes: “But you are not in the flesh,

but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ is not [?] his. But if Christ is in you, the body is dead because of sin, but the spirit is alive because of righteousness.” It is settled, then, that the Spirit belongs to the Son as his own. And he is not this only as the Word who came forth from the Father. Even when he is understood as having become man like us, he does not lack the properties of the Godhead, which belong to him as in his own nature. Indeed, though he himself is the life of all things because of his ineffable begetting from the living Father, he is said to be made alive along with us. Nevertheless, one can see him granting his own flesh the glory of his godlike working, while in turn making the things of the flesh his own and, as it were by the union of the economy, clothing his own nature with them.

38. Or will anyone deny that it is above all fitting for the Word who is by nature from God the Father, who came from above and from heaven, to be able to give life to whomever he wishes to infuse with life? And creating, tell me, would anyone grant that it is a divine thing, or a human one? Not human at all. How then? He gives us life as God. Yet he does this not only through our sharing in the Holy Spirit, but also by setting before us as food the flesh of the Son of man that he assumed. For he said: “Truly, truly I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of man and drink his blood, you have no life in yourselves.” Once the Jews mocked him and, how I do not know, tried to give the better verdict to blessed Moses, saying openly: “Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, as it is written, ‘He gave them bread from heaven to eat.’ What sign do you do, that we may believe you? What work do you perform,” as though to say, that you should bring down for us the food [?] from above and from heaven? He says: “Truly, truly I say to you, it was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven. For the bread of God is that which comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.” And besides this, almost pointing to himself in the body with his finger, he says: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever [?]; and the bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him. As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever eats me will also live because of me.” Yet is it not true to say that the flesh did not come down from heaven, but was from the Virgin, according to the Scriptures? That it is

not the Word that is edible [?], but that he gathers both into one, the properties of the natures, by a concurrence belonging to the economy, can be seen from countless sayings. Nicodemus did not understand the mystery and cried out in ignorance, “How can these things be?” To him he says: “If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things? No one has ascended into heaven except the Son of man who came down from heaven.” Again, the Jews suffered from the same ignorance as he did and chose, how I do not know, to laugh at him because he said that his own body was life-giving and from heaven. To them he says: “Does this offend you? Then what if you were to see the Son of man ascending to where he was before?” Do we not say that Emmanuel was born of a woman? Where then was he before, and how has he ascended to where he says he was, when the flesh united to him was born through the holy Virgin? Would I not also admit that flesh taken from the earth is powerless to give life, as far as its own nature goes? How then, tell me, is the flesh life-giving? And how could what is from the earth be understood to be from heaven? Clearly by union, I mean union with the living Word from heaven. That is how we shall think what is entirely right and in harmony with the sacred words. For he would be none other [?] than the Creator, acting as God, even when he is not understood apart from the flesh.

39. Again I shall call the heavenly-minded and inspired Paul to support the argument, who writes: “Giving thanks to God the Father, who has made us fit to share in the inheritance of the saints in light. He has rescued us from the power of darkness and brought us into the kingdom of the Son of his love, in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins. He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation; for in him all things were created, in the heavens and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities; all things were created through him and for him. He is before all things, and in him all things hold together. He is the head of the body, the Church; he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that he might be first in all things. For in him all the fullness was pleased to dwell, and through him to reconcile all things to himself, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether things on earth or things in heaven.” Here again he says openly that all things were created through him and for him, that he is before all things, and that all things hold together in him. He also says that he is the firstborn from the dead, who made peace through the blood of his cross for things in heaven and things on earth.

Then who is the firstborn from the dead, if not Christ Jesus, that is, the Word in the flesh and with the flesh? For the Word, being God, could by no means have died as far as his own nature is concerned. Nor could he be understood as the Creator of all things insofar as he is a man like us. He created as God, even though after the union he is not understood apart from the flesh. But he is firstborn from the dead insofar as he appeared as a man, without casting off his being God because of the incarnation.

40. You can see the Spirit-bearers going through the same arguments elsewhere too. John says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God.
