All things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being.” And Paul in turn says: “One God, the Father, from whom are all things; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things.” But if, after the Word was united to flesh, something came between them and split into otherness the duality in the Son, as some suppose, how were all things created through Jesus Christ? Yet all things were indeed created through him. It is evident, then, that what belongs by nature and properly to the Word who is from the Father was kept by him even when he appeared as man. It is dangerous, then, to dare to divide him. For there is one Lord Jesus Christ, and through him the Father created all things. He is therefore Creator as God and life-giver as life, composed into a single being between the two, out of human properties and those that surpass man. For he is the mediator between God and men, according to the Scriptures. He is God by nature, and not without flesh; and he is truly man, yet not a mere man like us, but still what he was, even though he became flesh. For it is written: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.”

41. Do we not say and believe that Emmanuel was born through the holy Virgin, the Mother of God, in the last times of the age? Then how is this not [?]? Now “yesterday and today,” Christ-loving emperor, would signify for us both the present time and the time already past. How then could he be the same in the past, when he had not yet received his birth according to the flesh? So the Word was in the beginning, and since he came forth from the eternal and unchangeable God and Father, he too has eternity and unchangeability in his own nature. Is not the name “Christ Jesus” quite new for the Word, coinciding with the time of the incarnation? Indeed this has already been shown to us by a great many arguments. Notice, then, that he says it is Christ Jesus, and not the Word considered in one aspect only, who is the same yesterday and today and forever. How then could [Notes: variant readings: “in a duality of sons”; “signifies.”]

[?] and permanence in sameness — when human nature undergoes change, and above all the change from not being into being and living? Has the sacred Scripture, then, missed the truth for us, in saying that he who did not exist yesterday existed before? I would not say so; far from it. For Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever. I will by no means deny that the Word is most ancient and unchangeable, even though he became flesh. But I will hold that, through the union with his own flesh, he is shown once more as being yesterday and pre-existing. Indeed, in his madness the Jew loathed him and tried to stone him, refusing to believe. He had perceived that, though seen as a man like us, he was bearing witness to his own supreme antiquity, an antiquity beyond any human one [?], when he said, as God: "Truly, truly I say to you, before Abraham came to be, I am." That was when they said to him, "You are not yet fifty years old, and you have seen Abraham?" John too said: "This is he of whom I said to you, 'After me comes a man who has come to be before me, because he was first, before me.'" Yet how can he know Emmanuel as a man, and call him one, and still say that the one born later, after him, came to be before him and first? Someone may say, "He says he came before him and was first in glory, and that is how I am inclined to understand it." It will not take a long argument to show us that this reading is counterfeit and ignorant. If we take "before" to mean "better in glory," then by the same reasoning we will say that "after" plainly means "second in renown." It will then follow of necessity that Christ is inferior to John in glory and runs behind him, as we would be foolishly confessing, for he said, "After me comes a man." What an absurdity! We will judge that it is not so, once we have rightly understood what is written in the Psalms: "Who among the clouds shall be equal to the Lord? Who among the sons of God shall be likened to the Lord?" Supreme antiquity must therefore be ascribed to him even with respect to the flesh. He is God united by nature to flesh, and he is accustomed to share the goods of his own nature with his own body. 42. If you wish, you may learn at once from other testimonies too that this is so and rightly said. For God said somewhere through one of the holy prophets, about the Christ who according to the flesh is of the seed of David: "And you, Bethlehem, house of Ephrathah, are by no means least among the thousands of Judah. From you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel, and his goings forth are from the beginning, from the days of eternity." And the most holy Paul says of the children of Israel: "All were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same

spiritual drink; for they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ." See, then, how the supreme antiquity that belongs properly to the Word is shown in Christ Jesus by the union of the economy. Or is the point not plain? Scripture says, and says well, that the man of Bethlehem, as man and born of a woman, has his goings forth from the beginning of eternity. For God the Word, who became man, was in the beginning and before every age. He himself was the rock, giving thirsty Israel streams beyond all hope and expectation to drink their fill, even though according to the flesh and the human nature he was born in the last times of the age, and was anointed by God the Father for his mission to this world. That, and nothing else, is why he is named Christ. And according to the law and to Paul, the rock was Christ. The wise John will also join the contest and fight well alongside this argument, all but bringing the natures together and binding into union the force of the properties that belong to each. See what he says: "That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon and our hands have touched, concerning the Word of life — and the life was made manifest, and we have seen it, and bear witness, and proclaim to you the eternal life, which was with the Father and was made manifest to us." See: he says that he who was from the beginning was plainly seen, and also submitted to touch. For Thomas cried out, "My Lord and my God!" after measuring with his finger the side of the body and the holes of the nails. Our divine Luke also says that the holy apostles became eyewitnesses and ministers of the Word. For the incorporeal became visible and the intangible tangible. He did not wear the flesh from the earth as a foreign covering, but made it his own [?], and he is known in it and with it as God and Lord. You know, surely, that the most holy Paul has also written: "For none of us lives to himself, and none dies to himself. If we live, we live to the Lord, and if we die, we die to the Lord. So whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord's. For to this end Christ died and lived, that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living." 43. It is truly established, then, that he truly became Lord of the dead and the living for this reason alone and no other: that he died and was raised. Whom, then, do we say underwent death and came back to life? The Son, clearly. That it is the Son, I think everyone would agree. What, then, shall we say? Is the Word from God the Father mortal and subject to corruption? Or is he beyond death and corruption, superior to them as life itself? Yet how can it be anything but plain to all that he is stronger than death, since he is life? Then how did he become "free among the dead," according to the Scriptures? For the Word would by no means die in himself. We say

then that when his flesh died, he himself is said to have suffered this. So it was not without the flesh, but rather with it and in it, that he received the glory of lordship. He died by the law of the flesh and of our nature, and he was raised. He showed that dying is a human suffering and that coming back to life is a divine work, so that through both he might be known as at once like us and, as God, above us, and might be seen to have become Lord of all, he who reigned with his own Father even before the flesh. Recognizing him in this way, Nathanael said: "Rabbi, you are the Son of God, you are the King of Israel." And he himself said to his disciples: "You call me Lord and Teacher, and you say well, for so I am." He confirmed this by deeds. He forgives sins, and he gave authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out and to heal every disease and every sickness among the people. For in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth the man crippled in both feet, who sat at the Beautiful Gate, was healed. And Aeneas shook off his long illness and escaped a disease that was very hard to escape, when the inspired Peter said to him: "Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you." 44. Driven, then, from every side toward the truth, earnestly striving to track down [?] what the sacred Scriptures hold, and following the teachings of the fathers, we believe that he is truly the Son of God: he who is from the root of Jesse, from the seed of David, from a woman according to the flesh; who as man was with us under the law, and as God is above us and above the law; who for us and like us was with us among the dead; who, above us, gives life through himself and is life. We neither strip his humanity of divinity, nor divest the Word of humanity after the inexpressible and inconceivable union. Rather, we confess one and the same Son, who has inexpressibly appeared as one out of two realities, by the highest kind of union and not by any alteration of nature. 45. How great a gain awaits those who believe this, the disciple of Christ will make plain when he writes: "Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God abides in him, and he in God." That Jesus Christ, who is from David according to the flesh, is by nature and truly the Son of God, since the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, the wise John will seal when he says: "And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know the true God. And we are in the true one, in his Son Jesus Christ. He is the true God and eternal life." Through him and with him, glory be to God the Father, with the holy, worshipful and life-giving Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.

[Of Cyril,] Archbishop of Alexandria: An Address to the Most Pious Princesses. 1. One might say, and with every reason, that you are a theme of praise for the whole world and the boast of the holy churches of Jesus Christ, the Savior of us all. You, most pious and God-beloved princesses, are his holy and all-pure brides. In you shines the many-colored beauty of virtue, sweet and most familiar to the eyes of the Godhead. By study and zeal it has been achieved, or rather is already accomplished, and it stands out in a right faith that is in no way shaken. The most wise Paul, truly so named, who served as a priest the mystery of Christ among the Gentiles, writes somewhere: "Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord." For where a right and blameless faith goes well together with the glories that come from good works, and the two keep equal pace, there surely is perfection in every good thing and completeness unto sanctification. Every word of ours, then, falls behind the glory that is in you and confesses defeat without blushing. It would deserve pardon if it shrank from praising what it could not reach in worth. If it had the power to achieve what it desires, it would be blamed as gravely sick with sloth. And let no one acquit its delay of the charge of laziness: why should it grieve, by choosing silence, those whom it could have adorned with praises of their virtue? But if it is weak, and afraid, and confesses defeat, we shall not lay the blame on it, but rather on you, who are so illustrious that by the excellence of your own noble deeds you have shown all the words that commonly adorn everyone else to be nothing. For royal blood has come down to you from on high and from ages long past, and it continues to the present and beyond, as we believe. But see,

and very plainly, you also lay hold of the kingdom in Christ, and you are eager to think and do what pleases him. On the one hand, as I said, you are distinguished by works and by a blameless faith, and you make your royal courts shine with the glory of virginity. On the other, you raise most costly churches to Christ. For this too, among other things, he has granted to your holy souls. 2. Therefore (I will say something taken from the sacred Scriptures): "Rejoice in the Lord always; again I will say, rejoice. Let your gentleness be known to all people." And it has indeed become known and been celebrated. Like an image that bears a portrait of piety toward Christ, its beauty has shone out clearly to people in every land and city, and it has been thought worthy of [?] wonder. I thought it right to give some spiritual gift to you, who are so well disposed toward every good thing, as holy brides of Christ: this book, which I have lately labored over. I think it can offer no small benefit to those who read it. Those who have been taught, or persuaded, to think wrongly about Christ the Savior of us all, it will bring back to correction and instruct well in the mystery. Those who stand firm in right understanding and make their home in the doctrines of truth, it will make more secure, by its manifold discoveries of sound thought and by its proofs from divinely inspired Scripture. For they will learn that Emmanuel is God by nature and in truth, and that the Virgin who bore him is, because of him, Theotokos, the Mother of God. Those who are afraid to say and believe this have probably not understood the deep mystery of godliness. I think it necessary to set out briefly the apostolic and evangelical tradition concerning Christ, the Lord of all, and the aim of all divinely inspired Scripture concerning him, and what the force of the doctrines of truth points toward. 3. We believe, then, in one God, the Father almighty, maker of all things visible and invisible. And in one Lord Jesus Christ, his Son, begotten from him by nature before every age and time. For he is without beginning in time together with his own Begetter and co-eternal with him; he shares his throne, is equal to him in glory, and is crowned with equality to him in every respect, for he is the exact imprint and radiance of his substance. Likewise we believe also in the Holy Spirit, not reckoning him foreign to the divine nature. For he is from the Father

by nature, and is poured out through the Son upon creation. In this way the holy and worshipped Trinity is understood to be one and consubstantial, and in identity of glory. And we say this: his only-begotten Word, ineffably begotten from the substance of God the Father, maker of the ages, through whom are all things and in whom are all things, the true light, the nature that gives life to all things (for he has appeared as life, as from the life of the Father), in the last times of the age, by the good pleasure of the Father, took hold of the seed of Abraham, according to the Scriptures. He did so to save the earthly race, which had fallen under the curse and through sin had been brought down to death and corruption. He shared in blood and flesh, that is, he became man; and taking flesh and making it his own, he was born according to the flesh through the holy Theotokos Mary. 4. But although he became like us, and in the economy put on the form of a servant, he remained in his natural divinity and lordship. For he did not cease to be God, even though he became flesh, that is, like us, and man. And since he is unchangeable by nature as God, remaining what he always was and is and will be, he has been called Son of Man. 5. Since he willingly came down into the measures of humanity (for he lowered himself into self-emptying), he necessarily underwent birth from a woman as well. Yet his divine nature did not receive a beginning of being when he is said to have been born according to the flesh, for the Word was and is, as I said, from God the Father by nature and in truth. But the one born of the holy Virgin is not thought of simply as a man like us. He is the Word himself made flesh, and the body from her is his own. Therefore he is said to have been born according to the flesh, since he makes the birth of his own flesh his own. 6. Those who foolishly say that the holy Virgin is not Theotokos necessarily fall into saying that there are two sons of God. For if the holy Virgin did not bear God made flesh according to the flesh, they are compelled, even against their will, to confess that she gave birth to an ordinary man, having nothing more than we have. Then how will every knee bow to him, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father? How do angels worship him, and the holy multitude of the highest powers? Has the whole of heaven, then, been serving an ordinary man along with us? Far from it! For we worship Emmanuel as true God. But he will not be worthy of worship in any other way unless we believe that the Word from God himself, who is worshipped by all creation, became flesh according to the Scriptures: not changed into flesh, but taking flesh from the holy Virgin,

as I said, and undergoing human birth along with us. This was so that, having become man for us, he might die in a human way but rise in a divine way, trampling down the power of death. For in this way we too, as having conquered in Christ, could prevail over sin, strip off corruption and escape death, and so say out of the joy that is in Christ: "Where is your victory, O death? Where is your sting, O Hades?" For as in Adam we fell, so in Christ we have conquered. 7. If Emmanuel were an ordinary man, how would the death of a man have benefited human nature? Many prophets died before him: that renowned Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, Moses and Samuel, and the saints who came after them. Yet their death did nothing for the earthly race of men, whereas the death of Christ saved it. For he offered his own flesh for us, and by giving it up to death for our sake he delivered all from the bonds of death. The one who is worth more than all sufficed, dying for all, because the Word from the Father is God by nature, and the body offered for us as a fragrant aroma to God the Father is his own. It is therefore impious, and among the most absurd of things, to divide the one Lord Jesus Christ into two sons. The most wise Paul will stand against them, saying: "One Lord, one faith, one baptism." For if there is one Lord, and some then divide the one into two sons, to whom shall we ascribe the glory of lordship? To the Word who sprang from the Father? The name and the reality of lordship befit him above all, and he is truly Master of all. Then where shall we put the other? He will be left outside being Lord, yielding place to the one who pre-existed and is incomparably exalted. Or shall we attach the glory of lordship to the one from the woman, separating them as they do? Then how will the Word from God the Father be Lord, if, there being one Lord according to the Scriptures, we grant the name of lordship to a mere man? And how is there one faith? Or how one baptism? For if there are two sons, as they say, in which one do we believe? Their ignorance would have to tell us into whose name we have been baptized, though there is only one baptism. 8. But your keen mind surely sees that my discussion of this has grown long, has taken on something unlovely, and is already verging on utter tedium. Yet I think that you, [?] the divine

mystery of him, since your mind searches it out with care, clearly see with the sharp eye of understanding those who want to lead others astray. They wrap their words in a mask of piety, yet are themselves sharper than any dart. As far as the force of truth is concerned, they deny the Master who bought them, that is, Christ. But because they fear the grief this causes those who are devout, and indeed their admirable zeal, they confess that the one born of the holy Virgin is God, and indeed Lord and Son of God. If one of the simple-minded hears their words, he will probably think they speak rightly and reasonably, and in no way out of tune with the doctrines of truth. But if someone chooses to press them hard with questions and test their words precisely, he will find the matter far from simple. For there are many gods and many lords, in heaven and on earth, as the blessed Paul writes to us; "yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and we are for him; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him." But when we name Jesus Christ, we mean the Word from God the Father, who has appeared in human form. He does not hold his dignity as a favor, imported from outside; he truly is what he is believed to be. For being God by nature even without flesh, he remained God also with flesh. Being Son by nature even before the flesh, he remained Son also when he became flesh. And being truly Lord of all, he is again seen in that same glory even after coming to be in humanity. So if they say that the one born of the holy Virgin is true God, that is, the Word from God the Father united by nature to flesh, why are they afraid to confess that the holy Virgin is Theotokos? Their aim is to pretend, and to say, "Yes, he is God and Lord, and sits with the Father." Yet that is not what they truly believe. They say instead that the glory of divinity and lordship was given as a favor, and by way of advancement, to an ordinary man like us born of the holy Virgin. 9. I thought it necessary to show truly that the word Theotokos was customary to the holy Fathers before us, who are admired for their right faith, and that it remains so to this day for everyone throughout, so to speak, the whole world under heaven. So that I may not seem simply to say whatever comes into my head without examination, I will gather from the books they composed in the Church the passages useful for this, and set them out as proof. In this way I will seal my words with truth. So then, the thrice-blessed and

…[?] in piety, Athanasius, who in his time was bishop of the Church of the Alexandrians, in the discourse On the Incarnation, concerning Christ. Of Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, or from the Discourse On the Incarnation. Concerning Christ. "For we confess," he says, "that he is the Son of God and God according to the spirit, and Son of man according to the flesh. We do not confess the one Son as two natures, one to be worshipped and one not to be worshipped. We confess one nature of God the Word made flesh, worshipped together with his flesh in a single worship. Nor are there two sons, one the true Son of God and worshipped, and another a man from Mary, not worshipped, who became Son of God by grace, as human beings also do. There is the one who is from God, as I said, one Son of God, and he himself is God, and not another. And he was born from Mary according to the flesh in the last days, as the angel told Mary the Theotokos when she said, 'How will this be, since I do not know a man?' He said: 'The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who is born will also be called Son of God.' So the one born of the holy Virgin is Son of God by nature and true God, not by grace and participation. He is man only according to the flesh that is from Mary, but according to the spirit he himself is Son of God and God. He suffered our sufferings according to the flesh, as it is written: 'Christ suffered for us in the flesh.' And again: 'He who did not spare his own Son, but gave him up for us all.' But he remained impassible and unchangeable according to the Godhead, as the prophet says: 'I am God, and I have not changed.' He died our death according to the flesh for our sins, so as to destroy death through the death he died for us, as the Apostle says: 'Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O Hades, is your sting?' And again: 'Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures.' But he remained immortal and unconquered by death because of the Godhead, as the impassible power of the Father, as Peter says: for it was not possible for him to be held by death." Then, after inserting other material in between, he adds the following: "But if anyone teaches from the divine Scriptures anything contrary to this, saying that the Son of God is one and the one from Mary another, made a son by grace as we are, so that there are two sons, one Son of God by nature, the one from God, and one by grace, the man from Mary; or if anyone says that the flesh of our Lord is from above and not from the Virgin Mary; or that the Godhead was changed into flesh, or confused, or altered; or that the Godhead of the Lord is passible; or that the flesh of our Lord is not to be worshipped, as being the flesh of a man, and is not to be worshipped as the flesh of the Lord

and God, such a one the holy catholic Church anathematizes, obeying the divine Apostle who says: 'If anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be anathema.'" So much for the blessed Athanasius. [?] I think I should also set out the words of other holy bishops which have the same aim. Of Atticus, bishop. "Today Christ the Master took on the birth of his loving-kindness; for the birth that belongs to his divine dignity he already had." Then he adds again: "The Word of loving-kindness is emptied, though by nature he cannot be emptied; for he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. The fleshless one takes flesh: 'The Word became flesh.' He who cannot be touched, because his nature has no body, is handled. He who has no beginning comes under a bodily beginning. The perfect one grows, the unchangeable one advances, the rich one is born in an inn. He who wraps the heaven in clouds is wrapped in swaddling clothes; the king is laid in a manger." Of Antiochus, bishop. "Whom yesterday Mary brought forth for us as Savior in undefiled childbirth: she who bore life, who bore a fair child, who bore greatness, the light-bearer, the hope-bearer, the Theotokos, she who bore a stranger's birth, the virgin mother." Of Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium, from the work On the Birth according to the Flesh. "The truth has been made known, grace has come, and life has appeared. He who is the Son of God, the Word from God, became flesh for our sake, to raise mortals to eternal life and to raise them up from the dead. The Maker of all things, who before all creation, visible and invisible, exists immortal together with the Father and the Spirit alone, today, behold, is born for us of a Virgin, without any sin, without a human father, that is, without a husband." Of Ammon, bishop of Adrianople. For he too said somewhere concerning God the Word: "If he himself, being God by nature as the only-begotten Son of God, coming to be in the assumption of the form of a servant, and deigning to be called the firstborn son of the holy Virgin, gave himself as a ransom for all…" And to this he adds: "I have already shown the impiety into which the Arians fall when they say that Mary the Theotokos needed the sacrifices that were then offered under the law for women who had given birth."

…of the divine birth. And concerning the holy Virgin he says: "Instead of the sun," he says, "she contained the Sun of righteousness without his being circumscribed. And do not ask how; for where God wills, the order of nature is overcome. For he willed, he was able, he came down, he saved. For God all things run together. Today he who is is born, and he who is becomes what he was not. For being God, he becomes man without ceasing to be God. He did not become man by departing from the Godhead, nor did he become God from man by advancement. Being the Word, and remaining impassible, he became flesh, his nature remaining unchanged." And to this he adds: "He who sits upon a throne high and lifted up is laid in a manger; the untouchable, simple and incorporeal one is wrapped by human hands; he who tears apart the bonds of sin is bound in swaddling clothes." Of Severian, bishop. "For the Word, born from above of the Father ineffably, inexpressibly, incomprehensibly and eternally, is himself born in time below of the Virgin Mary, so that those who were first born below might be born from above a second time [?], that is, of God." Of Vitalius, bishop, from the Discourse on Faith. "Further, concerning the Savior's economy in the flesh, we believe that the incarnation took place for the renewal of humanity while God the Word remained unaltered and unchangeable. For being truly Son of God by his eternal birth from God, he also became Son of man by his birth from the Virgin. And he is one and the same: perfect God according to the Godhead and consubstantial with the Father, and the same perfect man according to his birth from the Virgin and consubstantial with human beings according to the flesh. If anyone says that Christ has a body from heaven, or that he is consubstantial with God according to the flesh, let him be anathema. If anyone does not confess that the Lord's flesh is from the holy Virgin and consubstantial with human beings, let him be anathema. If anyone says that our Lord and Savior, born according to the flesh of the Holy Spirit and Mary the Virgin, is without soul, or without sense, or without reason, or without mind, let him be anathema. If anyone dares to say that Christ suffered in his Godhead and not in the flesh, as it is written, let him be anathema. If anyone divides and separates our Lord and Savior, and says that God the Word is one Son and the assumed man another, and does not confess one and the same, let him be anathema." [?] renewal.

Of Theophilus, bishop, from the Address [?] to those who hold the views of Origen. He spoke as follows concerning Christ: "So that the one who appeared might be believed to be true God not in word only but also in power, he showed the certainty about himself by the magnificence of his deeds. He was fully God, and he became man completely, leaving out nothing of human likeness except unholy wickedness alone. For even when he became an infant he was confessed as Emmanuel, when the magi came to him and by their worship proclaimed that the one who had appeared was God. And when he was crucified in the flesh he withdrew the rays of the sun, making his own Godhead plain by that strange wonder, nowhere scattering himself or splitting himself into two saviors. He also said to the disciples: 'Do not call anyone on earth teacher; for one is your teacher, the Christ.' When he gave this command to the apostles he did not separate his own Godhead from the visible body, nor, when he testified that he was the Christ, did he divide himself into soul and flesh. So he was both God and man, seen as a servant and known as Lord. He hid the loftiness of the Godhead beneath the humble disposition of the incarnation, and raised the lowliness of the visible body by the working of the Godhead." 11. It would be easy to add many other true testimonies to these, but I pass them over, knowing what is written: 'Give an occasion to a wise man, and he will be wiser; instruct a righteous man, and he will increase in learning.' This much, however, we say: behold, all the most excellent and wise Fathers who have lived in our times name the holy Virgin Theotokos. Firmly maintaining that the Word from God was united by nature with the flesh, they say that he came to be in the virgin's womb and came forth from her according to the flesh, although he had his birth from the Father without beginning and before every age and time. But since it was likely that a mind inclined to grow weary of longer compositions running on line after line would wish rather to see, briefly and concisely, the purest beauty of what concerns Christ, I have gathered from the divinely inspired New Scripture the very hearts, so to speak, of its ideas, set out on their own, and have sent them to your godly piety. Reading them little by little and section by section, you may yourselves make the mind within you shine still more brightly, and, guiding toward the truth those whom you choose to help, you may crown your holy heads with apostolic boasts. Very great is the reward for this, for it is written: 'He who turns a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul [?] completely.

from death and will cover a multitude of sins.' Now in the findings of the ideas, that is, in the conclusions, when we say 'Therefore Christ is God,' or 'Therefore the Son and Lord Jesus Christ is one,' we do not mean it as they do: that Emmanuel was named God, or Son, or Lord, by grace, or came to this glory by advancement or progress, as one ordinary sanctified man like us. We mean rather that the Word, being God, then lowered [?] himself into emptying and came down in the form of a servant, and is none the less true God, and by nature Lord of all, and alone and truly [?] Son. Conformed to him by the grace that comes through him, we too ascend to the glory of adoption. 14. Some maintain, I do not know how, that the name 'Christ' befits, properly and by itself, the Word sprung from God, existing and conceived apart from flesh. They say it likewise befits the one born of the holy Virgin, even if he were conceived as still existing by himself and on his own. Thirdly, they say it befits both, by reason, as it were, of the conjunction, as they themselves put it, binding them together into one person. For they have no account of the natural and true union, though this is the right and most unerring way of the mystery. Their pretext is not innocent, but full of bitterness and deceit. Since the divinely inspired Scripture, when it names Christ, assigns to him everything that befits God (for it knows, it surely knows, that the Word of God appeared in human form and was made flesh), the aim of those who choose to think otherwise is to declare that the one born of a woman is an ordinary man, who by progress, as I said, and by his own human virtue proved himself worthy to be honored by a conjunction of person with the Word from God, and to be chosen according to foreknowledge. [?]. This is what they say: that the name 'Christ' befits the Word that appeared from God the Father alone, separately, and conceived and existing by himself. But we have not been taught to think or speak this way. For we say that when the Word became flesh, then he was also named Christ Jesus. For since he has been anointed

and sanctified [?] the Word from God with his own Spirit, as if by another, superior to him in nature and pre-eminent. 'For beyond all dispute the lesser is blessed by the greater.' But since being sanctified and anointed befits the measures of humanity, it is altogether necessary that the Word from God be named Christ, not when he was still bare and not yet incarnate, but when he had become like us, that is, man: he was anointed according to his humanity. So the name 'Christ' could in no way befit the Word sprung from God the Father before he had become like us. If he is anywhere called Christ, understand him, I beg you, as having become man; and if you hear 'Word' once the incarnation has already taken place, do not forget the flesh united to him. To think that the term befits this one and that one separately is utterly senseless, and indeed unholy, whether to think or to say. For there is one Lord Jesus Christ, and he is not divided, as the most wise Paul himself says, who had Christ within him speaking the divine mystery to him. When you turn to the chapters that follow, you will find my argument straight and finely polished in accordance with the truth. I think it good also to state this solemnly beforehand: just as the Word from God the Father is perfect in Godhead, so he is also perfect in humanity, according to what humanity is. He did not take a soulless body, but one animated by a rational soul. May the God of all, who distributes the goods of heaven to those who love him, fill your holy souls with his gifts, so that, ascending to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, you may make your admirable life glorious and approved, holy brides of Christ.

THE FOLLOWING ARE CONTAINED IN WHAT FOLLOWS. That Christ is God, the assumed temple also ascending into his glory by its union with God the Word: from the apostolic writings. Selections from the Catholic Epistles on the same point. Selections from the Gospels on the same point. That Christ is life and life-giver: you will find this from the passages in the apostle Paul and in the apostolic writings. That faith in Christ is faith as in God: from the Catholic Epistles and from the Gospels. That Christ is life and propitiation: various selections. That the death of Christ brings salvation to the world: selections from the apostolic and Gospel writings. [?] but. ensouled. himself. selections. [?]. findings.

…Word, the assumed temple also ascending into his glory. From the Epistle to the Romans. 'Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God, which he promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures, concerning his Son, who was born of the seed of David according to the flesh, who was declared Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by the resurrection of the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord.' If, then, the preaching about Christ is the Gospel of God, how is Christ not God? And if every prophecy looks to it as its goal, and the Scriptures proclaim the one from the seed of David to be Son of God, even if he is said to have been declared so according to the Spirit of holiness because of the mystery of the incarnation, how is he not truly Son, attested as he is by the resurrection of the dead? For it was not an ordinary man like us who was raised, but one stronger than death, since he is both life and God. Concerning those who worship the creation rather than the Creator: 'For though they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks to him, but they became futile in their reasonings, and their senseless heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools.' Paul writes somewhere to those called from the Gentiles, that is, to us: 'But now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God.' Whom, then, have we come to know through faith, if not Christ Jesus? So if we have known him as God and glorify him as God, we have been enlightened in truth; but if we exchange his glory, we too have become futile in our reasonings. For if we have believed in him at all, we believe in him as in God. Otherwise we shall have to confess, wholly and without reserve, that even now we are caught in the snares of the ancient deceit, directing our faith to an ordinary man. But this is not true [?]. 'And since they did not see fit to acknowledge God, God gave them up to a debased mind, to do what is not fitting.' If we have known Christ as God, let us not reject the knowledge of him by saying that he is an ordinary man. But if we dare to do this out of ignorance, we shall surely go along with the others into a debased mind. 'But by your hardness and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the righteous judgment of God, who will render to each according to his works.' The blessed Paul says: 'We must all appear [?] this is not true.

before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive what was done through the body, according to what he has done, whether good or bad.' And another of the holy apostles said: 'There is one lawgiver and judge.' And David himself sings: 'For God is judge.' Since, then, he says that the verdict on each person at the divine judgment seat, which Christ himself will pronounce, is the righteous judgment of God (for we shall stand before his judgment seat, not as before one like us, but as before judge and God and lawgiver), how is Christ not God? 'For through the law comes knowledge of sin. But now, apart from the law, the righteousness of God has been revealed, attested by the law and the prophets, the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe.' He says that the righteousness apart from the law (which, he says, was also attested by the holy prophets) is the righteousness that comes through faith in Christ Jesus. How, then, is he who justifies those who believe not God, since he is truly God? For the goal of faith looks to this. And since the holy prophets bear witness to faith in Christ, who dares to say that he is not God because of his humanity, that is, once the Word became flesh? 'For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.' Sinning makes us fall short of the glory of God, because he knows no sin. Now it is written of Christ that he committed no sin, and in this respect we who transgress fall short of his glory. Therefore the Word is God even with the flesh, for he committed no sin. 'Do we then nullify the law through faith? By no means! Rather, we uphold the law.' The law given through Moses taught the people of Israel to worship one God: 'For the Lord your God,' it says, 'is one Lord.' And God himself addressed them, saying: 'You shall have no other gods besides me.' Has faith in Christ, then, led those called through it away from worshipping the one God who is God by nature? Do we then nullify the law by bringing [?] to the one true God? 'By no means,' he says, 'rather, we uphold the law.' So we approach Christ as God, so that we may not be accused of undoing the law, but may rather be praised for upholding the law through faith. Concerning Abraham he says: 'In the presence of the God in whom he believed, who gives life to the dead and calls into being the things that do not exist as though they did.' Now the power to give life to the dead could befit no one else but the one who alone is God by nature; yet Christ gives life

…if through his own flesh he [gave life to] those who had been corrupted, touching the dead and raising them up, how is he not the true God, he who also gave others authority to raise the dead through his name? “So, my brothers, you too were put to death to the law through the body of Christ, so that you might belong to another, to him who was raised from the dead, in order that we may bear fruit for God.” We are put to death to the law when we cease from the worship it prescribes; and we come to belong to another, to him who was raised from the dead, that is, to Christ, when we strive to follow his gospel commands, so that we may bear fruit for God. The chief of the gospel commands is faith in him. And this is our fruit, offered to Christ as to God. So he who rose from the dead is God, since the Word became flesh. “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God. But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if the Spirit of God dwells in you. Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him. But if Christ is in you, the body is dead because of sin, but the spirit is life because of righteousness. And if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you.” See, the Spirit of God is here clearly called the Spirit of Christ. But if he is a man in his own right, set apart on his own, having the Word of God merely dwelling in him, how is the divine Spirit called his? Yet the Spirit is his own; therefore he is God, and nothing else. For the Word of God did not come to be in a man; he truly became man, while remaining God. Only in this way could the Spirit of the Father be understood to be the Spirit of Christ. “For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God. For you did not receive a spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father.’” The blessed Paul writes: “And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father.’” If, then, it is in the Spirit of the Son that we have the boldness to call God Father, as of the one who according to [?]…

…with all our strength and to the uttermost,¹ even to the point of life and blood, and we offer it to Christ himself, who dares to say that he could not be God? For the aim of the saints has in no way missed what is fitting. “For I am convinced that neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.” If nothing at all can separate us from the love of God, and we practice this love in Christ Jesus, how is Christ not plainly God, if in loving him we love the God of the universe? And when I say Christ, I mean the Word from God who became man…

“For we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ,” he says; and so we shall stand before Christ. For [he will sit?] on the throne of his glory, judging the world in righteousness. Yet David says that God is judge; therefore Christ is God. “But on some points I have written to you rather boldly, by way of reminder, because of the grace given me by God to be a minister of Jesus Christ to the Gentiles, serving the gospel of God as a priest, so that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit.” Those entrusted with the work of priestly service minister to God alone; for priests do not stand in attendance on men. See, then: the divine Paul says that grace was given him by God to be a minister of Christ Jesus and to serve the gospel of Christ as a priest among the Gentiles. So Christ is God, if in preaching Christ to the Gentiles Paul says that he serves the gospel of God among them as a priest, so that they may be accepted as sanctified in the Spirit. “In Christ Jesus, then, I have reason to boast in what pertains to God. For I will not dare to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me to bring the Gentiles to obedience, by word and deed, by the power of signs and wonders, by the power of the Spirit of God, so that from Jerusalem and all around as far as Illyricum I have fully proclaimed the gospel of Christ.” He says he boasts in Jesus, while saying that he has his boast before God. And how can anyone doubt that it is no human thing for Christ to be able to work wonders in the holy apostles by the power of the Spirit? For just as each of us does his own works by his own power, so Christ too, using the Spirit as his own power, works wonders through the holy…

“All the churches of Christ greet you.” And yet elsewhere, writing to Timothy, he says: “so that you may know how one ought to behave in the house of God.” If, then, he knows the churches to be Christ's and has testified to it, Christ is God. “The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet.” Peace is said to be God's; and Christ once said to the holy apostles, “My peace I give to you, my peace I leave with you.” How, then, is he not truly God, the giver of peace, who gives it to the worthy as a good that is his own? From the First Epistle to the Corinthians. “Paul, called to be an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Sosthenes our brother, to the church of God.” Notice that, having said earlier to the Romans, “All the churches of Christ greet you,” when writing to the Corinthians he says that the church is God's. “What I mean is this: each of you says, ‘I belong to Paul,’ or ‘I belong to Apollos,’ or ‘I belong to Cephas,’ or ‘I belong to Christ.’ Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you, or were you baptized in his name?” So if Christ is not divided, all things are his, and all people are his. And if he was crucified for us and we were baptized in his name, we are clearly indebted to him; and we belong not to a man, one of our own kind, but to God. Therefore Christ is God over us. “For Jews demand signs and Greeks seek wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Greeks.” Would not anyone at all admit that the gospel preaching calls those throughout the whole earth to the true knowledge of God? How then, or on what grounds, could this be doubtful? In what sense, then, do the teachers of the mysteries preach Christ crucified? As one of us, who endured death on the cross, so that the faith of the world [?] in a man? Far from it! We have believed in the living and true God. So Paul knows the crucified Christ to be God, and preaches him to the world, confident that he is not mistaken. “When I came to you, brothers, I did not come with lofty speech or wisdom, proclaiming to you the testimony of God. For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.” See, then: having clearly said that he proclaims the testimony of God to the world, he added “Christ Jesus, and him crucified.” So Christ Jesus, who endured the cross for our sake, is God; and his testimony is proclaimed to the world through the…

…holy apostles, not with loftiness of speech and worldly wisdom, but as in the power of the Spirit. “Yet among the mature we do speak wisdom, but not a wisdom of this age or of the rulers of this age, who are passing away. Rather, we speak God's wisdom in a mystery, the hidden wisdom, which God decreed before the ages for our glory. None of the rulers of this age understood it; for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.” If the mystery of Christ is God's wisdom, and it is then preached to the world, and yet he is not truly God, as some for some reason suppose, while faith is in him,¹ how is the mystery wise, if it carries those on earth away from the true knowledge of God and [leads] the whole world into the worship of a man? But that is not true. The mystery is wise because it brings those who had gone astray to God; therefore Christ is God. And the crucified one has rightly been called the Lord of glory. “According to the grace of God given to me, like a wise master builder I laid a foundation, and someone else is building on it. For no one can lay any foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ.” If we rest upon Christ as upon a foundation, and are built up on him through faith, and he is the security of all, how could he not be truly God, in whom are all things and in whom is the faith of all, not as in one of us, since we have not worshipped a creature, but God who is God by nature and in truth? “Do you not know that you are God's temple and that the Spirit of God dwells in you? If anyone destroys God's temple, God will destroy him. For God's temple is holy, and you are that temple.” If by receiving the Spirit of Christ we are called God's temple, how is he not truly God, he through whom we are temples…

“Therefore do not pass judgment on anything before the time, until the Lord comes, who will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness and will disclose the purposes of the heart. Then each one will receive his praise from God.” We expect our Lord Jesus Christ to come down from heaven in due time, and we shall all stand before him as he judges what is hidden and discloses the purposes of the heart. And we are fully assured that he will also praise the righteous. For he will say to those standing at his right: “Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.” Since, then, it is Christ who gives the praise, and yet Paul says that each one will receive his praise from God, how is he not plainly God?

“Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God, and that you are not your own? For you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body.” If by receiving the Spirit of Christ we have become temples of God, and are not our own, having been bought with his blood, so that we no longer live for ourselves but for him who purchased us, how is Christ not plainly God, he through whom we are temples of God and whom we serve as God? “Now concerning the eating of food offered to idols, we know that an idol is nothing in the world and that there is no God but one. For although there may be so-called gods, whether in heaven or on earth (as indeed there are many gods and many lords), yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and for whom we exist, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and through whom we exist.” If there is only one God and no other besides him, and the one Christ Jesus, through whom are all things, is included together with him in the one nature of the Godhead, then he is God, understood in divine terms as consubstantial with the Father, even when he was called Jesus Christ, having been born of a woman. And note that, having named Christ Jesus, he says that all things came into being through him, since he is one Son by the union of the economy. “To those outside the law,” he says, “I became as one outside the law, not being outside the law of God but under the law of Christ.” If one who has the law of Christ has the law of God, how is not…
“Give no offense to Jews or to Greeks or to the church of God.” Note that, while calling the church God's, elsewhere he knows it as Christ's…

“But I want you to understand that the head of every man is Christ, the head of a woman is her husband, and the head of Christ is God.” When the blessed Luke composes for us the genealogy of Christ, he begins from Joseph, then, having reached Adam, he adds, “son of God,” assigning to man as his origin the God who made him. In this sense we say that Christ is the head of every man: for man was made through him and brought into being, not with the Son creating him as an assistant, but rather by divine action, as being Creator by nature. The husband is the head of the woman because she was taken from his flesh, and she has him, as it were, as her origin. And likewise God is the head of Christ, because Christ is from him by nature; for the Word was begotten of God the Father. How, then, is not…

…Christ God, whose head by nature is set down as the Father? And whenever I say Christ, I mean the Word of God who appeared in human form. “Therefore I want you to understand that no one speaking in the Spirit of God ever says, ‘Jesus is accursed!’ and no one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit. Now there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of service, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of activities, but it is the same God who works all things in all.” If saying that Christ is not God by nature and in truth is nothing other than saying “Jesus is accursed,” then those who strip him of truly being Jesus do not do so in the Holy Spirit. And if he says that the varieties of gifts are worked now by the Spirit, now by the same Lord, now by the same God, he knows Christ to be God, who works as God through the Spirit and, as Lord by nature, distributes the gifts from above with authority, as he wills. And we must remember that Paul also spoke of Christ as having worked in the power of the Holy Spirit. “And God has appointed in the church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then miracles, then gifts of healing.” Though God is said to accomplish these things, it is Christ who worked them; for he himself appointed the apostles in the church, and teachers as well, and worked miracles; for he gave the holy disciples authority to heal every disease and every infirmity among the people. “I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand. If anyone does not love the Lord, let him be accursed. Maranatha!” Whom, then, does he call Lord here? For the Son too is confessedly Lord; and likewise the Spirit: “For the Lord,” he says, “is the Spirit.” But the blessed Paul's aim here was directed¹ at Jesus himself. “For there is one Lord,” he says, “Jesus Christ.” So he pronounces a curse on the one who does not love him. And he does not love him who says that he is Son of God neither by nature nor in truth, but [?] placing him in a second rank beside the Word from God, and who does violence to the mystery of the economy by cutting the one Lord Jesus into two. From the Second Epistle to the Corinthians. “But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ, and the fragrance of the knowledge of him,” and what follows.

¹ Another reading: “is directed.”

“…spreads through us in every place. For we are the aroma of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing.” How, then, is Christ not God, if he himself is the fragrance of the knowledge of the Father? For one could not learn the sweet fragrance of the divine [?] from human nature; rather, just as the scent of humanity surely signifies a man, so the scent of divinity signifies God. If Christ is said to be the fragrance of the Father, and truly is, how is Christ not God, even if the Word from God the Father became man for the sake of the economy? “You yourselves are our letter, written on our hearts, known and read by all people. And you show that you are a letter of Christ delivered by us, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts.” God once said through one of the holy prophets: “In that day, says the Lord, I will put my laws into their minds and write them on their hearts.” We have become, then, a letter of Christ, who writes on us what he wills, not in ink but in the Spirit of the living God; not as an assistant, but rather, if we may put it so, by his own hand; for the Spirit is his own. How, then, is he not God, who in his own Spirit writes on us the way to the knowledge of God? Of the Jews he says: “But their minds were hardened. For to this very day, when they read the Old Covenant, that same veil remains unlifted, because only in Christ is it taken away. Yes, to this day whenever Moses is read a veil lies over their hearts. But when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed. Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.” If Christ is the end of the law and the prophets, and the veil over the reading of the Old Covenant is lifted only in Christ, what sense is there in supposing him to be an ordinary man, honored only with the title of sonship? For if that were so, the goal of our faith would turn out to be, not God, but one of us, which is utterly absurd. “And even if our gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing. In their case the god of this age has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, to keep them from seeing the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God.” If, as some suppose, Christ is an ordinary man, having his conjunction with the Word from God only by a union of person (for this is what they say), how is the gospel of God veiled to those who are perishing? For…

…the Gentiles are disposed to think, not that he is God, but that he is a man like us. And how have those who say of a man that he is a man been blinded by Satan? And what light is there in the gospel of Christ, if he is not God and is not glorified as such? And how could he be the image of God, if he reaches only as far as the things of humanity and does not truly possess being Son and God? “So whether we are at home or away, we make it our aim to please him. For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive what is due for what he has done in the body, whether good or evil.” If the whole endeavor of the saints is to please God, and we make it our aim to appear so before Christ, renouncing the pleasing of men, how is Christ not plainly God? And if he will judge the world, when there is said to be one lawgiver and judge, it is evident that on this ground too he is God, even though the Word became flesh. “For the love of God controls us, because we have concluded this: that if one has died for all, then all have died. And he died for all, that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who for their sake died and was raised.” If we are all one, and we pray to live for him, clearly ennobling our own lives by fulfilling his will, and we live for Christ, how could he not be God, to whom we are indebted and for whom we strive to live, as for one who died for us and purchased all with his own blood? “Therefore we are ambassadors for Christ, God making his appeal through us. We implore you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.” Notice that they are ambassadors for Christ, yet they say that we are appealed to by God. And again: “We implore you,” he says, “on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.” So Christ too is God, and in being reconciled to him we have been reconciled to God. “But as servants of God we commend ourselves in every way.” Those who are said to be servants of God are also called servants of Christ. Therefore Christ is God. “For we are the temple of the living God; as God said, ‘I will dwell among them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.’” If we are temples of the living God because the Spirit dwells in us, and the Spirit is also said to be Christ's (“For if anyone,” he says, “does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him”), how is Christ not God? “We destroy arguments,” he says, “and every lofty thing raised up against the knowledge of God, and take every thought captive to obey Christ.”

In what way shall we tear down every lofty thing raised up against the knowledge of God? Or how shall we take every thought captive to the obedience of Christ? For the Word willingly emptied himself and became obedient to the Father unto death. So when some, on the basis of things done or said in the economy, on account of the flesh and the human element, exalt themselves against the knowledge of the Son, saying that the one in human form is not true God and Son by nature, then we shall tear down every lofty thing raised up. We shall overturn the opinions of those who have chosen to say such things, and turn every thought round to the economy of obedience. For once the Son had come to be within the measures of humanity, he could not refuse what is human. From the Epistle to the Galatians. "For through the law I died to the law, that I might live to God. I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me; and the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself up for me." We must look at what the divine Paul is saying in these words. A law was laid down by God through the voice of the prophets, and it was this: "The righteous shall live by faith." A law was also laid down through Moses. "So," he says, "having followed the law of faith, I died to the law given through Moses, no longer practising what was prescribed for the ancients as in shadow and types." For this is what it means to die to the law given through Moses, so that we may live to God, devoted to faith in Christ. So when we die to the law given through Moses, preferring the justification that is in Christ, how is Christ not God, since the law is abolished through him and faith in him is superior to it? If Christ were a mere man, how could faith in him have become better even than the law? "Does he who supplies the Spirit to you and works miracles among you do so by works of the law, or by hearing with faith?" The law given through Moses was God's law and was spoken through angels. Yet it does not bring the supply of the Holy Spirit, nor did it ever obtain for anyone the power to work wonders, while we gain both through faith in Christ. How then does faith not stand higher [?] than the old law? And if he were a mere man like us, how did faith in him abolish a divine law? And if we who live by faith are in a better state than those who perhaps lived in those times when the law was in force, how is Christ not God? "Now before faith came, we were held in custody under the law,

imprisoned until the faith that was to be revealed. So the law became our guardian until Christ, that we might be justified by faith. But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian. For you are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus. For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ." The law was a guardian that led to nothing else but to Christ alone, even though it taught the true knowledge of God. If so, how is Christ not God? The law is abolished through faith in him, and it hands over to him the completion of its tutelage, as though bringing its pupils up to the highest good. And the final good can be nothing other than the knowledge of the true God. How then could anyone doubt that he is God? We are baptized into the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. How then have we been baptized into Christ, if he is not the true Son, when the Son by nature is one? Yet we have indeed been baptized into him. He is therefore God, as one Son and one Lord, having become flesh by a union in the economy.

"Formerly, when you did not know God, you were enslaved to beings that by nature are not gods; but now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God, how can you turn back again to the weak and beggarly elemental spirits?" If we have come to know God by confessing Christ, and say that we have been known by God because we have become known to him, how is Christ not God? "But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world." The blessed David sings: "I will boast in God my Savior." The saying is wise and befits the saints, for we ought not to take pride in a man, but rather in God. How then does Paul say that he boasts in the cross of Christ? He ought rather to have done this in God, for that is the aim of the other saints. Yet, as one who bears the Spirit, he says that he boasts in the death of Christ. He knows, then, that Christ is God, and true God, and that he suffered in the flesh for us. From the Epistle to the Ephesians. Concerning God the Father he says: "According to the working of his mighty strength, which he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places, far above every Rule and Authority and Power and Dominion, and above every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come." See, the Father has seated the one raised from the dead at his right hand, above every Rule and Authority and Power and every name that is named. Does he share the throne of the nature that is above all as a man like us and nothing more? Or is it, as is the truth, as God made man, being consubstantial

with the Father because he came forth from him, but having taken on the human element in addition in the economy, so that in him the same one is understood to be God and man together, and is for this reason crowned with divine glory? "Therefore remember that at one time you Gentiles in the flesh, called 'the uncircumcision' by what is called 'the circumcision', which is made in the flesh by hands, were at that time without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants, having no hope of the promise, and without God in the world." The Gentiles lived on in godlessness in the world as long as they did not have Christ, but since they have come to have him they have not remained without God. How then is Christ not God [?]?

"For this reason I bow my knees before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named, that he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner man, so that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith." As we have said very often, the name Christ Jesus everywhere means the Word who came forth from God and appeared in human form. How then does he dwell in our hearts through faith, unless he is understood as God, since the Word united the flesh to himself and dwells in us in a divine way through the Spirit? But if Christ is an ordinary man, and a son other than the one who alone is Son by nature (I mean the one from God), who is it that dwells in us? Or how does he take up residence in human beings through faith? Yet John says plainly about Christ: "By this we know that he is in us, because he has given us of his Spirit." From the Epistle to the Philippians. Concerning the things he could boast of in the law he says: "Whatever gains I had, these I have counted as loss for the sake of Christ. Indeed, I count all things as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus our Lord, for whose sake I have suffered the loss of all things, and I count them as refuse, in order that I may gain Christ." What is this surpassing worth of the knowledge of Jesus Christ? And why are the things in the law loss and refuse? After all, the law through Moses proclaimed to the people of old the God who is God by nature and true, whereas those who initiate us into the mysteries of the New Covenant have proclaimed Christ to the world. But suppose he is a man like us, simply ordinary, and not believed to be God by the hypostatic union with the Word from God. How then will faith in him surpass the faith of the law? From the Epistle to the Colossians. "Now I rejoice," he says, "in my sufferings for

your sake, and in my flesh I fill up what is lacking in Christ's afflictions for the sake of his body, which is the Church. I became its minister according to the stewardship from God given to me for you, to make the word of God fully known: the mystery hidden from the ages and from the generations, but now revealed to his saints. To them God chose to make known how great among the Gentiles are the riches of the glory of this mystery, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory. Him we proclaim." If Christ is an ordinary man like us, how was the mystery hidden? How is it the word of God at all? And what riches of glory are in it? The mystery is not great, nor even worth mentioning, unless we approach Christ as God. We must understand that the Word, being God and in equality and form with the Father, lowered himself into self-emptying, becoming man while remaining what he was. For in this way the mystery is understood to be rich and full of glory.

"As therefore you received Christ Jesus our Lord, walk in him, rooted and built up in him and established in the faith." The wise John will teach us how we received Christ, when he says: "And the Word became flesh." But he did not cease to be the Word when he became flesh. For even so he sits with his own Father, and the one who was crucified has been named the Lord of glory. "Continue steadfastly in prayer, being watchful in it with thanksgiving; and pray at the same time for us also, that God may open to us a door for the word, to speak the mystery of God, for which I am also in chains, that I may make it clear, as I ought to speak." If Christ is not God but a man honored with divine grace, the mystery concerning him has nothing deep in it. What door, then, did Paul need in order to speak it openly and as he ought? It is nothing great or difficult to say of a man that he is by nature a man. But if the Word from God is proclaimed as having become man, then there is certainly need of God, who opens the door and grants us to speak the mystery in the fitting way. From the Epistle to the Hebrews. "And when he brings the firstborn into the world, he says: Let all God's angels worship him." The Word from God the Father has been named Only-begotten by nature, because he alone has been begotten of the Father alone. He has also been called firstborn, when he entered the world, having become man

and a part of it. Yet even so he is worshipped by the holy angels, although being worshipped is reserved for God alone and befits him alone. How then is Christ not God, when he is worshipped even in heaven? "Of the angels he says: He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire. But of the Son: Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; and: The scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated lawlessness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions." The one who has a throne forever and ever is the maker of angels. He has loved righteousness and hated lawlessness, and for this reason he is said to be anointed with the oil of gladness by God the Father. What then shall we say as we come to reflect on what is said of him? If he makes his angels spirits and has the throne of Godhead, in what way is he anointed with the oil of gladness? As God, then, he creates angels, but as man he is anointed. The anointing does not touch the nature of the Godhead; it belongs to the skilful design of the economy. Christ, then, is God and man: God by nature, and the same one man like us in the economy, when he was born of a woman according to the flesh. "Take care, brothers, lest there be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, leading you to fall away from the living God." If by denying Christ we fall away from the living and true God, while by remaining in faith in him we commit no apostasy at all, how is Christ not God? "For if the blood of bulls and goats, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled on those who are defiled, sanctify for the purification of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God?" If Christ is not true God, what benefit comes through his blood? Or how will it purify our conscience from dead works? What more does the blood of an ordinary man have than the blood of goats? Nothing at all, except that the one belongs to an irrational animal and the other to a rational one. But the one who is from God by nature took flesh and laid down his own blood for all. For this very reason he is able to purify those who believe in him, to free them from dead works, and to bring them to the service of God. "Anyone who has set aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses. How much worse punishment, do you think, will be deserved by the one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, and regarded as common the blood of the covenant

by which he was sanctified, and insulted the Spirit of grace?" One who has insulted a divine law, that is, set it aside, does not bear a charge equal to that of one who has sinned against a man; his charge is much heavier. Indeed, the one who transgressed the law fell under the penalty of death, while the one who has wronged a man might also deserve pardon. How then does the one who regarded the blood of Christ as common fall under a worse penalty than the one who offends against the law of Moses? Yet he does fall under a worse one, and very fittingly. The blood of Christ, then, is not common, for the Word who became flesh was God. "See that you do not refuse him who is speaking. For if they did not escape when they refused him who warned them on earth, much less shall we escape if we turn away from him who warns from heaven. His voice then shook the earth; but now he has promised, saying: Yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also heaven." Who is the one who warned them on earth, whom the fathers of the Jews refused and so fell into danger? Is it not clear that it was Moses? But Christ is not from the earth; rather, he is from heaven. For God the Word, who is from above and from the Father, became man while remaining God. The penalty, then, is worse for those who turn away from him, and very fittingly. For as the wise John says, "He who is of the earth speaks of the earth," that is, of human things, "but he who comes from above is above all," plainly as God. And such Christ was and is. "Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever." We shall find that the Word who sprang from God was called Jesus Christ at the time when he became man of a woman. How then is he the same yesterday and today and forever? Clearly by the union with the Word from God, since the flesh he assumed is understood together with him as one Son. For in this way the Word will still keep his natural immutability, even when he is understood together with the flesh. From the First Epistle to Timothy. "Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by command of God our Savior, to Timothy, my true child in the faith." The name Savior would properly and truly befit no one else but him alone who is God by nature, and so here too the initiator into the mysteries has named him. But our Savior and Lord is Jesus Christ. For he was named Jesus, and the blessed angel made clear the force, that is, the meaning, of the name when he said: "And you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people

from their sins." Christ, then, is God, since he is the Savior of all men, as the divine Paul says. From the Epistle to Titus. "For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all men. It trains us to renounce ungodliness and worldly desires, and to live soberly and fairly [?] in the present age, as we await the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ. He gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people of his own, zealous for good works." What grace has appeared to us, and the grace of what God, since it is said to bring salvation to all men? But it is clear: "God is the Lord, and he has appeared to us," as the blessed David says. It is his appearing in glory from heaven that we await. And he is the great God and our Savior Jesus the Christ, who gave himself for us, so that he might free us from all sin and present to himself genuine worshippers. Who then says that Emmanuel is not true God, when the blessed Paul says of him: "of the great God and our Savior Jesus

FROM THE CATHOLIC EPISTLES. From the Epistle of James. That Christ is God. "Do not be deceived, my beloved brothers: every good gift and every perfect present is from above, coming down from the Father of lights." "Every good gift," he says. And a good gift is the Holy Spirit, and the power to perform signs in him. Since Christ grants the Spirit to the saints, and the power to perform wonders as well, how would Christ not be true God? "Submit yourselves therefore to God; resist the devil, and he will flee from you." See, here he has said plainly that we must submit to God. And Christ says: "Take my yoke upon you." Since, then, those who take up his yoke submit to no one other than God, how would he not be

From the First Epistle of Peter. "Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, to the called sojourners of the dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia, according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, in the sanctification of the Spirit, for obedience and for sprinkling with the blood of Jesus Christ: may grace and peace be multiplied to you." See, according to the foreknowledge of God

the Father he named himself an apostle of Christ.
