In explaining to us the manner of his apostleship, he says that it was carried out in the sanctification of the Spirit, for obedience and for sprinkling with the blood of Jesus Christ. Since, then, we who believe in him are sanctified by the Spirit, and he sprinkles us with his blood for cleansing, how would he not be understood to be God, when he sanctifies those who believe by his own Spirit and cleanses them by his blood? For he was God in the flesh. "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy has begotten us again to a hope of life through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, to an inheritance imperishable, undefiled and unfading, kept in heaven." If God has begotten us to a living and abiding hope, and Christ has accomplished this through his own resurrection from the dead, how would he not be

"Concerning this salvation," he says, "the prophets who prophesied about the grace that was to be yours searched and inquired diligently. They inquired what person or what time the Spirit of Christ within them was pointing to." See, here again the Holy Spirit is called the Spirit of Christ, although it is the Spirit of God. Christ, then, is God, since he has the Holy Spirit as his own. From the Second Epistle of Peter. "But there were also false prophets among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you, who will secretly bring in destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them." For we have been bought with a price, not with perishable things like silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ. We belong, then, to the one who purchased us, and yet we serve the living and true God. How then is Christ not God, when we have enrolled ourselves under him as Master and know him to be living and true? From the First Epistle of John. "And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know the only and true God; and we are in him who is true, in his Son Jesus Christ. He is the true God and eternal life." Jesus Christ does not mean the Word from God the Father understood bare and by himself, apart from the flesh. It was when he became man that he was also named Christ Jesus. Since, then, he is true God and eternal life, which of those who think otherwise will be able to bear it? From the Epistle of Jude. "Though I was very eager to write to you about our common salvation, I found it necessary to write to you, urging you to contend for the faith once

…once delivered to the saints. For certain people have crept in who were long ago written about beforehand for this condemnation: ungodly people, who turn the grace of our God into licentiousness and deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ." How might one of those who have once believed deny our Lord Jesus Christ? We have indeed accepted the teaching of the Incarnation. But if we say that the Son, the Word from God the Father, is one, and the one from a woman is another, separately, then we have denied the only Master. For there is one Lord Jesus Christ through the union of the economy, I mean his union with the Word from God, since his flesh rises up into the glory of the Godhead. So there is one Christ and Son, for only so will he be Master of all.

From the Gospel according to Matthew. That Christ is God.

"But as he was considering these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying: 'Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife, for what has been conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit. She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins.'" Here he states two things together that befit God and do not befit human nature. He said that those saved through him are the own people of the one born of Mary, and that he himself will free them from their sins. But all things belong to God, and it befits him alone to be able to free sinners from their sins. So the one born of the holy Virgin is God. We are his own people, and he freed us from our sins because he has the authority to do this too.

"Now when Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea." He was born in Bethlehem of Judea, from the root of Jesse. And God the Father says of him through one of the prophets: "And you, Bethlehem, house of Ephrathah, are by no means too few to be among the thousands of Judah. For from you one shall come forth for me to be ruler in Israel, and his goings forth are from the beginning, from the days of eternity." How then can the one born in Bethlehem of Judea be said to have his goings forth, that is, the beginning of his existence, from the beginning of eternity, when he was born in the last times of the age? So Christ is God, and the great antiquity of the Word of God belongs to him. For he was God, and for our sake he endured a birth in the flesh from a woman.

"For I baptize you with water," he says, "for repentance. But he who comes after me is mightier than I, and I am not worthy to carry his sandals. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire. His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will thoroughly clear his threshing floor." We say that baptizing in the Holy [?] Spirit is not the work of humanity. Nor do we say that the spiritual threshing floor, that is, those on the

earth, belongs to a man. For all things belong to God, and to him alone it befits to be able to baptize believers in the Holy Spirit. Christ accomplished this, the one who came after John according to the flesh, that is, in the time of the flesh. [?] He also cleanses his own threshing floor. So he is God

"And behold, a leper came and knelt before him, saying: 'Lord, if you are willing, you can make me clean.' And he stretched out his hand and touched him, saying: 'I am willing; be made clean.' And immediately his leprosy was cleansed." To be able to act in a way that befits God is not proper to a man. It would rather befit [?] only the nature that is beyond all things. Christ acts in this way, so he is not a mere man like us, but rather God in human form. Understand it the same way in the case of Peter's mother-in-law, and when he is seen rebuking the winds, the sea and the waters. So the divine disciples too, seeing the sea and the winds subject to him, marveled and said: "What sort of man is this?" For no mere man could do such things. So he is at once God and man, the one

"And the demons," it says, "begged him, saying: 'If you cast us out, send us into the herd of swine.' And he said to them: 'Go.'" Whose task is it to provide for all things and preserve them, if not his alone who is God by nature? So the Saviour also said: "Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? Yet not one of them will fall to the ground without your Father who is in heaven. And even the hairs of your head are all numbered." See, then: Christ's providence over all that exists was so great that the unclean demons were not allowed authority even over a herd of swine. When they begged him he allowed it only reluctantly. He was not granting their request; he wanted to persuade us to believe that he provides for all things as God. How then is he not God, who has taken on authority befitting God and dominion over all things, and who preserves the things made through him as his own?

"Then he said to his disciples: 'The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few. So ask the lord of the harvest to send out workers into his harvest.' And he called his twelve disciples to him and gave them authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to heal every disease and every sickness." He knows that the lord of the harvest is the God of all, for his is the spiritual threshing floor, that is, humanity, and his also is the harvest. But see: having commanded them to ask

Matt. 10:29. Variant: "permit us to go away." Variant: "to rule." Variant: "having taken away."

the lord of the harvest, he showed that he himself is that lord by sending out the workers, that is, the holy apostles. As God he also gave them authority over unclean spirits. For giving anyone the working of the Holy Spirit lies beyond the measure of humanity, yet Christ gave it. How then is he not God by nature and in truth, even though the Word became flesh?

"So everyone who acknowledges me before people, I too will acknowledge before my Father who is in heaven. But whoever denies me before people, I too will deny before my Father who is in heaven." Many of the saints have been called to the glory of martyrdom, and have been made perfect through suffering and death, having confessed Christ. Were they crowned, then, for affirming and declaring that he is an ordinary man, or rather for [honoring?] him as God in their confessions? The answer is clear. Those who denied this have [fallen away from?] the glory of martyrdom, and on the day of judgment they will find Christ himself denying them. How then is he not God, who crowns with the glory of martyrdom those who confess him to be what he truly is?

"Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you." If Emmanuel is not truly God, how does he lay his own yoke upon us? For all things are God's servants. The law too is called a yoke. Yet Christ lays his own yoke upon us and subjects us to himself, even though he refers [?] all things to the Father. So he is God, and it is therefore fitting for all things to be subject to him.

"Or have you not read in the law that on the Sabbath the priests in the temple profane the Sabbath and are guiltless? I tell you, something greater than the temple is here." If the priests who profane the Sabbath are guiltless because they are offering service to God, how is service to Christ thought greater than what is done in the temple? Clearly, those under the law served a shadow and copy of heavenly things. The divine disciples, however, who attended on Christ and ministered to him, had greater [honor] and glory. And if ministering to Christ ranks above the worship under the law, how could he not be thought true God?

"If I cast out demons by Beelzebul," he says, "by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges." If the disciples healed the demon-possessed in the name of Christ (for they cried out, "In the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene"), how could he not be thought true God? For a man's glory and power would not have been enough to prevail over Satan.

"Just as the weeds are gathered and burned with fire, so it will be at the end of the age. The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all causes of stumbling and those who do lawlessness, and will throw them into the furnace of fire." It is written of God: "Bless the Lord, all you his angels." An angel does not have angels of its own; rather, all things belong to God. How then does he say of the Son of Man that he will send his angels? So he is God, since he has the angels as his own and is served by the spirits above.

Christ asked: "Who do people say that I, the Son of Man, am?" And they said: "Some say John the Baptist, others Elijah, others Jeremiah or one of the prophets." He said to them: "But who do you say that I am?" And Peter answered, it says, and said: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." And Jesus answered and said to him: "Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, for flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but my Father who is in heaven." If Christ is a mere man, why is Peter admired for confessing him? How is he taught by God, or what illumination from above did he need to learn the mystery concerning him? No: he knew that Christ was God, and he confessed him the Son of the living God, and that is why he was admired. Yet he speaks of one Son, not two sons. So it is impious to divide him into two.

"For the Son of Man is going to come in the glory of his Father with his angels." See, again he calls the spirits above his angels, even though he is called Son of Man.

"When they came to Capernaum, those who collected the two-drachma tax came to Peter and said: 'Does your teacher not pay the two-drachma tax?' He said: 'Yes.' And when he came into the house, Jesus spoke to him first, saying: 'What do you think, Simon? From whom do the kings of the earth collect tolls or tribute? From their own sons or from others?' He said to him: 'From others.' Jesus said to him: 'Then the sons are free.'" How can he say that he is free, outside the law, exempt from the tax and truly Son, unless he is God who has shared in flesh and blood through hypostatic union? Yet he paid the two drachmas, as the Son who is above the law having come under the law. As a man he is not thought to be above the law. How could he be? Nor would he have freedom by nature unless he is understood to be God in human

and saying: "Hosanna to the Son of David." This doxology is entirely befitting God. "The Pharisees were indignant and came to him, saying: 'Do you hear what these are saying?' Jesus said to them: 'Yes. Have you never read, "Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have perfected praise"?'" Here we must recall blessed David, who says: "O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth! For your majesty is exalted above the heavens. Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have perfected praise." The children cried out in acclamation: "Hosanna to the Son of David," and he accepts the doxology when they acclaim him. But blessed David did not ascribe this praise to an ordinary man. He ascribed it to the Lord, whose name is wonderful in all the earth, for [his] majesty is exalted above the heavens. How then is the Son of David according to the flesh, Christ, not God?

"When the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the angels with him, then he will sit on the throne of his glory." Will Christ, then, sit there as a man like one of us, with all the angels standing beside him, and judge the world that way? What sense would that make? For it is written: "There is one lawgiver and judge." So Christ is God. He is in the glory of God, has a throne and angels standing by him, and judges the world in righteousness.

"And the high priest," it says, "said to him: 'I adjure you by the living God to tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of the living God.' He said to him: 'You have said so. But I tell you, from now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the Power and coming on the clouds of heaven.'" How does the Son of Man sit at the right hand of the Power? It is clear that even though the Word from God became Son of Man, he did not cease to be God, but is what he was. That is why he sits with the one who begot him and is seen resplendent in the dignities of the Godhead, even though he became flesh.

"And Jesus cried out again with a loud voice and gave up his spirit. And behold, the curtain of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom, and the earth shook, and the rocks were split, and the tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep were raised." If Christ was an ordinary man, why was there such turmoil among the elements when he died? The sun drew in its rays and made darkness by day. The earth split when it saw its own Master abused by the Jews, and Hades released the souls of the saints. Who did these things? Was it not God? For he was God

in the flesh, and when he was outraged, creation in a sense shared his anger.

From the Gospel according to John.

"But Jesus himself did not entrust himself to them, because he knew all people. He had no need for anyone to testify about man, for he himself knew what was in man." Of God it is written: "He who fashioned their hearts one by one." And he himself says somewhere: "Will anything be hidden from me?" If Christ knows all things and knows what is in man, how could he not be God, since he searches hearts and minds?

"You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, for salvation is from the Jews." Do you hear him say that salvation is from the Jews? Yet we have acknowledged God as our Saviour, for according to the Scriptures it was not an envoy or an angel who saved us, but the Lord himself. He is named Christ Jesus, having come from the Jews according to the flesh, and "Jesus" means salvation. So he himself is the salvation that is from the Jews. Thus, even though the Word became flesh and took hold of the seed of Abraham, he is God even with the flesh.

"Truly, truly, I tell you, whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these, because I am going to my Father. And whatever you ask in my name, this I will do." He is going, he says, to the Father, even though the Son is God by nature and is himself the one who fills all things. He goes in a human way, for he was taken up into heaven. [?] As God he promises to fulfil the requests of those who pray, if they make their supplications in his name. Whom, then, would it befit to fulfil the prayers of the saints and grant their requests, if not him alone who is God by nature and in truth?

"You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you so that you would go and bear fruit, and that your fruit would remain, so that whatever you ask the Father in my name, he may give [?] it to you." See how he shows everywhere that he acts with authority equally with the Father. He said: "Whatever you ask in my name, I will do." Now he says: "Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give [?] it to you." Does the Father give on his own, then, apart from the Son, and the Son on his own and in his turn, apart from the Father? Are the requests made in prayer granted to the saints by two gods, then? But that is not how it is. May it not

Variant [?]: "to go." Read: "to God the Father."

be! For there is one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ. The Father distributes good things through the Son in the Spirit. But the requests made in prayer are made in Christ Jesus, and the Lord Jesus who became man is understood and named the Word.

"And on that day you will ask me nothing. Truly, truly, I tell you, if you ask the Father anything in my name, he will give it to you. Ask, and you will receive, so that your joy may be complete." This too, briefly, carries the same meaning as the passages above, and so does what follows. It runs: "On that day you will ask in my name. I do not say to you that I will ask the Father for you, for the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and have believed that I came forth from the Father."

"And this is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent." If the knowledge of Jesus Christ must be joined to the knowledge of the only true God and enter in with it, and this brings eternal life, how is it not evident to everyone that Christ is true God? For the Word became flesh, and remained the Word.

"So that the world may believe that you sent me. The glory that you have given me I have given to them, so that they may be one, just as we are one: I in them and you in me, so that they may be perfected into one." Let us fix the eye of the mind closely on the force of this passage and consider what is in it. What glory does the Son say he received from the Father and gave to us? He himself spares us the inquiry by saying: "So that they may be one, just as we are one." In natural identity the Word from God is one with his own Father, even though each is understood to exist in his own hypostasis. And how has he also come to be in us? In the same way, I mean essentially and naturally. And yet the nature of God would be entirely unmixable with creation, as far as identity of essence is concerned. How, then, has he who is above creation come to be in us naturally? He became man, so that just as he is one with the Father in the nature of the Godhead, so too he might become one with us through the relation that comes from humanity. In this way we too have been perfected into one.

"When it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and the doors were shut where the disciples were gathered for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood in the midst and said to them: 'Peace be with you.'" Someone might reasonably raise this question: If the Word was in a body even after the resurrection, just as before the precious cross, how

did he unexpectedly appear in the midst of the disciples when the doors were shut? To this we reply: by [his own?] power. We should remember Paul's words: "So from now on we know no one according to the flesh. Even if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, we know him so no longer." After the resurrection from the dead, the economy had already been completed, [?] in which the taking up of the flesh had necessarily been accomplished. So he made use of authority and power befitting God, wishing to be recognized through these rather than through the measures of his self-emptying, as was proper at that time.

"And when he had said this, he breathed on them and said to them: 'Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained.'" What took place befits God and deserves to be [?] spoken of. First, breathing on the apostles and giving them the Spirit is not a human act. Next, granting such authority is great and above creation: to retain the sins of whomever they choose and to forgive those of whomever they might wish. And why does he give the Spirit through a bodily breath? Because the flesh did not become foreign to the Word; it was his own. The breathing through the flesh is human, but to make those who were counted worthy partakers of the [Spirit?] is the work of divine power.

From the Gospel according to Luke.

An angel of God says to Zechariah about the holy Baptist: "And you will have joy and gladness, and many will rejoice at his birth. For he will be great before the Lord, and he will drink no wine or strong drink, and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother's womb. And he will turn many of the sons of Israel to the Lord their God." When the Jews asked blessed John, "Who are you?" he said: "I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight." And Zechariah himself, prophesying over his own child, says: "And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High, for you will go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways, to give his people knowledge of salvation in the forgiveness of their sins." John went ahead of Christ and became his forerunner. He proclaimed that the ways were being prepared for him and foretold the message about him, turning people to him as to God, who is able to justify those in sin. How then is Christ not God?

"He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High, and the Lord God will give him the throne of David

…of his father; and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.” Are we then to be placed under one of our own kind, ruled by him perpetually and without end? Or shall we rather be under God, who reigns over us in Christ, and not as though some mediator from outside had been brought in for this purpose, but as God the Father ruling over all things through the Son and in the Son? If this is true, then Christ is God. “And Mary said to the angel, ‘How will this be for me, since I do not know a man?’ And the angel answered and said to her, ‘The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who is born will be called Son of God.’” Has he then merely been called Son, the one ineffably born, or rather created, from the holy Virgin through the Spirit? Or is he believed to be Son by nature and in truth, and God? This last is the truth. Let the Word, then, be understood to have become flesh hypostatically, that is, having made his own the flesh that came from the holy Virgin through the Spirit; for in this way he will also be truly God. “And it happened that when Elizabeth heard Mary's greeting, the babe leaped in her womb; and Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit, and cried out with a loud voice and said, ‘Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb. And how does this happen to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?’” When God works the grace of prophecy, a person will be a prophet; in any other way, not at all. Since, then, the greeting of the holy Virgin Mary, while she was still carrying Jesus, moved John in the womb to prophecy, how is Christ not God, who even from within the Virgin's womb moved the Baptist, in a manner befitting God, to the power of prophecy? “Now, Master, you are dismissing your servant in peace, according to your word; for my eyes have seen your salvation, which you have prepared before the face of all peoples: a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and the glory of your people Israel.” Simeon, taking Jesus into his arms, says these things about him. How then is he salvation, and how a light for revelation to the Gentiles, unless he is truly God, the one and only Son, who is by nature from the Father as Word, and the same from the Virgin according to the flesh? For what revelation came to the Gentiles, other than that in him they came to know that he is God, and by worshipping him escaped the charge of worshipping some god other than the one who is God by nature and in truth?

…answering, he said to them, “Why do you reason in your hearts? Which is easier, to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven you,’ or to say, ‘Rise and walk’? But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins” (he said to the paralytic), “I say to you, rise, take up your little bed, and go to your house.” If the God of all alone frees us from our offenses, this befitting no one else, and Christ grants this too with an authority befitting God, how could he not be God? For he is called Son of Man because he was born of a woman according to the flesh, although he is God, the…

“In that hour he healed many of diseases and plagues and evil spirits, and to many who were blind he granted sight. And he answered and said to them, ‘Go and report to John what you have seen and heard: the blind see again, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, the poor have the gospel preached to them. And blessed is whoever is not scandalized in me.’” Having shown himself by the very deeds to be the accomplisher of mighty works befitting God, Christ calls to mind what had been said about him through the voice of the prophets. For the blessed Isaiah said: “Be strong, you slack hands and paralyzed knees.” Then, all but stretching out his hand, he points out Emmanuel, saying: “Behold our God; behold, the Lord comes with strength, and his arm with lordship.” And elsewhere he said: “Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will hear; then the lame will leap like a deer, and the tongue of the stammerers will be clear.” And besides these: “The dead will rise, and those in the tombs will be raised; for the dew that comes from you is healing for them.” And again he said, in the person of Christ: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach the gospel to the poor, to proclaim release to captives and recovery of sight to the blind.” Since, then, he makes the words of the prophets the sign, that is, the proof, for faith in himself, and the prophets proclaim him to be God, who would dare to say the opposite of them? The disciples, it says, were caught in a storm on the lake; then “they came and woke him, saying, ‘Master, we are perishing.’ And he arose and rebuked the wind and the raging of the water; and they ceased, and there was a calm.” It is said of Christ through the voice of the blessed David: “You rule the might of the sea, and you calm the tossing of its waves. Yours are the heavens, and yours is the earth; you founded the world and its fullness.” Since, then, to the one who calms the sea it would also belong to rule over all things, to have the heavens as his own, and to be able to found
the world and its fullness, how could Christ not be understood to be truly God, who rebukes sea and winds, and this with…

“The man from whom the demons had gone out begged him that he might be with him. But he sent him away, saying, ‘Return to your house, and tell how much God has done for you.’ And he went away through the whole city proclaiming how much God had done for him.” In the country of the Gergesenes Christ healed the savagely possessed man, who also begged to stay with him. But although he had healed him and cast out the spirits, he ordered him to go away to his house and proclaim how much God had done for him. So it was he himself who acted, being true God; for we do not say that he became a minister of divine grace like one of the prophets or of the holy apostles; rather, he himself was crushing Satan by his own power befitting God. It was in his name, then, that the demons were subject even to the holy disciples; and they themselves confessed this. Regarding the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, Christ says: “Do not weep; for the girl has not died, but is sleeping.” Was he then lying? Far from it! He speaks the truth; and in what way, Paul explains, saying: “He is not the God of the dead, but of the living.” For those who are going to live are alive to God. So the dead are dead in human terms, but in relation to the life-giving nature, that is, the divine, they have not died. For he speaks the truth as God when he says of the girl, “She has not died, but…”

Speaking with his own disciples, he said: “Who is greater, the one who reclines at table or the one who serves? Is it not the one who reclines? But I am among you as one who serves.” You see how, so far as concerns what befits the Godhead and the glory of the Master, he all but shakes off being thought of as in the rank of a servant; but he accepts this because of his humanity: “For I am,” he says, “among you as one who serves.” So even if he came down among servants, he is nonetheless himself the one who reclines as Master, and is served by all creation as God. Then Christ said to them (that is, to the chief priests of the Jews, who were asking, “Are you the Christ?”): “If I tell you, you will not believe; and if I ask you, you will not answer. But from now on the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God.” If the Son of Man sits at the right hand of the power of God, how is Christ not God, resplendent on the highest seats and sharing the throne [? marginal notes: “was lying”; “therefore as God”]

with the Father? For no created nature at all sits beside the one who is God by nature. Yet the Son of Man does sit beside him, since the Word born from God became flesh by an economic union. That Christ is life and life-giving. From the First Epistle to the Corinthians. “I speak as to sensible people; judge for yourselves what I say. The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not a communion in the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not a communion in the body of Christ? Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body; for we all partake of the one bread.” The flesh of a man, considered in its own nature, could not be life-giving; nor could human blood, if it were ordinary and on its own. But the body of Christ gives life, and so does his precious blood, since it befits God alone to be able to give life to what lacks life. Christ, then, is God; for only so will his body be life-giving. But if he is thought of as a man apart, honored merely with the title of Christ and having only the bare person of a son, how could his body be life-giving? “The first man Adam became a living soul; the last Adam became a life-giving Spirit.” And again: “The first man was from the earth, earthy; the second man is the Lord from heaven. As was the earthy one, so are those who are earthy; and as is the heavenly one, so are those who are heavenly. And just as we have borne the image of the earthy one, let us also bear the image of the heavenly one. This I say, brothers: flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does corruption inherit incorruption.” And to this he adds: “The trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed. For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.” The first man became a living soul; for as a thing made he needed God, who gives life. But the last Adam, that is, Christ, since as God he did not need life, became for us a life-giving Spirit, which is a prerogative proper to the divine nature. And the first is from the earth, earthy; but the second is from heaven, even though he was born through a woman. For the Word who is from above, from heaven, and from God the Father, even if he became man, is no less from heaven. And if, because we are held fast by corruption and death, we are said to bear the image of the earthy one, then when we have put on incorruption we shall bear the image of the heavenly one. And incorruption, again, is a good proper to the Godhead by nature; for the dead are changed, and the corruptible is clothed with incorruption, since [? note: ibid. 15:50; “second man”]

the Only-begotten became like us, transferring the mortal into immortality and the corruptible into incorruption, and refashioning it first in himself. For in this way he became for us too a way to life. From the Second Epistle to the Corinthians. “But we ourselves,” he says, “have had the sentence of death within ourselves, so that we might not trust in ourselves, but in God who raises the dead.” If we say that raising the dead is most fitting for the one who is God by nature, because he is life and life-giving; and Christ said, “I am the resurrection and the life”; and he is also plainly seen to have raised the dead: then he is God, as being life by nature. From the Epistle to the Hebrews. “Since, then, the children have shared in blood and flesh, he himself likewise partook of the same, so that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil.” Just like us who are ranked among the children of God, the Word from God shared in blood and flesh, so that, having given his own body to death, he might bring it to life again, being life by nature, as God. For how has the power of death been destroyed, unless the body that fell into death came back to life, being the own body of him who is life by nature, that is, of the Word who is from God? That the Son and Lord Jesus Christ is one. From the First Catholic Epistle of John. “That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have beheld, and our hands have touched, concerning the Word of life—and the life was made manifest, and we have seen it, and bear witness, and proclaim to you the eternal life, which was with the Father and was made manifest to us.” See, he says that he has seen with his eyes, and indeed touched with his hands, the one who was from the beginning, that is, the Word from the Father, the eternal life; and yet according to the proper nature of the Word who is from the Father he is both invisible and intangible, for what is incorporeal is intangible. But he says that he saw and touched the Word when he had come to be in the flesh. There is, then, one Son and God and Lord, even though the Word became flesh. That faith is in Christ as in God. From the First Epistle of Peter. “So that,” he says, “your faith and hope may be in God.” And yet it is Christ who is proclaimed through the holy

apostles; and he himself says somewhere: “Truly, truly I say to you, whoever believes in me has eternal life.” Since, then, faith is in God, and Christ says, “Believe in me,” how could he not plainly be God? From the First Epistle of John. “And this is his commandment, that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ.” If it is not contrary to the will of God the Father that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ, and faith is exercised by us not as in a mere man but as in the living and true God, then Christ is God. “By this the Spirit of God is known: every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ come in the flesh is from God; and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God; and this is the spirit of the Antichrist, which you have heard is coming, and now is already in the world.” Do we, then, confess Jesus as a man and one of us? Or rather that the Word, being God, became flesh, not neglecting to be God, but rather remaining what he was, even though he became man? This is beyond doubt. So whoever does not say that Christ is truly God, but divides and belittles his glory, has the spirit of the Antichrist.

“And we have beheld and bear witness that the Father has sent the Son as Savior of the world. Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God abides in him, and he in God.” We say that the Son, that is, the only-begotten Word who is from him by nature, was sent by God the Father; and that he was named Jesus when, in accordance with the economy, he also underwent birth from a woman according to the flesh. So the Word from God became man. And if anyone confesses him in this way, he has God abiding in himself, and he himself will also be in God; for God will remember him and will count him as his own, as one who shares in him. But whoever does not confess that the Word from God the Father, who lowered himself into humanity, is himself Jesus, would neither be enriched with God within himself, nor will he himself be in God, at least in the manner of spiritual kinship. “Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God.” So whoever does not believe would not be counted among the children of God either. For if “to as many as received the Son he gave authority to become children of God,” as the evangelist says, those who have not received him would not be counted among the children of God, since they have not known the one through whom this comes about. “And who is it that overcomes the world, if not the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God? This is the one who came through water and blood, Jesus Christ, [? note: John 3:25]

not in the water only, but in the water and the blood. And it is the Spirit who bears witness, because the Spirit is truth. For there are three who bear witness: the Spirit, and the water, and the blood; and the three are one.” The one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God overcomes the world. And who Jesus is, Jesus' own disciple makes clear to us, saying: “This is the one who came through water and blood, Jesus Christ.” But he says also in blood and in Spirit, and he says that the three are one. So the Word became flesh, and he sanctifies us by the Spirit, cleanses us by the blood, and washes us again with pure water. Yet the Son is surely one, to whom, we say, the Spirit, the water, and the blood belong. “If we receive the testimony of men, the testimony of God is greater; for this is the testimony of God, that he has testified concerning his Son. Whoever believes in the Son of God has the testimony in himself. Whoever does not believe God has made him a liar, because he has not believed in the testimony that God has given concerning his Son.” The Father has testified to the Son through the Spirit and through a voice. For that the Son is truly his would be attested by his being able to supply the Spirit to the saints and to work miracles through it. And indeed he said, “He will glorify me.” He also testified in another way, for he glorified him at the Jordan, saying, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” All those, therefore, who make a division and say that the one born of a woman is not a true Son, but apply the name of sonship to the Word from God, bare and alone, make the Father a liar; for at the Jordan he showed forth the Word made flesh, and then the Spirit bore witness to him that he is both God and truly Son. That Christ is one [?]. From the Gospel according to Matthew. Concerning the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue it is written: “When the crowd had been put out, Jesus went in and took her by the hand, and the girl arose.” Why did he not rather, as in the case of Lazarus, content himself with a word to raise the girl, but also took her by the hand? To show that his own body is life-giving; for it is the body of Life. So the union of the Word with the flesh is rather natural and true, and not, as some say out of ignorance, accomplished merely in persons, or by mere good pleasure and will, or a simple conjunction. From the Gospel according to John. “Work,” he says, “not for the food that perishes,

but for the food that endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give you; for on him God the Father has set his seal.” The Son of Man has given us food that endures to eternal life, that is, his own flesh; for it is indeed life-giving. How then is he not God, who is able to give life even through his own flesh, and who is like God the Father in all things? For I know that this is what is meant by saying that he has been sealed by God, since “being sealed” signifies exact likeness. For just as, if someone presses a seal of gold, or one made of some other material, into wax, it imprints its whole likeness completely, so also God the Father has the characteristics of his own nature essentially shining forth in the Son. And this is what it means to say that he has been sealed by the Father. From the Gospel according to Luke. Christ raised Lazarus, the little daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, and the widow's son. How then is he not life by nature, who was able to make death fall not only by a word alone, but also by the touch of his hand? For it was consistent and necessary that the body of him who is life by nature should be life-giving. That he is a propitiation through faith. From the Epistle to the Romans. He says of Christ: “whom God put forward as a propitiation through faith in his blood, to show his righteousness, because of the passing over of former sins in the forbearance of God, to show his righteousness at the present time, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus.” If there was no other way for Christ to become a propitiation for those under sin, curse, and the penalty of death, except through blood, which was to be poured out for the passing over of former sins, how was it not necessary for the Word to become flesh, so that by his own blood, clearly the blood of his own flesh, he might justify all who believe in him? That we have been redeemed and have obtained reconciliation with God through his blood. From the First Epistle to the Corinthians. “It is from him that you are in Christ Jesus, who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption, so that, as it is written, ‘Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.’” We have been redeemed, then, in Christ, and sanctified, and made wise. “But every good gift and every perfect present is from above, coming down from the Father of lights,” that is, from God. How then is Christ not God [? note: John ii, 45]

[...Chri]st, who has granted us wisdom and sanctification and redemption. That we have been redeemed through the blood of Christ. From the First Epistle of Peter: "Knowing that you were redeemed from the futile way of life handed down from your fathers, not with perishable things, silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot." For we have been redeemed because Christ gave his own body for us. But if he is understood to be an ordinary man, how could his blood be worth [?] the life of all? But if he was God in the flesh, worthier than all, then the redemption of the whole world through his own blood would be sufficient, and quite rightly so. That the death of Christ is saving for the world. From the Epistle to the Romans: "But God shows his own love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Much more, then, having now been justified by his blood, we shall be saved through him from the wrath." And again: "For if while we were enemies we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved by his life." So then: there was no other way for the world to be saved except by blood and a death usefully [?] undergone, by divine dispensation, for the passing over of sins previously committed, in the forbearance of God; and we have been saved through Christ. How, then, was the way of incarnation not necessary for the Word born from God, so that he might justify by his blood those who believe in him, and reconcile [them] to God [?] through the death of his own body, so that we might also live with him? "Or do you not know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were buried with him, then, through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life." If it was in every way necessary for those [?] on earth to be buried with Christ through baptism into his death, so that, just as he has been raised from the dead, we too might walk in newness of life, as those buried and raised together with him who died and was raised for us, then the mystery of the incarnation was accomplished most usefully and necessarily, and the Word shared in flesh and blood, so that with him who is said to have died according to the flesh, and indeed to have been raised, we might die and rise together. "For if we have been united with him in the likeness of his death, we shall certainly also be united with him in the likeness of his resurrection."

You will understand this too in the same way as the first: "For since death came through a man, the resurrection of the dead has also come through a man. For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive." Christ has been called the second Adam; and just as the first Adam brought us down into corruption, so the second has brought us back to life. He did not die for us as a mere man, for then we would remain dead even in him; he died as God in the flesh, having suffered humanly in it, so that we might be raised together with him who divinely raised up his own temple. From the Epistle to the Galatians: "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us; for it is written: Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree; so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the gentiles, so that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith." Observe for me from this passage too that Christ's death has become saving for the world. For he became a curse for us, enduring the cross and being hung on a tree, in order to undo the sin of the world, so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the gentiles—that is, so that the gentiles might be justified by faith, according to the promise given to Abraham—so that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith. Since, then, Christ's death has also undone the curse in the law, and procured for the gentiles the blessing of Abraham, that is, the grace that comes through faith, and has made us partakers of the Holy Spirit as well, his death could not be understood as that of an ordinary man. Rather, one ought to consider that the Word, having become flesh, suffered in the flesh for the world, and his suffering became sufficient for the redemption of the world. From the Epistle to the Ephesians: "But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ. For he himself is our peace, who made both one and broke down the dividing wall of the barrier, abolishing in his flesh the enmity, the law of commandments expressed in decrees." If the blood of Christ has brought near those who were far off because they wandered about in the world and lived continually in godlessness, how was the incarnation of the Word not necessary for those on earth? It gathers together what was divided, brings those far off into kinship with God, and creates the two peoples into one new man through his flesh. For it was given for the redemption of those in sins, and through it he won all things for God the Father. And in addition to this, the old law has also been abolished, since faith stands above it—clearly faith in Christ. And if this is true, how is faith above the law, unless we have believed in Christ as God?

From the Epistle to the Hebrews: "Therefore, when he comes into the world, he says: Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but a body you prepared for me; in burnt offerings and offerings for sin you took no pleasure. Then I said: Behold, I have come—in the scroll of the book it is written of me—to do your will, O God." The suffering of Christ has become saving for the world. But we must see who it is that comes into the world. For he was outside the world wholly and entirely; otherwise, how could he have entered into it if he was [already] in the world? Therefore, being by nature above the whole world, as the only-begotten God, he entered into it, having become part of it, that is, a man; and so, offering the sacrifice on our behalf and dedicating himself, he has saved all that is under heaven. "Therefore Jesus also, in order to sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside the gate." In what way could the blood of an ordinary man make us holy? Yet the blood of Christ did sanctify. It is therefore divine, and not simply human; for he was God in the flesh, cleansing us with his own blood. From the Epistle to Timothy: "For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all." It is acknowledged that the death of Christ is saving for the whole world. But if he is not God, how could he, one alone, suffice to become a ransom for all? Yet he did suffice, dying alone for all, because he is above all. He is God, therefore, who by the death of his own flesh did away with [?] the death of the world. FROM THE CATHOLIC EPISTLES. From the Epistle of Peter. That the death of Christ is saving for the world: "For Christ died once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, so that he might bring us to God, having been put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit; in which he also went and preached to the spirits in prison, who were once disobedient." Many of the holy prophets were killed, but none of them is said to have died for us, nor to have brought us to God through his own death; nor did any of them preach to the spirits in prison. But Christ did this, and through him and in him we have been redeemed, and his suffering was saving for the world. He died for us, then, not as one man among us, but as God in the flesh, giving his own body in exchange for the life of all.

"Since, therefore, Christ suffered for us in the flesh." Because Christ is God, the disciple wisely and prudently says that he suffered in the flesh, withdrawing from suffering the ineffable nature, to which suffering is foreign. So the Word from God suffered in his own flesh, although it is his nature to have no share in suffering. Christ, then, is God: impassible as God, but passible according to the flesh. That the death of Christ is saving for the world. From the Gospel according to John: "His disciples did not understand these things at first; but when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered that these things had been written about him." And again: "Jesus answered them, saying: The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified. Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit." It is beyond dispute that the whole world has been saved, since Emmanuel died for it. But we ask this: how was he glorified by dying? Indeed the thing rather carries the reproach of weakness; that is why he is said to have despised the shame, having become obedient unto death. But perhaps you will say that he was glorified through the resurrection. The argument is correct [?]. Did he, then, come back to life divinely rather than humanly? Divinely, I think. So whenever the Word himself is said to have suffered in the flesh, let us not be ashamed of the suffering; for its outcome holds glory, and this [...]

From the Epistle to the Romans: "So then, I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh the law of sin. There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. For the law of the Spirit of life has set me free from the law of sin and death. For what the law could not do, weak as it was through the flesh, God did: sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin, he condemned sin in the flesh, so that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit." For admittedly the flesh and the spirit fight against each other—that is, the mind of the flesh and the stirring of the pleasures innate in us, against the power of life according to the Spirit. And even if the divine law carries us toward choosing the good, the desire of the flesh forces us toward the opposite.

But now in Christ the opposing force has been undone; the law of sin has lost its strength, and the law of the Spirit has prevailed. For what reason? "For God sent his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, so that he might condemn sin in the flesh." How, then, is the incarnation of the Word not supremely needful? For in this way sin has been condemned in our flesh too. But if the Word had not become flesh, our condition would have remained uncorrected, and we would be serving the law of sin with the flesh, with no one having abolished it in us. Therefore we say that the hypostatic union of the Word with the flesh is necessary, and not merely the union in persons and by will, or a simple conjunction, as some say. "What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who is against us? He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him freely give us all things?" If God the Father gave his own Son for us—clearly the one from his own substance—and he suffered according to the flesh and not in the nature of the Godhead, then the body that suffered was his own [?], so that he too might be understood to have suffered by dispensation, he who knows no suffering. To divide the one into two, therefore, is impious; for the Father would no longer be found to have given his own Son for us, if he is a man separately, and not rather the Word from God in the assumption of flesh. "Who will bring a charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies; who is the one who condemns? It is Christ Jesus who died, or rather who was raised, who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us." If Christ justifies by faith, and it is God who justifies, then Christ is true God. And if he is at the right hand of God, though he died and was raised, and sits together with the Father, then the body is the Word's own. For in this way he sits with the Father together with the flesh he assumed, as Son by nature, even though the Word became flesh. "But the righteousness that comes from faith speaks thus: Do not say in your heart, Who will ascend into heaven?—that is, to bring Christ down—or, Who will descend into the abyss?—that is, to bring Christ up from the dead. But what does it say? The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart—that is, the word of faith which we preach. For if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth one confesses unto salvation." If, as some think, Christ is understood as a God-bearing man, having only the union in persons with God the Word, for what reason, believing

in him as in the Lord, and confessing his resurrection from the dead, are we justified by faith in him? Clearly, faith is exercised as in God. The hypostatic union of God the Word with humanity is therefore necessary. For in this way we shall confess one Christ as Lord by nature, and, acknowledging the resurrection of his flesh, we are justified as those who believe in God. "For none of us lives to himself, and none of us dies to himself. If we live, we live to the Lord; and if we die, we die to the Lord. So whether we live or whether we die, we are God's. For to this end Christ died and lived, so that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living." Blessed Paul says somewhere to those from the gentiles: "But now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God, how can you turn back to the weak and beggarly elements of the world, which you want to be enslaved to all over again?" We have been redeemed, then, through faith in Christ from slavery to the elements, and have been brought to serve the living and true God. If Christ died so that he might be Lord of both dead and living, and we live to him as to the living and true God, how was a true union with flesh not necessary for the Word? For by dying in it, he became Lord of both living and dead. From the First Epistle to the Corinthians: "For they drank," he says, "from the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ." The name Christ was given to Emmanuel when he was born through the holy Virgin. How, then, was he the rock that gave Israel water? But it is clear that the sacred Scripture knows one Christ and Son. For the Word, having become flesh, is again himself the spiritual rock, not casting off the great antiquity of his own nature because of the newness of the dispensation. From the Second Epistle to the Corinthians: "So from now on we regard no one according to the flesh; even though we once knew Christ according to the flesh, we know him thus no longer." What, then, is Paul saying? Does he deny Christ after the resurrection? Does he not know that he was raised in the flesh and taken up with it into heaven? And who would dare to say that? For he knows him as taken up and as coming again at the appointed time in the same way he ascended into heaven. How, then, does he say that he does not know the Son according to the flesh? Because after his return to life from the dead it is better to know and confess him no longer in terms of the measures of the flesh, but in terms of his divine pre-eminence. For while the dispensation was not yet fulfilled, he was preached according to the flesh, so that the Only-begotten might be believed to have become man; but since the mystery has been accomplished, it is better to confess him in terms of what makes him God than in terms of his having emptied himself [?]

[...] the flesh. One, then, is Christ and Son and Lord. "For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, for your sake he became poor, so that by his poverty you might become rich." If Christ is only a man, and not rich as God by true union with God the Word, how did he become poor? For what wealth does humanity have at all? It has been said to every man: "What do you have that you did not receive?" But he became poor, though he was rich as God; for the Word from God the Father, who is truly rich, became poor by making the lowliness of humanity his own by dispensation. One, then, is Christ and Son: rich as God, and poor because he became man. From the Epistle to the Galatians: "Paul, an apostle—not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead." Does not the teacher of the mysteries show us through these words that God became man [?], and that the one from both is Son and Lord? For he said that he was sent neither from men nor through man, and added: "but through Jesus Christ." Yet how could he not know that Jesus Christ is a man, he who proclaimed him in this way to the whole inhabited world [?]? But he knows him to be not simply a man, but rather the Word from God made man; not God understood to be in a man, but one who actually became man while remaining God. So when he says that he was not sent from man but through Jesus Christ, how is it not evident to everyone that he knows him also to be true God, even after he came to be in flesh like us? He describes him, then, not in terms of the measures of the emptying, but in terms of his divine pre-eminence over all. "When we were children, we were enslaved under the elements of the world. But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons." Whom did God the Father send, who was born of a woman and also came under the law? Is it not fitting to say, and worth considering, that he sent the one who would not have been born of a woman, nor have lived under the law, had he remained what he was, that is, without flesh and blood? But the statement is clear: the Word from God the Father was born of a woman according to the flesh; the Lord of the law, as God, came [?]

under the law, so that he might also become a brother to those under the law; for in this way we received adoption. So if he had not come under the law and been born of a woman, we would not be brothers to the one who is by nature Lord and God. But since this came about through him, we have been enriched. The divine Paul gives a clear proof of the matter, adding at once: "And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father." How, then, is the spirit of the one born of a woman and under the law the Holy Spirit, through whom we cry "Abba, Father," unless Christ is God, being one, and Son? From the Epistle to the Ephesians: "One Lord, one faith, one baptism; one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all. But to each one of us this grace was given according to the measure of Christ's gift. Therefore it says: Ascending on high, he led captivity captive, and gave gifts to men. Now what does 'he ascended' mean, except that he also descended into the lowest parts of the earth? He who descended is the same one who ascended far above all the heavens, so that he might fill all things." Observe for me again how much this passage shows most clearly and plainly, if you know how and are able [to see it] [?]: that Christ is one Lord by a union of dispensation, the Word having been brought together with humanity; for the one from both is true Son. Otherwise, how is there one Lord? How one faith? Or how is the baptism one? For if there are two sons, there are certainly two lords as well; the faith is twofold, and the baptism is not one. For in whom have we believed? Or into whose name have we been baptized? But in fact there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism; it is therefore plain that there is also one Son, even if the Only-begotten is understood to have become like us. Who, after all, is the one who ascended on high? Or who is the one who descended into the lower parts of the earth? He himself, then, descended humanly, for he lowered himself into emptying and humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death; and he ascended with the flesh far above all the heavens, so that he might fill all things. From the Epistle to the Philippians: "Let each of you have this mind among you which was also in Christ Jesus, who, being in the form of God, did not regard being equal with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a slave, being made in the likeness of men; and being found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also highly exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven [?] and to God."

[?] …and on earth, and under the earth; and every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father." Notice how he says that God the Word, being in the form of God the Father, did not consider being equal to God something to be grasped. For although by nature he had being in equality with the Father, he emptied himself and took the form of a servant. That is, he became man and was found, as it were, in our likeness, and he humbled himself even to emptying. And since he endured even the cross itself, Paul says that he was exalted, and that he was given the name above every name, so that every knee should bow and every tongue confess him. How then is the one who is in the form and equality of God said to have lowered himself into emptying, and afterwards to have been exalted? Is not the mystery of Christ perfectly plain? Being God by nature, he became man in humility and lowliness. And having become like us, he returns to his own glory, even with the flesh. Exaltation would therefore belong to the economy, and not to the very nature of the Word. So Christ is one: God in humanity, and existing together with the humanity.

From the Epistle to the Colossians. "Giving thanks," he says, "to the Father, who has made us fit for a share in the inheritance of the saints in light. He rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love, in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins. He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation. For in him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or authorities; all things were created through him and for him. He is before all things, and in him all things hold together. He is the head of the body, the Church; he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that he might come to have first place in everything. For in him all the fullness was pleased to dwell, and through him to reconcile all things to him, having made peace through the blood of his cross, whether things on earth or things in the heavens." See, once again he calls him the image of the invisible God. He clearly affirms that thrones and principalities and dominions were created through him. He says that all things are for him and hold together in him, and that he is the head of the body of the Church and the firstborn from the dead. Who then is the image of God, the creator of all things, if not the only-begotten Son of God himself? He also became the firstborn from the dead, since he died in his own flesh and not in that of someone else. So there is one Christ and Son, at once both God and man. From the Epistle to the Hebrews. "In many parts and in many ways God of old, having spo-

-ken to the fathers in the prophets, in these last days has spoken to us in a Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom he also made the ages." We believe that the only-begotten Word of God is by nature Lord of all things together with God the Father. Yet he is appointed heir because he became flesh. For it was said to him, as one who had become man like us for our sake: "Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession." Yet the writer says that the ages themselves were made through him, who is God and heir by reason of his humanity, and here the statement refers to the supreme antiquity of the Word. So there is one Christ and Son, the same at once God and [?]

"He is the radiance of his glory and the exact imprint of his substance, and he upholds all things by the word of his power. Having made purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high, having become as much superior to the angels as the name he has inherited is more excellent than theirs." He is the radiance of the glory and the imprint of the substance of God the Father, that is, the only-begotten Son who is from him by nature. In what way, then, having made purification for our sins (plainly, through his own blood), has he sat down at the right hand of the Father? And how is he said to have become superior to the angels, when by nature, and by the preeminence of his divinity, he surpasses all things? It follows that even having become man he surpassed the invisible creation as God, for he is the same one who is the radiance and imprint, and who accomplished the purification of our sins by his own blood. So there is one Christ and Son,

"For he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified all come from one. For this reason he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying: 'I will proclaim your name to my brothers.'" What is holy by nature is not sanctified, because it has no need of sanctification. And what has become holy by participation in another cannot sanctify others. So we must ask how the same one both sanctifies and is sanctified. He sanctifies as God, since the power to sanctify belongs to him as a property of his own nature; but he is sanctified with us, as man. So there is one Christ and Son and Lord, who sanctifies divinely

but is sanctified with us humanly. "Now the main point of what is being said¹ is this: we have such a high priest, who sat down at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens, a minister of the holy places and of the true tabernacle, which the Lord pitched, and not man." If every priest, as the blessed Paul says, is appointed to offer gifts [?]… [Notes: ¹ upon; ² what has been said.]

and sacrifices, then those called to the priesthood do not perform their service to themselves. They perform it rather to God, to whom the reverence of all creation is due. And whoever ministers to God will not stand on equal footing with God, nor bear the glory that befits him alone. How then does Christ, who became our high priest, sit at the right hand of God, and hold the throne of majesty in the heavens, while also being a minister of the holy places and of the true tabernacle above, bringing to himself and to the Father the worship offered by all? So there is one Christ and Son. He sits divinely on the throne of his own Godhead, but he is called priest and minister by reason of the economy, because of his humanity. "Therefore we also, since we have so great a cloud of witnesses surrounding us, should lay aside every weight and the sin that so easily entangles us, and run with endurance the race set before us. Let us look to Jesus Christ, the pioneer and perfecter of faith, who for the joy set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God." If Christ is an ordinary man in the flesh like us, and not truly God, what joy does the writer say was set before him? Or how has he sat down at the right hand of the throne of God? Joy was indeed set before him, for the supreme nature dwells in unending delight. Yet he endured the cross, having made his own a body that could be crucified, and the very one who was crucified has sat down at the right hand of God the Father. So there is one Lord Jesus Christ, crucified humanly but enthroned with the Father divinely. That there is one Son and Lord. From the Gospel according to Matthew. "All things have been handed over to me by my Father. No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him." Since no one knows the Son except the Father alone, how can some set aside the Father's testimony? For at the Jordan he pointed out his own Son, saying: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." But he did not show us his own Word bare. He showed him united to flesh. Nor did he say, "In this one is my Son," but "This is," meaning the one with the flesh. So he is one, both Lord and Son. From the Gospel according to John. "The true light, which enlightens every man, was coming into the world. He was in the world, and the world came into being through him, yet the world did not know him. He came to his own, and his own did not receive him." The evangelist has spoken sufficiently of his divinity. He has said that every man coming into the world is enlightened by the true light, and that the world itself was made through him. Now he says that he came to his own. The Only-begotten came, having become man, as to

his own, and above all to those of the blood of Israel. Since, then, he himself is the true light, through whom all things exist, and he is the one who came with flesh to his own, how can we fail to confess one Christ and Son? "And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we beheld his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth." The Word became flesh: that is, he shared in blood and flesh just as we do, and took hold of the seed of Abraham, so as to be made like his brothers in every respect. If so, how could anyone doubt that he remained the Word even when he had become flesh? For the nature of the Word is unchangeable. And if he has been called our brother, how does he have the glory of the Only-begotten? It follows that even though he became flesh, he is no less God. He is Only-begotten as God, and firstborn by reason of the cross he underwent as man. "John testifies about him and cried out, saying: 'This was he of whom I said, "He who comes after me has come to be ahead of me, because he was before me"'; for from his fullness we have all received." John says of Christ: "He who comes after me" (that is, he who is manifested after me, the one whom John himself plainly proclaimed) "has come to be ahead of me," that is, he holds first place in glory, for as God he was also first in existence. How then is the one who was before him in time also after him? Because the Word was God and became flesh. He has the first place insofar as he is the Word, but the second place according to the flesh. And all the saints have partaken of his fullness. Since only the divine is full, as Scripture says through the voice of Isaiah, it befits him alone to fill others from his own fullness and make them partakers of himself. And Christ has done this. So there is one Son and Lord, the Word from God become flesh, himself at once God and man. The next saying bears the same sense: "This is he of whom I said, 'After me comes a man who has come to be ahead of me, because he was before me.'" For see: he calls him a man, and one who comes after, yet he says that he is first, as God. "For in the beginning was the Word, and God…"

"And John testified, saying: 'I have seen the Spirit descending like a dove from heaven, and it remained on him. I did not know him, but the one who sent me to baptize with water said to me, "The one on whom you see the Spirit descend and remain is the one who baptizes with the Holy Spirit." And I have seen and have testified that this is the Son of God.'" In these words you can see clearly and plainly our Lord Jesus Christ receiving the Spirit humanly, because of the economy with the flesh (for though he was rich, [Note: to accomplish.]

he became poor for our sake), and yet baptizing divinely in the Holy Spirit. For to whom could it belong to bestow the grace of the Spirit, except to the one who is God by nature and in truth? So there is one Christ and Son, and the evangelist will testify to it, saying: "And I have seen and have testified that this is the Son of God." This one, the same [?] whom he beheld receiving the Spirit humanly, he knows as the one who baptizes divinely in the Holy Spirit. "If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things? No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man." How has the Son of Man descended from heaven, when the holy flesh was born of a woman? Because the body belonged to the Word who came down from heaven and who also became Son of Man. So there is one Christ and Son. In this way the properties of the Word became the flesh's own, and the properties of the flesh became the Word's own, sin alone excepted. "And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may have eternal life." The serpents were biting the Israelites in the wilderness, and then the God of all commanded Moses to set up a bronze serpent. "And if a serpent bites a man," he says, "and he looks at the serpent, he shall live." What, then, is the riddle? Why does the one who looks at the serpent [?]? The only-begotten Word of God, who is Life by nature, came to be in our likeness, that is, he became man, and man is wicked, like the serpent. Yet although he became like us, anyone who looks to him conquers death. And what is it to look to him, if not to understand precisely the mystery concerning him? For then one will see him in the likeness of the wicked, that is, of men, yet life-giving as God, and wiping out the bites of the spiritual serpents. So there is one Lord and Son, the same one, both life-giving as God and in the form of the wicked by reason of the economy. "The children, holding palm branches, went out to meet him," it says, "and cried out: 'Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel!'" How then does the sacred Scripture say that he came in the name of the Lord? Suppose it means a mere man in his own right, the one born of the holy Virgin, with God the Word not united to him hypostatically. Then the name of lordship will belong to him just as it does to us, and there will be nothing great about Christ. But if he was foretold to come as Lo- [Notes: him; in him; the serpent; of the wicked; cried aloud; to have come.]

-rd in truth, as is indeed true (for the Only-begotten came into this world not without flesh), then he is one: Lord, Christ and Son by nature and in truth. "And for their sake I sanctify myself, so that they too may be sanctified in truth." Christ sanctifies himself. Does he do so as man, or rather because he is God by nature and has the Holy Spirit as his own? The latter is the truth. Since no man sanctifies himself, and yet Christ sanctifies himself, there is one Son and Lord. He is sanctified humanly, but divinely he sanctifies his own [?] by his own Spirit.

"Now Jesus did many other signs in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book. But these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name." Emmanuel, born of the holy Virgin, has been named Jesus by the voice of the Gospel. Since he himself, and not another, is the Son of God, and the one who believes has eternal life in his name, are they not mad who divide him and claim that the Word from God is one Son and the one from the holy Virgin another? For in these words the evangelist quite clearly knows and proclaims one Jesus Christ only, made of both: the Word from God the Father who shared in blood and flesh just as we do, as it is written. From the Gospel according to Luke. "And while they were there, the days were completed for her to give birth. She gave birth to her firstborn son, wrapped him in swaddling cloths, and laid him in the manger, because there was no place for them in the inn." The holy Virgin bore one only Son, Emmanuel. Why then does it say "her firstborn son"? There were no others after him, for she remained a virgin. The divinely inspired Scripture is pointing something out here. The only-begotten Word of God has been called firstborn because he shared in blood and flesh and partook of the same things just as we do. In this way he became the firstborn among many brothers.
