Yet as God he is worshipped both by us and by the powers above

"And his mother said to him," it says, "'Child, why have you treated us like this? Look, your father and I have been searching for you in anguish.' And he said to them, 'Why were you searching for me? Do you not know that I must be in my Father's house?'" Observe how [Notes: perhaps, of an angel; did you not know.]

he names the Father in heaven as his own Father. If he were a mere man by himself, understood simply as one like us, should he not rather have said, "Did you not know that I must be in the house of the Father of all?" But he makes him his own, for he alone was begotten from him by nature, in a divine way. And the same one, having also become man, has his own Father, and that by nature

"And while he was in one of the cities, there was a man full of leprosy. When he saw Jesus, he fell on his face and begged him, saying, 'Lord, if you are willing, you can make me clean.' And he stretched out his hand and touched him, saying, 'I am willing; be made clean.'" You will marvel at Christ in these words, acting divinely and bodily at the same time. To will is divine; to stretch out the hand is human. So there is one Son, made of both. For even though the Word became flesh, he acts as God with his own flesh, [?] imparting to it the power that comes from himself. "And he said to them, 'How can they say that the Christ is the son of David? For David himself says in the book of Psalms, "The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet." David calls him Lord, so how is he his son?'" You hear how in these words Christ himself seeks to show that, although the Word came from the seed of David according to the flesh, he is even so Lord by nature, as Son and God. "For if he is the son of David," he says, "how does David call him Lord?" In these words he does not deny that he was born of David's seed according to the flesh, nor does he give up being Lord by nature. He says that both belong to him, since he wishes it to be made known that the one is made of both. So there is one Christ, and he is truly Son. That faith is directed to Christ as to God. From the Epistle to the Romans. "Through him we have received grace and apostleship to bring about the obedience of faith among all the nations for the sake of his name, and among them you too are called to belong to Jesus Christ." The nations have been called through faith. Christ was the one proclaimed among them by the holy apostles, and those being initiated practiced their faith not as in a man but as in God. Surely we do not say that the nations, in accepting faith in Christ, were called from one error into another. Rather, they abandoned the falsely named gods and turned at last to the living God. Since, then, the initiators say that they received apostleship for the obedience of faith for the sake of Christ's name, how could he not be God, if faith is directed to him as to God? "For God, whom I serve in my spirit in the gospel of his Son, is my witness that I unceasingly make mention of you, always, in my prayers." Those who serve God do not serve Christ as a God other

than him. Yet Paul says the gospel is Christ's. For Christ is proclaimed to the world as God, even though the Father is God by nature and rules over all. Christ, then, is God, through whom and in whom the Father himself is proclaimed as God, and is honored with the [?] of all

"Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. Through him we have also now obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand, and we boast in the hope of the glory of God." We are justified by believing as in God. If our faith is in Christ Jesus, and through him we have obtained access (for we have been joined to God the Father, Christ having, as it were, raised us up with him), how is he not God, even if according to the flesh he came from the seed of David, as the Scriptures say? "As it is written," he says, "'Behold, I lay in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense, and everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame.'" When the righteous Simeon received the divine infant into his arms, he said to God: "Now, Master, you are dismissing your servant in peace, according to your word; for my eyes have seen your salvation, which you have prepared in the sight of all peoples," and so on. And he added: "Behold, this child is set for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and for a sign that is spoken against." The same one, then, is the stone of stumbling and the rock of offense. Some stumbled against him through disobedience and were broken, but those who embraced faith in him escaped being put to shame. Have we, then, believed as in a man, or as in God? Clearly as in God. So Christ is God, for it was of him that the righteous Simeon spoke the words we have just cited.

Concerning the Jews he says: "For being ignorant of the power and righteousness of God, and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to the righteousness of God. For Christ is the end of the law, bringing righteousness to everyone who believes." Christ is the end of the law, and he is himself righteousness, justifying through faith in him. If the power to justify belongs to God alone as his own, how is Christ not God? "But the righteousness that comes from faith speaks thus: 'Do not say in your heart, "Who will ascend into heaven?"' (that is, to bring Christ down), 'or, "Who will descend into the abyss?"' (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead). But what does it say? 'The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart,' that is, the word of faith that we proclaim. For if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes and is justified, and with the mouth one confesses

…unto salvation. For the Scripture says: "No one who believes in him will be put to shame." If [?] surrounds the [name?] of Christ, and if we who confess his death and resurrection as those of God are saved [?], who is it that dares to say he is not God, if upon him [rests] the salvation of all, [?] the confession of faith in him? For through him and in him the Father himself is also acknowledged by us. "Now to him who is able to strengthen you according to my gospel and the proclamation of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery that was kept silent for long ages but has now been disclosed through the prophetic writings, according to the command of the eternal God, and made known to all the nations for the obedience of faith — to the only wise God, through Jesus Christ, to whom be the glory and the might to the ages of ages. Amen." See, he says plainly that the gospel is the proclamation of Jesus Christ, and that the mystery concerning him was hidden and kept silent for long ages, but has now been revealed to all the nations for the obedience of faith. For the nations have obeyed [?] Christ, delivered from their falsely named worship, and have recognized him as God by nature and in truth. And if God was clearly made known through Jesus Christ, how is the mystery of Christ not great? But if we think of him as simply a man, and not rather as God made man, the mystery is no longer wise [?]. "For I say that Christ became a servant of the circumcision for the sake of God's truth, to confirm the promises made to the fathers, and that the nations might glorify God for his mercy." For it is written: "Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness." And it was said to him: "In you all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed." Paul made this clear to us when he said: "For the promise to Abraham that he would be heir of the world did not come through the law, but through the righteousness of faith." And again: "So then, those who are of faith are blessed together with faithful Abraham." If, therefore, the promises are given to the fathers by God on the basis of faith, Christ has become a servant, that is, a mediator, to confirm the promises given to the fathers by God, that is, justification through faith. Christ has become a servant, then, that is, a mediator — not as one negotiating faith for someone else, but rather for himself, and through himself for the Father. He is therefore God by nature. For blessed Abraham was justified by believing in God; and so

the nations too would be justified in him, following in his footsteps and believing in God, that is, in Christ. From the First Letter to the Corinthians: "And such were some of you; but you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God." If we are justified in the name of Christ, having honoured him as God by our faith and receiving his Spirit, how is Christ not God? From the Second Letter to the Corinthians: "For if someone comes and proclaims another Jesus whom we did not proclaim, or if you receive a different spirit from the one you received, or a different gospel from the one you accepted, you put up with it well enough." Before the time of the incarnation no one is found to have called the Word who is from God "Jesus" or "Christ" — unless by foreknowledge, as one who would be so named in due time, when he also became flesh. So the name "Jesus" was new for him when he became man. Now if he is proclaimed as God, and as being one (for there is no other besides him whom anyone could proclaim), all would be well, and we worship God. But if his measure is only that of humanity, and he has been honoured by a mere union of persons, then the word of our faith has been emptied, for it brings us to a man and not to God. But this is impious. Christ, therefore, is God and Son, since the Word of God became flesh. From the Letter to the Galatians: "I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ, for a different gospel — not that there is another, but there are some who are troubling you and want to pervert the gospel of Christ. But even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be accursed." If the gospel spoken to all the world under heaven through the holy teachers of the mysteries is one, and this is faith in Christ, how could he not be true God, if indeed we must confess that we have been called out of the ancient error to the knowledge of him who is God by nature? And blessed Paul is so bold that he even pronounces angels accursed, should they pervert the gospel of Christ. "But when God, who set me apart from my mother's womb, was pleased to reveal his Son in me, so that I might preach him among the nations, I did not immediately consult with flesh and blood, nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me." For one who had once received initiation and revelation from God had no need of instruction from human beings. But we say this: whom did the Father reveal to blessed Paul, or whom did he command him to preach

among the nations? Was it God the Word, the only-begotten Son, not united to flesh and not having become man in the divine economy? Then how is this true? For he proclaimed one and the same to be at once man and God, calling him Son and Lord Jesus Christ: "Knowing that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, we too have believed in Christ Jesus, so that we might be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law." If believing God has justification as its reward (for so were those before us justified too; for it is written, "Abraham believed God, and his faith was reckoned to him as righteousness"), how is Emmanuel not God, if it is true that by believing in him we are justified? From the Letter to the Ephesians: "In him you also, when you heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, and believed in him, were sealed with the holy Spirit of promise, who is the pledge of our inheritance, for the redemption of God's own possession, to the praise of his glory." One could see many things at once in the meaning of these passages, from which one may learn that Christ is true God, and that the faith of all in him is not faith in simply one of us, but in one Lord and Son and God. For first, he himself is the gospel of salvation, in whom also is our faith — clearly, as in God. Then follows the reward of faith, that is, the Spirit of promise, the pledge of our inheritance; for we have been redeemed to the praise of the glory of Christ. For he saved us not as an ordinary man, but as God who came to be in the flesh for our sake. For in this way we shall be to the praise of his glory. "For this reason I, Paul, the prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles — if indeed you have heard of the stewardship of God's grace that was given to me for you, how the mystery was made known to me by revelation, as I wrote briefly above; by reading which you can perceive my insight into the mystery of Christ." What need would there be of insight, and of revelation from God, for the mystery of Christ to be made known, if he is a man [?]…

[?]: "To me, the very least of all the saints, this grace was given, to preach to the nations the unsearchable riches of Christ, and to bring to light for all what is the stewardship of the mystery hidden from the ages in God, who created all things." "Husbands," he says, "love your wives, just as Christ also loved the Church and gave himself up for her, that he might sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word." What, then, is the word in which we have been cleansed, when our bodies were washed with pure water? Surely it is the one of which the divine Paul says: "This is the word of faith that we proclaim: that if you confess with your mouth Jesus Christ as Lord, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth one confesses unto salvation." If, then, we are saved by confessing Christ in faith, how is he not true God, in whom, when the word of faith comes to be [?], we have been cleansed and sanctified? From the Letter to the Philippians: "What then?" he says. "Only that in every way, whether in pretence or in truth, Christ is proclaimed." Is he, then, proclaimed to the world as a man honoured with grace? Yet the world recognized Christ as God, honouring him with its faith. How then is he not God, who is proclaimed to the world in the glory of the Godhead? "Striving side by side," he says, "for the faith of the gospel, and not frightened in anything by your opponents. This is to them a sign of destruction, but to you of salvation, and that from God. For it has been granted to you on behalf of Christ not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him." If we receive from God, as a gift of grace, the power to believe in Christ, and are not led astray by this, but rather have come to know him who is God by nature and in truth, how could anyone doubt that Christ is God? From the First Letter to Timothy: "The saying is trustworthy and worthy of full acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost. But for this reason I received mercy, that in me first Christ Jesus might display his perfect patience, as an example to those who were to believe in him for eternal life." If Christ saves sinners and is patient with their offences, accepting their repentance, and if all our faith is in him, and through faith in him we have gained eternal life, how would he not be God? For it would fittingly belong to God alone to be able to save the world, that is, those in the world, to be patient with sinners, and to give life through faith in

"And confessedly great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifested in the flesh, vindicated in the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory." Who is the one manifested in the flesh? Is it not clear that it is wholly and in every way the Word who is from God the Father? For thus the mystery of godliness will be great. God was manifested in the flesh, and was seen by angels as he ascended into the heavens; he was proclaimed among the nations through the holy apostles, and was believed on in the world — and not, we say, as simply a man like us, but as God who came to be in the flesh and like us. And he was taken up in glory, that he might hear God the Father saying: "Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet." From the Letter to Titus: "The saying is trustworthy; and I want you to insist on these things, so that those who have believed God may be careful to devote themselves to good works." Have those who believe God, then, not believed in Christ? Yet blessed John is plainly seen saying of him: "But to all who received him he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name." And indeed blessed Paul himself says: "Knowing that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, we too believed in Christ Jesus, so that we might be justified in him." When, therefore, those who bring their faith to Christ are believing in God, how could he not be true God? For the faith is in Christ. From the Gospel according to John: "But to all who received him he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name." He sets down two things at once that are fitting for God. For Christ is received by us in no other way [?]; and that the faith is in him, the passage before us makes clear: "to those," it says, "who believe in his name." And we believe in his name not believing him to be an ordinary man, one of us, but God made man. And to give power to become children of God is not something human, but rather fitting for God and beyond the created order. When, therefore, faith is in him, and he himself gives the grace of adoption, how is Christ not God? "This, the first of his signs, Jesus did at Cana in Galilee, and manifested his glory; and his disciples believed in him." When the sign had taken place, then, and Christ had manifested his glory, in whom, and as what, did the blessed disciples believe? In a holy man [?]? Yet before the sign they had followed him, marvelling at him as a holy man; but through the sign they beheld

[?] him possessing a power and authority beyond that of man. Therefore they believed as in God. It should be noted that many of the saints also did many extraordinary things, and they were marvelled at, but no one believed in them. The following passage would bear the same sense: "Now when he was in Jerusalem at the Passover, during the feast, many believed in his name when they saw the signs that he was doing." "For God did not send his Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him. Whoever believes in him is not judged; but whoever does not believe has been judged already, because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God." If faith in the Son is the way of salvation, how then do we believe in him? Or how shall we escape the penalty of being judged [?]? By accepting him as a man, and nothing else besides? Then how shall we not be worshipping a man? No — we believe in him as in God; for this is the truth. Who, then, dares to say that he is not God in truth, faith in whom has justified the whole world under heaven? "So the father knew that it was at that hour when Jesus had said to him, 'Your son lives'; and he himself believed, and his whole household." Christ raised the official's son from the dead, saying to him: "Go; your son lives." Then he believed with all his household. Did the official, then, through so great an authority, one befitting God, believe in him as in a man? Or did he recognize him as being God by nature, giving life with authority to whomever he would, and to him alone [?]? It is clear that he believed in him as God. "Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life." God the Father sent us his own Son from heaven, "so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life." How, then, does he say here that the one who believes him who sent him has eternal life? In whom [?], then, is the faith? Is it as in two gods, the Father and the Son? Far from it! It is as in one true God. Therefore, if anyone believes in Christ, he has believed in God; and if he believes in God the Father, he will also have believed in the one Lord Jesus Christ. "Jesus answered and said to them: This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent." If we accomplish what pleases God by believing in Christ (for the Father truly sent him into the world when he became man like us), how could he not be true God? For otherwise believing in him would not be the work of God. "But Jesus cried out and said: Whoever believes in me does not believe in me, but in him who sent me.

And whoever sees me sees him who sent me." Then he adds to these words: "I have not spoken on my own authority; but the Father who sent me has himself given me a commandment, what to say and what to speak." When, therefore, in accordance with the Father's commandments — even though he speaks as a man — he refers faith in himself to the one who sent him, and whoever sees him sees the one who sent him, who dares to say that he is not God, and that truly so? Similar to this is: "Believe in God, believe also in me." From the Gospel according to Luke: "Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth?" When Christ comes from heaven, what kind of faith will he look for in us [?]? For if he wishes to be believed in as a man like us, who has ever disbelieved him? For the Jews accused him, saying: "Why do you, being a man, make yourself God?" And the Greeks, hearing of a cross and death, are disposed [?] as if toward an ordinary man, one of us. What faith, then, does he seek, if not clearly the faith proclaimed by those who spoke of God, who became eyewitnesses and ministers of the Word? John, then, said: "The Word became flesh." And he became flesh while remaining God. This, then, is the faith in us [?] from him [?]…
End of the first oration addressed by Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, to the most pious ladies.

SECOND ORATION OF CYRIL, ARCHBISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA, ADDRESSED TO THE MOST PIOUS PRINCESSES, ON THE RIGHT FAITH. 1. To those who perform the sacred service of the divine and heavenly proclamation, the God of all gives this command through the voice of Isaiah: "Go up onto a high mountain, you who bring good news to Zion; lift up your voice with strength,

you who bring good news to Jerusalem; lift it up, do not be afraid." For my part, I say that those appointed to the sacred ministry, who speak of the mystery of Christ, the Saviour of us all, must not have a mind that is cast down and grovelling on the ground, overcome by sloth and shrinking in timidity. Rather, their mind should stand firmly on high, set as it were upon the mountains, and so be eager to gaze on the surpassing beauty of the doctrines of truth; and they should speak their words with boldness, even if those they are initiating into the mysteries are hard and difficult to lead, like arrogant and unbridled horses — of whom blessed David himself says somewhere to the God of all: "With bit and bridle you will bind the jaws of those who do not draw near to you." But if one must take on even people of such a mind, how would it not be among the most perilous of things to choose silence, and not to pour into your pious ears again and again, like a sweet and life-giving stream, the knowledge of the sacred Scriptures? This God promised us long ago, saying through the voice of Isaiah: "And draw water with joy from the springs of salvation." By the springs of salvation we mean the holy prophets, evangelists and apostles, who pour forth for the world the saving word that is from above and from heaven, the Holy Spirit supplying them, and so gladden the whole world under heaven. Come, then, let us lower our minds into the depths of the thoughts they contain, and draw from there the discovery of the truth. Farmers, at the right seasons, cut the most fragrant flowers from the fields, place them in baskets, and carry them to their masters; and these receive them most gladly and delight in the fruits of the season. But we who have taken up the calling of teaching bring, as from the field of the God-inspired Scripture, not a display of quickly fading flowers, but rather words and the mystagogy that comes through the Spirit, which has the unfading beauty of devotion to Christ and breathes forth most richly the fragrance of his mystery. For it is written: "We are the aroma of Christ to

2. I come, then, to dedicate this discourse to you, most pious princesses; I have composed it on the right and blameless faith that you should hold toward our Lord Jesus Christ. For it is especially fitting for you, who are so holy and so dearly loved by God, to wear the crown of love for Christ together with the supreme glories of royalty. Indeed, it already rests upon your celebrated heads, and the God of all makes you radiant with unending renown. So that you may shine still more brightly, holding in your minds the precise and unadulterated knowledge of the mystery of Christ, I have composed this little treatise, through all

[?]… showing that, just as there is one God the Father, from whom are all things, so also there is one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things; and surely the Holy Spirit is also entirely one. "And those who divide the one Christ and Son and Lord into two sons we will not tolerate, since we have come to know right belief. For we do not say that the Son begotten before every age from the essence of God the Father is one, and the one who in the last times came to be from a woman, came to be under the law, is another; but that he is one and the same, both before his coming together with flesh and true union, and still after it. For the Son who is by nature from God the Father, having taken to himself a body endowed with soul and mind, was born according to the flesh through the holy Virgin and Theotokos Mary. He was not changed into flesh (God forbid!), but rather took it on, and did not neglect to be God; for even so he has remained Master of all things." 3. This is what we have been taught to believe. For the words of the saints furnish us with wise precepts: that we must cherish above all what seems good to the Holy Scriptures, and examine closely the truth in the divine doctrines, applying a subtle mind to what is said about Christ, "casting down reasonings and every high thing that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and taking every thought captive into obedience to him." For it stands firm and is agreed by all that the Word who is from him by nature, existing in the form and equality of God and the Father, "did not count being equal to God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, coming to be in the likeness of men; and being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to death, even death on a cross." Since that is so, it is altogether necessary that whoever aims to discern well the force of what is written about him should have a mind full of God-loving thought, so that the same one may be recognized as at once both God and man: possessing his being God unimpaired (for the nature of the Word is unchangeable), and not refusing the measure of the emptying. For he who for our sake, in the economy, endured a voluntary emptying does not blush in the least at his own conditions. He must therefore be seen as distinguished by the dignities of the Godhead, and yet, because of his humanity, not wholly free of our lowliness, since the economy demands this. For if the Word, being God, became flesh, that is, man (in the sense of "I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh"), let no one be disturbed if the divinely inspired Scripture says something about him that befits a human being. Let one rather contemplate his trans- [?]

-cendent glory, which comes from the power and pre-eminence that befits God and is highest of all. 4. The passages most likely to unsettle the minds of the simpler, these I shall try to make clear as far as possible and as well as I can, setting beside each passage the solution that suffices to clarify it, with God once more directing our path in this too. "For he gives a word to those who preach the good news with great power," as the divine Psalmist says. In the treatise we composed for the holy virgins we cited as many as possible of the more readily understood passages, which present no difficulty for comprehension; in the present one, however, we have taken up the more obscure ones. For it was necessary, truly necessary, that your God-loving Majesty should know these and not be ignorant of those, so that through both the correct knowledge might, like a light, take up its dwelling in your most pious minds. My aim in interpreting each passage is to be as brief as possible, and the passage about the emptying will be placed before the others. Yet this must be understood: whenever we name Christ Jesus, we ought to understand the Word from God the Father, made man and incarnate.

…"the head is Christ; and the head of the woman is the man; and the head of Christ is God." "The first man was from the earth, earthy" (that is, Adam); "the second is from heaven" (clearly Christ); "but just as we have borne the image of the earthy, let us also bear the image of the heavenly," as it is written. So the first head of our race, that is, its beginning, was the one from the earth and earthy. But since Christ has been named the second Adam, he has been appointed head, that is, beginning, of those who are refashioned through him into his likeness, unto incorruption, through sanctification in the Spirit. So he is our beginning, that is, our head, inasmuch as he has appeared as man. Yet he himself, as God by nature, has as his head the Father in heaven; for the Word, being God, was begotten from him by nature. That "head" signifies "beginning" is confirmed, for those of doubtful mind, by the fact that the man is called the head of the woman; for she was taken from him. There is therefore one Christ and Son and Lord, who as God by nature has the Father in heaven as his head, but who has become head for us because of his kinship with us according to the flesh. 6. "For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, he became poor for your sake, so that by his poverty you might become rich." Observe, I pray, how very clearly these words show the pre-eminence of the divine and pure nature, the

lowliness of the measures of humanity, and besides this the coming together of both into unity, when the Only-begotten lowered himself to this. For no word could express the wealth of the Godhead, while humanity is very poor: all that it has is given by God and comes from above, and before all else its very being, for it was called into existence by God, not having existed before. But he who was rich as God willingly became poor and became like us, so that henceforth human nature, having come to be in Christ amid the heights of the divine pre-eminence, might put away the shame of its poverty. "For God the Father raised us up together in Christ and seated us together in the heavenly places," as it is written. But we would not have come to be there, had not he who was rich as God put on the nature that is poor. For a man who is by nature very poor could hardly become poor. This would more fittingly befall the one who is truly rich, that is, the Word from God the Father, when he became like us. Therefore Christ and Son is one. 7. "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us; for it is written: Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree." Since the letter of the law declared accursed the one living in transgression and sin, he who knew no sin, that is, Christ, submitted to the penalty. He endured an unjust sentence and suffered what befits those under a curse, so that, being of equal worth to all, by dying for all he might cancel the charges arising from the disobedience of all, and purchase the world under heaven with his own blood. He would not have been one who was of equal worth to all, if he had simply been a man. But if he is understood as God made man, suffering in his own flesh, then the whole creation is little in comparison with him, and the death of one flesh suffices as the ransom of the world under heaven; for it was the own flesh of the Word who sprang from God the Father. 8. "But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honour because of the suffering of death, so that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone." Now the divine Paul, speaking of Christ, the Saviour of us all, says: "And when he brings the firstborn into the world, he says: Let all the angels of God worship him." And again: "He, being the radiance of his glory and the imprint of his being, and upholding all things by the word of his power, having made purification for our sins, sat down at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty on high, having become as much superior to the angels as the name he has inherited is more excellent than theirs. For to which of the angels did he ever say: You are my Son, today I have begotten you?" So when the Only-begotten became firstborn, even among

many brothers, then, he says, he was brought into the world; for according to his own nature, as God, he was outside creation. Then too he says he was made lower than the angels, although he had obtained a name more excellent than theirs. For "angel" signifies ministry and points to a servant's rank: "For they are sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation." But "Son" signifies an existence from the Father that is essential and natural, since we believe that the begetting truly took place. How, then, was he made lower than the angels, he who is worshipped by them and sits with the Father? The reason is plain. He descended into the measures of humanity, and, taking a body that by nature could die and making it his own, he willingly suffered in it. And he is crowned with the highest glories because of the suffering, since through it he abolished death and rendered corruption powerless, being himself incorruption and life. So when Scripture names Jesus and says that he was made lower than the angels, we do not understand a man taken separately and individually, but the Only-begotten himself, yielding his superiority to the holy angels in the economy, because he truly became man and so was surpassed by their pre-eminence. The holy angels' pre-eminence lies in this: they are outside the flesh and superior to death; and the Son came to be in these conditions through his voluntary emptying. Yet he who was made a little lower than the angels because of the measure of humanity, existing in the pre-eminence of the Godhead, is worshipped by them and is seated on thrones which they surround, ever glorifying him and naming him Lord of the powers. 9. "Since, therefore, the children share in blood and flesh, he himself likewise partook of the same, so that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and set free those who through fear of death were subject to slavery all their lives." By "the children" he clearly means us who are on earth, as is sung in the Psalms as if from the person of God: "I said: You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High." For as far as it depended on God's will and on the gentleness inherent in his nature, we would all be children, and no one would have slipped away from intimacy with him. But, as David says, "we die like men, and fall like one of the rulers," subjecting our own mind to the passions of the flesh. How, then, have we come to share in blood and flesh? The human soul, though its nature differs from that of the flesh, by being joined with it in union, produced the one rational living being, that is, man. In the same way, then, the Word of God too, uniting himself ineffably to flesh endowed with a soul, and not to soulless flesh as some say,

partook of blood and flesh like us, clearly through birth from a woman. There is therefore one Lord Jesus Christ, since the Word of God united the human to himself, yet even so remained what he was. And if he himself, as life and God, destroyed the power of death, it is fitting that what suffered death be understood as his own, so that he may be said, having himself risen, to have abolished corruption and to have passed on the grace of incorruption to our whole race. "For as in Adam we all die, so also in Christ we shall all be made alive." And again: "For as death came through a man, so also the resurrection of the dead came through a man." But since trampling down death lies beyond the measures of humanity as we understand it, we say that the Word of God became man like us by union, or communion, with flesh and blood, yet even so remained superior to death; for he was God in flesh. 10. "For surely he does not take hold of angels, but he takes hold of the seed of Abraham. Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect, so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest in the things of God, to make expiation for our sins. For because he himself suffered when he was tempted, he is able to help those who are tempted." We say that the Word of God takes hold of the seed of Abraham, for according to the flesh he sprang from the Jews, and he was made like his brothers in every respect, in that he consented to take the form of a servant and to come to be in the likeness of men, as blessed Paul says. For thus he has been called Son of Man and has become a brother to those of the seed of Abraham, that is, to those in blood and flesh. What, then, is the reason for this? "So that he might become," it says, "a merciful and faithful high priest in the things of God." Christ became a merciful high priest for us, because the letter of the law condemned sinners and passed the sentence that those who dishonoured the divine commandment must be punished: "For anyone who has set aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses." But Christ justifies in faith and releases the weak from the ancient charges. So he has become a merciful high priest, no longer allowing the severities of the law to prevail. 11. And he is faithful because he is abiding and everlasting, and worthy of trust for what has been promised. For, as the divine Paul himself again says somewhere about the priests under the law: "The former priests were many in number, because they were prevented by death from continuing; but he, because he remains forever, holds a priesthood that does not pass away. Hence he is able to save completely those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to intercede for

them." Observe that he became high priest not to condemn sinners but rather to make expiation for their sins. And what might be the manner of the temptation and of the sacrifice? "For because he himself suffered when he was tempted," it says, "he is able also to help those who are tempted." For he held firm when tempted and endured the cross. And the Son offered himself as a spotless victim to God the Father, so that through his own flesh he might help those who struggle and are tempted. "For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified." He himself, then, became high priest according to his humanity, although in a divine way he receives sacrifices from all. He himself is the sacrifice, according to the flesh. He himself is the one who makes expiation for our sins, according to the power of the Godhead. Therefore there is one Lord Jesus Christ. 12. "You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, for salvation is from the Jews." Someone might perhaps say that worshipping is unfitting for the divine and supreme nature of the Word. How, then, if Christ is truly God, is he seen to have ranked himself among those who must worship? What do we say to this? If we believed that the Word who came forth from God the Father had come into this world in bare Godhead, the thing would be altogether unfitting for him; for he is worshipped rather than himself worshipping another. But if, having taken the form of a servant and not disdaining the measure of a humanity that worships, he has been called Son of Man, then the worship will belong to the economy, and will befit the measures of the emptying rather than the nature of the Word taken by itself alone. Otherwise, how is salvation from the Jews? For no one would say that he is from the Jews insofar as he is understood to be, and is, the Word; but rather insofar as he has become a brother to those in flesh and blood, through taking hold of the seed of Abraham. So Christ is one, even if he is said to worship on account of his humanity, although he is worshipped as God by all creation. 13. "Yet a little while I am with you, and then I go to him who sent me." For where is the Word of God not, if he fills all things by the nature of the Godhead? How, then, is he sent by the Father? And how does he go to him? He is sent, then, in a human way, according to the manner and meaning of a mission, to proclaim release to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind. But he goes to God the Father no longer in the same manner, but as one who has ascended into heaven, as it were, in the body, so that on our behalf he might appear [?: authority … according to … from the body]

before the face of the Father, as it is written. And if "was sent" is also taken of the Word himself, let no one be vexed. For it is the custom of the divinely inspired Scripture sometimes to use such expressions too, without subjecting the divine and transcendent nature to places and circumscriptions (for it knows that nature to be incorporeal, beyond all limits, and far from being conceived as in a place); rather, it tries by human expressions to make plain things that surpass our understanding. Thus the Saviour himself also said that he would send the Paraclete to us, although the Holy Spirit fills all things: "For the Spirit of the Lord," it says, "has filled the world." 14. "When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am." Blessed John, explaining the causes of the Jews' madness against Christ, says: "For this reason the Jews persecuted Christ, because he was not only breaking the sabbath but was also calling God his own Father, making himself equal to God." And somewhere he also presents them impiously saying: "It is not for a good work that we are stoning you, but for blasphemy, because you, being a man, make yourself God." Their faith in him, then, was unacceptable: they thought him to be simply and merely a man, not knowing that the Word, being God, took hold of the seed of Abraham and shared in blood and flesh like us. Yet he did not cease to be God, for he is unchangeable by nature and ever the same. "When, therefore," he says, "you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am." For he was crucified in a human way, but came back to life in a divine way, and through the resurrection it was believed that he is God and truly the Son of God. And if we believe that he did not raise someone else but rather was himself raised, then, because of the economy, it is altogether necessary that what suffered death be understood as his own body, so that he too may be said to have risen, although he is immortal by nature as God. For it is by proclaiming the death of one Christ and Son, and confessing his resurrection, that we are justified through faith. So the same one, being the one and only Christ Jesus, is said to have died in a human way according to the flesh, but to have been raised fittingly [?]

15. "The Jews once came to Christ and said: How long will you keep us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly. Jesus answered them: I told you, and you do not believe. The works that I do in the name of my Father, these ¹ divine. ² in a divine way [?]

bear witness about me." What, then, do they say even to this, those who ignorantly divide the one Lord Jesus Christ into a pair of sons and into two Christs? About whom did the Jews say, "If you are the Christ, tell us plainly"? And who is the one who says, "The works that I do in the name of my Father, these bear witness about me"? Whose own Father do we say God is? Is he the Father of the one from a woman, understood separately and individually, or of the Only-begotten? Yet the power to accomplish the works of the Godhead could hardly befit a human nature; far from it. But since Christ fulfilled the works of the Father, he would not be understood as a mere man, but rather as God in blood and flesh, remaining what he was. For being such, he will work equally with his own Begetter; and no one of sound mind would find fault with the account of the mystery.

16. "And the child grew and became strong in spirit, being filled with wisdom; and the grace of God was upon him." And again: "Jesus advanced in stature and wisdom and grace with God and men." We say that our Lord Jesus Christ is one, and attribute to him both the human things and those befitting God. So we affirm that it truly befits the measures of the emptying for him to receive bodily growth, and indeed to grow strong as the parts of the body gradually matured. The same holds for his very appearing to be filled with wisdom, since the manifestation of the wisdom within him advanced most fittingly, as if keeping pace with the progress of the body's age. These things, as I said, would befit the economy in the flesh and the measures of lowliness. But to the nature of the Word, on the other hand, it would befit always to be perfect and to be wisdom itself. His, therefore, in a human way, is whatever happens to be lowly, as belonging to the emptying; and his likewise, in a divine way, are the things befitting God. For the manner and meaning of the economy in the flesh know him as being both like us and above us: surpassing the measures of creation as God, yet in a certain way all but inferior to himself, inasmuch as he appeared as man. For where would be the humiliation he willingly endured, if he refused human things? Yet the nature of the Word is not understood to be in them; rather, he makes them his own together with his own flesh, just as, of course, he does hunger and thirst and being said to be tired from the journey. So when you hear, "And the child grew and became strong in spirit, being filled with wisdom," accept the mystery as a vindication of the economy in the flesh. For that he was God in flesh the blessed evangelist himself assures us, saying, "For the grace of God was upon him." He is not said to have the grace of God as though he had grace from another God, but because the child had grace such as befits God. For the Word both was and is God, even when he appeared in flesh, that is, as a man like us. And if he should be said to have grace,

…that he advanced in grace with God and men, there is nothing unfitting in this, since the Father himself approved the economy, and approved him as he made the things of the flesh his own, because this was both fitting to the mystery and useful.

XVII. "But of that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels of heaven nor the Son, but only the Father."

"If," they say, "you have resolved to confess one Christ, the Word of God incarnate, that is, made man, how was he ignorant of the day of the consummation?" We reply that to be ignorant of the mysteries hidden in God, if it should so happen, is neither unusual nor in any other way unfitting for a creature. "For who has known the mind of the Lord?" as it is written. And if the Son is said to have been made a little lower than the angels, clearly inasmuch as he became man, although in his divinity he is beyond all creation, what wonder is it if he is said, together with the angels, not to know the mystery hidden in God, although he is God's wisdom and power? Besides, how could the Wisdom of the Father be ignorant of what is hidden in him? And if the Spirit is said to search all things, even the depths of God, and the Spirit is Christ's, how could he himself be ignorant of what his own Spirit knows exactly? So although he is said to be ignorant in a human way, he knows in a divine way. Indeed, when he asked, "Where has Lazarus been laid?", as one permitted not to know in his humanity, he acted divinely, raising him from the dead. Assigning, then, the human things to the economy in the flesh, let us piously reserve the things befitting God for the Word who sprang from God and became as we are.

XVIII. "And Jesus cried out with a loud voice: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"

Are we then to say that the Word from God the Father himself needed help from above? Yet how could this be anything but utterly foolish? For he rules over all things together with God the Father; he makes the heavens firm by his own Spirit, and he is called Lord of hosts, and truly so. Was he weak, then, against the plots of the Jews, and was the hand of those who crucified him too strong for him to resist? Yet the prophet Isaiah says: "If all the nations are reckoned as a drop from a bucket and as the tipping of a scale, and shall be reckoned as spittle, to whom have you likened the Lord? And with what likeness have you compared him?" We should also bear in mind that the servants of the synagogue of the Jews were there, with the cohort of soldiers, and the traitor at their head. And when they sought to seize him, he went to meet them and said, "Whom are you seeking?" And they answered him,

"Jesus of Nazareth." Then the Saviour said to them, "I am he." And they drew back and fell to the ground. How then could he be weak who by his voice alone exposed the weakness of those plotting against him? What then does he mean when he says, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" We say, then, that when our forefather Adam trampled on the commandment given him and disregarded the divine law, human nature was in some sense forsaken by God; because of this it became accursed and was held fast by death. But when the only-begotten Word of God came among us to refashion what had suffered this into incorruption, and took hold of the seed of Abraham and was made like his brethren, it was necessary that, along with that ancient curse and the corruption that had been brought in, the forsakenness which human nature had endured from the beginning should also come to an end. So, as one of the forsaken, since he too shared in blood and flesh just as we do, he says, "Why have you forsaken me?" This was plainly the act of one undoing the forsakenness that had befallen us, and, as it were, entreating the Father in his own person, and calling him to show favour toward us as toward himself, the first; for Christ has become for us both the beginning and the provider of every good. So even if he is said to receive something in a human way from the Father, he procured this for our nature, while he himself was full and lacked nothing whatever, as

XIX. "Let each of you have this mind among yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus, who, being in the form of God, did not count being equal with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men; and being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also highly exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father."

See how clearly he says that God the Word, who is in the form of God the Father and equal to him, did not count being equal with God a thing to be grasped, but rather emptied himself of his own will, taking the form of a servant and being made in the likeness of men. And he adds that he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross. If, then, the one and only Christ and Lord is to be divided into two Christs and sons, and, as some think, the Word of God honoured the man born of the woman with equality in his own dignities, and joined him to himself after the manner of [?]

authority and by sharing with him the name of sonship, as though he were a different Son in his own right beside him, then who is it who emptied himself? Or in what way has he been emptied? For if, as they say, it is the man from the woman, considered in his own right, who is said to have undergone this, how, or in what way, has he been emptied? And how did he descend into humiliation, when he had been raised to equality with God the Word in the manner of dignity, that is, of authority, and had this conjunction with him? But if the emptying is said of God the Word himself, again considered separately and apart as Son, how has he been emptied by honouring another, as they claim, and clothing him with his own dignities? And in what way has he been humbled who gave the height of his own glory to the one joined to him? For if they should say that in glorifying another he himself undergoes humiliation, that is, emptying, then, it seems, there would be nothing absurd in thinking that by insulting another he is exalted. So they all but force us toward a necessary, and indeed a true, conclusion: that what is emptied is that which is full; and that what comes to be in the form of a servant is not that which is a servant by nature, but that which is beyond the measures of servitude; and that what comes to be in the likeness of men is that which was not so by nature before it came to be. And since it is the exalted one who is humbled, we believe that the Word of God himself came to be in these things in a human way, by his own will, for our sake, while remaining in a divine way in the heights of his own pre-eminence. For this reason he is said also to have been highly exalted and to have received the name above every name, to be worshipped by all, and to be called "Lord" to the glory of God the Father. For although he existed in the pre-eminence of the Father and in ineffable heights, since he lowered himself into emptying, he is said to have been humbled, taking the form of a servant; and he went up again into his own riches, having risen above the poverty of the nature united to him, clearly the human nature. For this reason he is said to receive in a human way what always and inalienably belongs to him, namely, to be God and Lord of all. And if it is glorious for the Father to have his own Son as Lord of all, how is it not true to say that, even when he had taken the form of the servant, there was kept for him once again his freedom and the surpassing dignity of lordship and authority over all?

XX. "Giving thanks to the Father, who has made us fit for a share in the inheritance of the saints in light; who has delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love, in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins; who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation; for in him all things were created, in heaven and on earth,

visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers; all things were created through him and for him; and he is before all things, and in him all things hold together. And he is the head of the body, the Church; he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in all things he might have the pre-eminence; for in him it pleased all the fullness to dwell, and through him to reconcile all things to himself, having made peace through the blood of his cross, whether things on earth or things in heaven."

He calls the Son begotten from God by nature, that is, God the Word, the image of the invisible God; and he says that through him all things were brought into being, whether visible or invisible, in heaven and on earth; and that he is before all things ("For in the beginning was the Word"), and that he is the creator of the ages and has an existence older than all time. Yet he says that he who is such by his own nature was given by the Father as head of the body, the Church, and that he is the firstborn from the dead. How then is he who is eternally God the Word, in whom all things hold together, said to have become the firstborn of the dead and the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, unless the body he took is truly his own? When that body suffered death, he himself would be understood to have suffered, and what happened has a reasonable explanation in itself; for it was what was his own that suffered. Thus he is understood as the firstborn from the dead, although he is immortal by nature and is himself called Life. So when he was given as head of the body, the Church, having lowered himself into emptying, he is then also said to have died in a human way for our sake, he who as God cannot suffer death.

XXI. Since the blessed Paul says that all the fullness dwelt in him, some might perhaps say: "See, he knows another Christ in his own right, the man from the woman, in whom the Word, as another Christ beside him and in his own right, that is, the Spirit, dwelt as the fullness of the Godhead bodily." To such objections we reply that the Spirit-bearer knows nothing of two Christs, but proclaims one, just as he proclaims one Father. "For to us," he says, "there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and we for him; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him." Come then, let us examine the force of what has been said, putting it to the touchstone. He says that the image of the invisible God, through whom and in whom are all things, the Son who is before the ages, the one who holds all things together, was given to the Church as head, and indeed that he became the firstborn from the dead. But since he is immortal by nature, we must surely say that the Word from God the Father was brought into a union with our humanity that was both economic and true, and that in this way one Christ was revealed to us, the same being at once God and man. In whom, then, did

the fullness of the Godhead dwell bodily? To suppose that this took place in the nature of the Word on its own and in isolation is utterly foolish, for it would amount to saying that the Only-begotten dwelt in himself. But since we believe that the Word became flesh, not by any transformation or change, but rather that he dwelt among us and made his own temple the body truly united to him, possessed of a rational soul, it is pious to say this: that the divine Paul, indicating to us the indwelling of the Word in the holy flesh, that is, a true union, says that all the fullness of the Godhead dwelt in him, not by participation or by relation, that is, as by a gift of grace, but bodily, which is to say essentially; just as it might be said of a man that his spirit dwells in him, though it is not something other than him. Often, when only one person is concerned, a form of speech implying two persons is used, and this in no way wrongs the truth. For example, it is said of God by the inspired Scripture: "He who forms the spirit of man within him." Yet surely it is clear to everyone that no one would think, in the case of man, of his spirit as something other than him, formed within him? And somewhere the blessed David also says: "By night I communed with my heart, and my spirit was troubled." Who, then, is it who communes with his heart, and whose own spirit is troubled [?]? We should not, therefore, be over-fussy about forms of speech, but should rather look to the very natures of the things, and, guided by them, make our way to the truth itself.

On the obedience of Christ. "Therefore, as through one trespass condemnation came to all men, so also through one act of righteousness justification of life came to all men. For as through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous."

Since human nature had been condemned to the curse and the sentence of death through the disobedience of the first-formed man, it had to recover once more what it had been in the beginning, by giving a wholly blameless display of obedience. But this was already far and away beyond the measures of humanity, for no one is pure from sins. Having once fallen into transgression, mingled with weaknesses from within, perceiving in its own flesh the origin of wickedness, and feeling the law of sin raging, how could it possibly escape altogether? "For the mind of the flesh," he says, "is utter enmity toward God; for it does not submit to the law of God, nor indeed

can it." Most skilfully, then, God the Father, summing up all things in Christ, and in his great gentleness bringing about for human nature its return, that is, its restoration, to what it had been, "sent forth his Son, born of a woman," so that, taking a body like ours and making it his own, he who knew no sin might be found as a man on earth, and so, having become obedient in all things to God the Father, might justify human nature in himself and rescue it from the bonds of death, crowned by God the Father with the leaves of sinlessness. For it would be absurd that we should become heirs of the sentence passed on the first man, who plunged us into corruption through his disobedience, yet should have no share in the righteousness of the second, who brings us back to life through his complete obedience. So when the sacred Scripture says that many have been justified through the obedience of one, we do not say that simply one man like us was taken up for this purpose, but rather the Only-begotten made man, who became obedient to the Father for our sake. "For he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth," as it is written.

XXIII. "For I tell you that Christ became a servant of the circumcision for the sake of God's truth, to confirm the promises made to the fathers, and that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy."

The divine Paul said that the promises given to the fathers belonged to the Jews. And the blessed prophets had cried out beforehand concerning Christ that he would be the expectation of the nations. So our Lord Jesus Christ, consenting to the will of the Father, became a servant to the circumcision, that is, to the Jews, to confirm what had been promised to the fathers (for it had been said, "The righteous shall live by faith"), and to those from the Gentiles he became a spiritual and life-giving blessing, so that they too, having received mercy through faith, might glorify God. But although he became a servant in a human way, he is nonetheless preached as God both to those of the circumcision and to those from the Gentiles. For they have been called to life believing in Christ, not as in simply one man like us, but as in God; and they do not confess that the Word from God exists apart from flesh, that is, from humanity, but worship him as incarnate and made man.

XXIV. "This is the word of faith which we preach," the blessed Paul declares, "that if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved." How then could he be said to have been raised from the dead,

although he is immortal by nature as God, unless one first accepts the teaching about the incarnation and is convinced that he made his own a body that by nature dies? In it he endured death in a human way, but came back to life in a divine way, as incorruption and life.

XXV. "For the weapons of our warfare are not fleshly, but mighty before God for the pulling down of strongholds, casting down reasonings and every high thing that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and taking every thought captive to the obedience of Christ."

The warfare of the saints is not coarse and bodily, but rather subtle and spiritual. For they strive [?] to win glory not by wielding fleshly weapons, nor by using the points of spears or the good aim of arrows, but fitted out with the weapons of truth, standing up spiritually and with great vigour against those who wish to counterfeit it and who twist the correctness of the divine doctrines toward whatever they have thoughtlessly decided. So the weapons of the saints are not fleshly, but rather mighty before God. For they cast down reasonings that carry us off into outlandish notions. And as though these were some accursed barbarians who had resolved to contend against the king's glory, they hasten to put them out of the way. And if anyone lifts up on high the horn of those who are accustomed to speak wickedness against God, they all but burn him up with thoughts that lead to correctness, turning him toward what is straight and setting him upon the words of truth. It would, then, be the work of a skill truly befitting the saints, and pleasing to God, always to [?] by means of the teaching of the economy whatever seems to be set against the glory of Christ. For although the Word was God, in the form of the Father and equal to him, he lowered himself into emptying and became obedient unto death. We must therefore deftly turn every thought around and, as it were, take it captive to obedience to him. For if anything human is also said of him, the lowliness belonging to humanity would in no way wrong the nature of the Word, if he is believed to have become man like us; and not by casting off his being God, but by assuming what is human while remaining God, and becoming obedient unto death according to the flesh.

XXVI. "Therefore, holy brothers, partakers of a heavenly calling, consider the apostle and high priest of our confession, Jesus, who was faithful to him who appointed him, as Moses also was in all his house. For he has been counted worthy of more glory than Moses, inasmuch as the builder of the house has more honour than the house. For every house is built by someone, but he who built all things is God. And Moses was faithful in all his house as a servant, for a testimony of the things that were to be spoken; but Christ as a Son over his own house, whose house we are."

Jesus became the apostle and high priest of our confession from

God the Father, that is, the Word from God appeared as man; for it was then that he was also given the name Jesus by the voice of the angel. The name and the function of priesthood and of apostleship are a very small thing for the nature of the Word; yet they would not be unsuited to the measures of humanity. For as he himself says somewhere, "The Son did not come to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many." To be served by creation would befit him, and quite reasonably, as God and Master, who has under his feet everything that has come into being. But to serve is a human thing; yet in so far as it belongs to the teaching of the economy in the flesh, it is not unfitting for one who has wholly lowered himself to human things. Observe how he acts as priest in a human way, and has been appointed mediator between God and men, for every priest is a mediator; yet he does not offer the sacrifice in the manner of one of our priests, as a servant, having himself no part in receiving it; rather, he performs it for himself, and through himself and in himself for the Father. For he offers in sacrifice our confession, that is, the faith, which we are rightly accustomed to make, saying: "We believe in one God, the Father almighty; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, his Son; and in the Holy Spirit." So, although he is said to act as priest in a human way, he himself nevertheless receives the sacrifice in a divine way, being one and the same, at once God and man. He is called faithful because he is always able to save those who draw near to God through him. And the Father himself is also called faithful. When he is compared in some way with the ministry of Moses in respect of his humanity, one may learn, and without much sweat, how great a pre-eminence he has in respect of his being God, by reflecting that the one was faithful as a household servant in the house, the other as Master over his own house; and that Emmanuel is the builder and maker of the house, whose house we are. And the difference between the Maker and what is made is beyond comparison, as is that between the Master by nature and what is truly a servant and understood as subordinate.

XXVII. "For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me. And this is the will of him who sent me, that of all that he has given me I should lose nothing, but should raise it up on the last day."

He says that he came down from heaven and was sent by God the Father, although he fills all things. In this, I think, he is showing and making clear to all that the Word, being God, lowered himself [?] economically into humanity for our sake; and not at all by letting go of his being God by nature, but rather by assuming the servant.

[?] ...was not, so that, though he gave over to death for a short time the body united to him and made his own, he might lose none of those given to him, but rather save them and raise them up on the last day. So when he says that he does the will of the Father, and not at all his own, he exposes the folly of the Jews and rebukes them indirectly, as people who always set up their own will, disregard the divine laws, and make it their concern to count for nothing what pleases the Master. For by bearing witness here to his own obedience, he accuses their disobedience. Indeed, he said to them somewhere else as well, since they wanted to persecute him, had chosen to hate him, and were passing an unjust verdict on him for this: "You judge according to the flesh; I judge no one. And even if I do judge, my judgment is just, because I do not seek my own will, but the will of him who sent me." So he says such things in keeping with the economy [?].

28. But come now, let us consider this. Having come down from heaven as God, he says that those who have believed in him were given to him by the Father, so that he might not lose them, but rather save them and raise them up on the last day. How, then, did he raise them, if not plainly through his own resurrection from the dead? For he first of all gave life to his own temple, and shook the power of death through the death of his own flesh, and so became for human nature a way to resurrection, and to being able from then on to prevail over corruption. It was therefore proper to God the Word, who came down from heaven, that through which he became firstborn from the dead [?], so that what was given to him might follow him, once he had risen, into life, no longer perishing through the transgression of the first-formed man, but rather being saved through the obedience of Christ. Again, he says that those who accept faith in him have been given to him as one who has become man. For all that belongs to the Father is his own inheritance. But since, as I said, he shared in blood and flesh, and we then believed in him as God, the word "giving" is brought in for this reason. For he who was king even before the flesh has reigned over us also with the flesh. And so, as one brought to the point of beginning to reign when he became like us, he says: "The Lord said to me, 'You are my Son; today I have begotten you.'" He receives, then, in a human way what is his own, even though as God he holds authority over all things.

On Christ's being sanctified, and on the priesthood understood with reference to him.

29. "For it was fitting that he, for whom are all things,

[Footnotes: ἀπολείπηται; αὐτό; αὐτῷ.]

and through whom are all things, in bringing many sons to glory, should make the pioneer of their salvation perfect through sufferings. For the one who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one. For this reason he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying, 'I will proclaim your name to my brothers; in the midst of the assembly I will sing your praise.'" Some of the more ignorant, perhaps, who are in the habit of dividing the one Lord Jesus Christ into two Christs and two sons, suppose that the one said to be made perfect through sufferings is the man born of a woman, thought of separately and apart from the Word who is from God the Father, and that he is the one called the pioneer of our salvation; and that he was made perfect by God the Word himself, having been given over to suffering as someone else in his own right. For they say it was fitting above all for him for whom are all things and through whom are all things, because the blessed evangelist says: "All things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being." "It was fitting, then," they say, "for the Word, for whom are all things and through whom are all things, in bringing many sons to glory, to make the pioneer of their salvation" (that is, simply a man, the one born through the holy Virgin) "perfect through sufferings." But that their argument is full of folly, as can be shown even now

30. First of all, the phrase "through whom" is used also of the Father himself. Indeed the blessed Paul says, "God is faithful, through whom you were called into fellowship with his Son." And again, to those called through faith to the dignity of freedom, he says: "So you are no longer a slave but a son; and if a son, then also an heir through God." Since, then, divinely inspired Scripture makes no distinction in using the expression, and applies it to the Father as well, nothing any longer compels us to refer the "through whom" necessarily to the person of the Son. And since this is true, why should we not rather leave his person aside for the present, and then, following the aim of the sacred Scriptures and keeping to the account proper to the Only-begotten's economy in the flesh, say that the Father made the Son, once he had become man, perfect through sufferings? "For he endured the cross, despising the shame," surely by the good pleasure of the God and Father, so that he might make us too, who have chosen to follow in his footsteps, courageous, as we obey him when he says: "Do not fear those who kill your body but cannot kill the soul." For since they were going to have tribulation in the world, to be persecuted by enemies, to contend strenuously for the doctrines of the truth, and to achieve virtue well by sweat and toil, he does not let them grow soft and cowardly, but rather makes them most bold, having himself travelled the road of sufferings, so that he might also

[Footnotes: ἀγαγόντι; πιθεῖν; τοῦτο.]

shame us into it, saying: "A disciple is not above the teacher, nor a slave above his master. It is enough for the disciple to become like his teacher, and the slave like his master." "If they persecuted me, they will persecute you too."

31. The aim of the Only-begotten, then, was to suffer for us in his own flesh. And what the reason for this was, the inspired Paul will teach us when he says: "Since the children share in blood and flesh, he himself likewise shared in the same, so that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and set free those who through fear of death were subject to slavery all their lives." Since, then, it was impossible for human nature to destroy death (for it had been overpowered by death, the ancient curse having brought it down to this), the life-giving Word of God necessarily put on the nature held captive by death, that is, ours, the human nature, so that death, leaping upon his flesh like some untamed wild beast, might cease from its tyranny over us, being destroyed by God. He himself, then, is the one who is made perfect in the flesh for our sake in a human way, but who perfects us in a divine way by destroying the power of death. For human nature lacked incorruption, though it had been made so in the beginning. "For God did not make death, nor does he delight in the destruction of the living; for he created all things so that they might exist; and the generative forces of the world are wholesome, and there is no poison of destruction in them, nor is there a kingdom of Hades on earth." "But through the envy of the devil death entered the world." So, having perfected us, he said to his Father and God in heaven: "I glorified you on earth; I finished the work that you gave me to do." For it is truly glory to God the Father to have destroyed death through his own Offspring. So for him the perfecting came through sufferings, but for us what took place is the supplying of what was lacking; for what is in Christ is a new creation.

32. That he is not saying that simply a man, with the Word set apart, was made perfect for us, but rather the Only-begotten appearing in human form, the inspired Paul will confirm again when he adds: "For the one who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one. For this reason he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying, 'I will proclaim your name to my brothers.'" It is well worth seeing who the one who sanctifies is, and who those who are sanctified would be, and how all are from one, or from whom. Well then, the Son sanctifies, since he is holy by nature as God, and we are sanctified by

[Footnotes: θανάτου; αὑταῖς; τό; unum?]

him through the Spirit. How then are all from one? As from a Maker and Creator; so that from this it follows that we must have brotherhood with one another. For between one created thing and another, insofar as they are created, there is a kind of natural brotherhood. Yet the Son is uncreated by nature, and not a brother to creation, since he is God by nature. How then are all from one, both the one who sanctifies and those who are sanctified? Then the account of the economy in the flesh is needed to clarify the matter before us. For when he became like us, then he too is said to be from one together with us, and he has been called brother to creatures, as one who has human kinship with us. That is why, very reasonably, he is not ashamed to call us brothers. As it seems to me, he would not consent to be called brother to those who came into being through him unless he had become like them, though without letting go of what he was. For then he too, whom the Seraphim praise and all creation worships, will sing praise with us without reproach.

33. "And confessedly great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed in throughout the world, taken up in glory." If the Word, being God, is said to have become man, without of course letting go of being God, but remaining always in what he was, then indeed it is great, and confessedly great is the mystery of godliness. But if Christ is thought to be an ordinary man, joined to God only by equality of rank or authority (for some of the more ignorant have held such views), how has he been manifested in the flesh? (Yet is it not obvious to everyone that every man is in the flesh and could not be seen by anyone otherwise?) And in what way does it say that he was seen also by the holy angels?
