Do the angels not see us ourselves as well? What then is strange or extraordinary in Christ if some of the holy angels beheld him, when he was like us and nothing more? And how was he proclaimed among the nations? And as being what is he believed in by those in the world? For if the disciples proclaimed him simply as a man, one of us, and not rather as God made man, and he is believed in by those in the world as being this, then we have been overcome by the worship of a man and have worshipped the creature; and he himself, who is by nature and in truth God of all, has driven us to this [?], for he himself appointed for us the choir of those who speak of God. But if Christ, after rising from the dead, said to the holy apostles, "Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,"

[Footnotes: 1 Timothy 3:16; γενητῷ, γενητόν; τίνα δὲ τρόπον; perhaps καὶ τίς ὑπάρχων.]

and we then believed in him and were baptized, proclaiming his death and confessing his resurrection, then, since this is our custom, we are in no way liable to charges of worshipping a man. Christ, then, is not a man honored by a mere conjunction with God the Word, but rather, through the coming together with the human in a union belonging to the economy, one Son and Lord. For then the mystery of godliness is great. For the Word, being God, was manifested in the flesh, and he was also justified in the Spirit, for our Lord Jesus Christ committed no sin. He was also seen by angels, who, not being ignorant of his human birth, said: "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will among men." He was also proclaimed among the nations; and that he is truly the Son of God the Father and has appeared in the flesh is believed by those in the world.

34. "And John testified, saying, 'I saw the Spirit descending like a dove from heaven, and it remained on him. I did not know him; but the one who sent me to baptize with water said to me, "The one on whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining, he is the one who baptizes with the Holy Spirit." And I have seen and have testified that this is the Son of God.'" Since we say that Emmanuel is one, and do not tolerate those who divide him into two Christs, what then do we say about the Holy Spirit flying down upon him from heaven and remaining on him? Are we to suppose that the Word from God the Father needed to partake of the Holy Spirit? Yet how would it not be truly shameful to think or say such a thing? For the Spirit is his own, just as it is also God the Father's. Indeed the blessed Paul says: "And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, 'Abba, Father.'" It is impious, then, even so much as to suspect that the Word from God the Father himself needed participation in the Spirit; and to think that something with so clear a proof requires further inquiry is utterly foolish. How then did the Spirit fly down upon him? He receives in a human way, for the economy in the flesh shows very well that his receiving is beyond reproach, or rather leads to it of necessity. For he receives not so much for himself as for us. Since the Spirit had flown away from those on earth, because the mind of man is intently set on evil from youth, it came down upon him as upon a second firstfruits of the race, so that it might lodge and rest again in us, who have now attained sinlessness in Christ and have, freed from every charge, a

[Footnotes: κἀγώ; οὐ πάναισχρον, or πᾶν αἰσχρόν.]

life. But although he receives in a human way for our sake, see him giving in a divine way. "The one on whom you see the Spirit descending," it says, "and remaining, he is the one who baptizes with the Holy Spirit." This is a divine work, for our Lord Jesus Christ instills the Spirit of the Father into the baptized as his own. And the inspired Paul confirms us in this when he writes: "Those who are in the flesh cannot please God. But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if the Spirit of God dwells in you. And if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him." So John testified that "This is the Son of God."

35. I would like to put a question again to those who divide the one Lord Jesus Christ into two sons (the Father pointed to one, and the blessed evangelist speaks about one: "This is the Son of God"). Tell me, then: of whom is this saying spoken? If it is spoken specifically and solely of the Only-begotten, that is, of the Word who is from the Father, how does he receive the Spirit, when he is God by nature and has it as his own? But if they say that the man born of a woman, separately and specifically, that is, on his own, needed participation in the Spirit, how is he the one who baptizes in it, when being able to make those who come to it partakers of the Spirit befits only the supreme nature? But if the same one both receives and gives, it is clear that he receives in keeping with the principles of the economy in the flesh, and gives inasmuch as he is God by nature and in truth. He receives in a human way, not so much for himself, but procuring it for the nature of men through himself and in himself first; and he gives in a divine way from his own nature, instilling it in those worthy to receive it. It would be possible to add other passages that resemble the text before us and have the same sense; but knowing that repetition is tiresome, we say this: for the more intelligent, the explanation of one passage is enough for an accurate clarification of those like it. So whenever Christ is said to be sanctified, perhaps, or to receive the Spirit, it should be understood in this very way. For it is better to be pious, piously turning the sense of the sacred Scriptures toward what is blameless, than to run against rocks, impiously raising fortifications against the glory of Christ out of what is rightly

36. "Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit in the wilderness for forty days, being tempted by the devil. He ate nothing in those days, and when they were over, he was hungry." Again, it was necessary that he who had come for this very purpose into a voluntary self-emptying should stand up on our behalf and, so to speak, strip for the contest against Satan, who had conquered of old, so that he might make us partakers of his own

[?achievement], and show that those who had grown weak in Adam have spiritual strength. For in Christ the effects of the ailments, both of body and of soul, that befell human nature in the first-formed man have ceased. For just as through his obedience the many were made righteous, though through that man's disobedience they had suffered condemnation, so again, through the strength understood to be in Christ (clearly a spiritual strength), we have repelled the harms that came from the first weaknesses, and we who fell in Adam have conquered in Christ. He therefore does battle for us as man, and conquers in a divine way. He is tempted, as Satan leaps upon him as upon one of us, supposing that the lack of self-control of desire [?] would help him fight against the one being tempted; but he went away put to shame, since human nature was renewed in Christ and had put to death the law of sin that rages in the members of the flesh, for it has been abolished in Christ. Having fasted long enough, and having kept his flesh unharmed without drink or food by a power befitting God, he at length allows it to undergo what is proper to it. For he is said to have been hungry. And for what reason? So that through both he might skilfully be recognized as being at once God and man, plainly one and the same: above us in a divine way [?], and like us in a human way. He is said to be led by the power of the Spirit in the wilderness, where "being led" means not so much being carried off as spending one's time, or continuing; just as it is often said of one of us, "So-and-so conducts himself rightly," that is, he lives and behaves blamelessly. He stayed, then, in the wilderness, that is, he spent his time there, not in a bodily way; for without drink and the food that bodies need, in the power of the Spirit and beyond our nature, he persevered in the fast. But observe this, for the force of the thought is most beneficial. He was not tempted before holy baptism, nor was he led by the Spirit in the wilderness, and in this he set us a pattern. For it is impossible for those not yet baptized to be able to withstand courageously the onslaught of Satan the tempter, hard as it is to bear, or to be led spiritually. The fitting time for such brilliant and admirable achievements is after holy baptism. For once we have been strengthened in this way by participation in the Holy Spirit, and sealed by grace from above for spiritual vigor, we shall be invincible to Satan and shall live as in the power of the Spirit, taking as a kind of wilderness the state of being outside worldly turmoil. For the all-powerful Word, conquering Satan was a very small thing; but for us, in turn, it is a great thing to obtain this too through his becoming man, just as it is to be renewed to incorruption. For just as through his resurrection from the dead we have risen above corruption, so through his victory in being tempted we in turn have prevailed.

Chapter 37. "Since then we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our confession. For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who has been tested in every respect in the same way, yet without sin." We make the confession of the right faith in one God the Father Almighty, and in one Lord Jesus Christ his Son, and in one Holy Spirit. The divine Paul writes that we must hold fast to this confession. There is, as all agree, one Son of God the Father, and clearly this is Christ Jesus, who is able to sympathize with our weaknesses and has been tested in every respect in the same way, yet without sin. Who, then, would our great high priest be? Is it not the one who became like us and suffered in the flesh for us? For it was then that he was named our high priest. He did not offer an alien and foreign victim, as the others were accustomed to do. He was himself the lamb, the most fragrant sacrifice, the spiritual whole burnt offering, the most vocal turtledove, the pure dove, the living bread, the golden censer. "For we are the fragrance of Christ to God," as it is written. But consider with me the depth of the apostle's thoughts. "We do not have," he says, "a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who has been tested in every respect in the same way, yet without sin." For even before the Word of God had become man, he says, he knew, yes, he knew human weakness as its Creator: "For he knew our frame," as it is written. But if we may say anything human of him too, he had not yet been called to the actual experience of our weaknesses. Once he had clothed himself in our flesh, however, he was tested in all things. We certainly do not say this as though he had been ignorant. We mean that, while divine knowledge already lay beneath it, it also came about that he learned through experience itself. Nor did he become sympathetic from having been tested in some way, for he was merciful by nature, and is, as God. But since he became like us while remaining what he is, these things too are said of him in a manner fitting for a man. The apostle says that he passed through the heavens both bodily and in a manner fitting for God. "For he ascended," as the most wise Paul himself says somewhere, "now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf." Yet he also passes through the heavens in another way, in that the blessed angels are surpassed and fall behind his glory. For he is, he truly is, as God, "far above all rule and authority and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come." For he sits as Son with his own

Father [?], even though he became like us in the economy of salvation. Chapter 38. "And no one takes this honor for himself; he is called by God, just as Aaron was. So also Christ did not glorify himself to become high priest. It was the one who said to him, 'You are my Son; today I have begotten you.'" He who emptied himself waits for the call from the Father that brings him into the priesthood. That priesthood was entirely customary and most fitting, not so much for his own nature as for ours, that is, for human nature. Since he became equal to that nature, he submits to what belongs to it. He suffers no harm at all from this, but rather makes skillful use of the economy in the flesh. Being Lord by nature, he remained what he was even though he came to be in the form of a servant. In the same way, we say, he has in heaven myriads who minister to him as priests, offering the spiritual and bloodless sacrifices, that is, hymns and doxologies; yet he also accepts the priesthood that belongs to us, preserving everywhere, within the limits of humanity, what is proper and fitting to it. He was called, then, just as Aaron was, but not in the same way. Aaron was anointed for priestly service and was a servant. Christ is called as Son, and serves as priest to the Father after the order of Melchizedek. The divine Paul explains the manner of this priestly service when he writes of Christ, the Savior of us all: "who has become such not according to the law of a fleshly commandment, but according to the power of an indestructible life." The manner of his priestly service is therefore incomparably better. Aaron, as I said, was a servant, even though called to the priesthood. But Christ is even so the Son of God the Father: as God and Word by nature, according to his birth before the ages, and as a man like us, according to his most recent birth in the flesh. The word "today" would point to this birth, since it signifies to us the present time. The Father, then, makes his birth in the flesh his own as well. For he knows, he knows that he is his own Son [?], from himself in a divine way and from a woman in a human way. Chapter 39. "In the days of his flesh he offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to the one who was able to save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverence. Although he was a Son, he learned obedience from what he suffered; and having been made perfect, he became the source of eternal salvation for all who obey him, being designated [Textual notes: variant 'high priest' (accusative); 1: variant 'carrying away'.]

by God a high priest after the order of Melchizedek." The all-wise Paul writes to those justified by faith and says: "Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ." And indeed the divine Peter says: "For what credit is it if you endure when you sin and are beaten for it? But if you do good and suffer and endure it, this is grace before God. For Christ died for us, leaving you an example, so that you might follow in his steps." So the Only-begotten, having taken our likeness, made it his aim to suffer in a human way. He wanted to teach those who know him how one must meet the attacks of temptation, and what kind of people those ought to be who are persecuted for the sake of piety toward God and have entered into danger of soul and body. He also wanted to show the glorious outcome of obedience, so that we too may prove to be excellent and wise imitators of what he did in the economy, and may live a truly commendable life as we strive to follow in his steps. From what he himself endured and did for our sake in a human way, he wants to teach this: those who are at all destined to suffer for love of him ought to have an unbreakable resolve, and ought to regard danger for the sake of piety as life. Yet he does not allow those who show courage to throw their lives away rashly. Nor does he allow them carelessly to neglect what must be done and the means by which they could reasonably be saved, and simply to wait, against all hope, for whatever those who wish them harm decide. Rather, he urges them to pray more intensely and to make their supplication to God unceasing. He teaches this by having offered prayers and supplications in the days of his flesh to the one who was able to save him from death. Chapter 40. See how full this matter is of a holy moderation. To be overbold in the face of temptations has a reputation for courage, but it seems somehow not entirely free of arrogance. To appear to fear and draw back, on the other hand, and to ask God, who has the power to save, gives the impression of reverence. Otherwise, why did he command the holy disciples, "When they persecute you in this city, flee to the next"? And how could the all-wise Paul himself, though he plainly tells us, "Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Will affliction, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or sword?", have escaped the governor of Damascus by being let down through a window in the wall? It was necessary, then, that Christ himself should appear to us as the guide and teacher of every good. For he approached with loud cries and supplication, as one who had become like us; and he was heard [Textual notes: 5: variant 'having given themselves over to the'; variant 'the supplication to him'.]

as one who is by nature and truly the Son, and is never disregarded. "For I knew," he says, "that you always hear me." To make our prayers acceptable as well, he himself once more makes the beginning of the matter. He all but widens the Father's hearing to human nature, and makes it, as it were, most ready for the prayers of those who are in danger for his sake. So it was we who were in him, as in a second firstfruits of the race, praying with loud cries and not without tears. We were asking that the power of death be abolished and that life prevail, the life given long ago to our nature. Chapter 41. That obeying God has a splendid and admirable end, we are again taught [?] in him. "For from what he suffered," he says, "he learned obedience." It is as if he were saying, for instance: "He humbled himself, becoming obedient to death, even death on a cross." But he did not remain humble, for he was highly exalted and received the name that is above every name. The form of the expression is human, yet the pattern it sets for us is excellent. It shows obedience to be glorious and admirable, and the source of every good for us. So the fact that Emmanuel, when tempted, prayed with loud cries and tears is also an example for us. This happened not before the incarnation but in the days of his flesh, when he could do this too without blame, and with no injury to the glory of the Godhead; rather, this itself was [?] of the economy in the flesh. Otherwise, how could Life have been terrified of death? He makes us ourselves most courageous and says, "Do not fear those who kill the body." How could he himself have been overcome by cowardice? Or how could he have been unable to drive death away from his own flesh? He removes it from all. He promises to raise those in the tombs with a single word, and shows that this is not beyond his power. For he called to Lazarus, "Come out!", and to the widow's son, "Young man, I say to you, arise." Chapter 42. But if there are some who dare to say that

he is a mere man like us, then by their own admission they are worshippers of a man, since they worship him. For it is written: "You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve." Suppose they say that he was called to equality of rank, that is, of authority, with God the Word, and that he then approaches God the Father with loud cries and in tears and begs the one who saves. In that case nothing prevents us from supposing that the Word himself is of the same measure as the one believed to have equality of rank, that is, of authority, with him. Then it would also be fitting for the Word to fear death, to be wary of danger, to weep in temptations, and to need another's hand in order to be saved, and besides this to learn obedience through what he suffered when tested. But, I think, to think or say this is utterly unsafe. For the Word of God is all-powerful, stronger than death, beyond suffering, and has no share at all in human fear. And yet, though this is his nature, he suffered for us. So Christ is neither a mere man nor a Word without flesh. Rather, being united to our humanity, he could suffer human things in his own flesh while remaining impassible. These things, then, happened in a human way as a pattern for us, as I said at the beginning, so that we might follow in his steps. "For he did this once for all when he offered himself. For the law appoints as high priests men who are subject to weakness; but the word of the oath, which came after the law, appoints a Son who has been made perfect forever." By a single offering, clearly the offering of his own body, "he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified," our Lord Jesus Christ. "For he offered himself for us as a fragrant offering to God" the Father. And he has perfected them spiritually, through faith and sanctification, although the worship of the law perfected nothing. Therefore the types have come to an end, and the uselessness of the Old Covenant, with its shadows, has ceased. In its place, necessarily, a better hope has been introduced, through which we draw near to God. Christ is the mediator, and he came into the rank of high priest because he took on our likeness. Chapter 43. But consider this. The divine Paul says of him [?] that he was crucified in weakness. How, then, can the law appoint as high priests men subject to weakness, while the word of the oath that came after the law appoints a Son made perfect forever, as one who is clearly not subject to weakness? For this, I think, is what it means to be made perfect, that is, to be complete in every good: he is not like those under the law, of whom it is not unusual to say that they are sometimes weak. [Textual notes: 13: variant 'of them'; variant 'altogether also'.]

How, then, is the same one believed to be above weakness, as a Son made perfect, and also crucified in weakness? It follows that we should understand it this way: he was weak in that he endured the cross in the flesh, yet as God he is beyond weakness. "For the spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak." But if they say that the weakness here shows that those who served as priests under the law were in sin, I will not object. I rather agree with those who choose to take it correctly in this sense too. The priests under the law, then, needed not one sacrifice but many. They offered daily for themselves and for the sins of ignorance of the people, because they were very often weak and gave way to a slackness that led to sin of many kinds. But he, being above sin as God, offered himself and became our high priest. He is said to minister in a human way, yet as priest he offers his own body to the Father. So, in a manner fitting for God, he does not admit of experiencing sin, since he was not of a created nature. A created nature does not have immutability by its essence, nor the power to escape sin entirely. He is therefore God, perfect in every way. He holds unshakable firmness in holiness without help from another, and has sinlessness as the fruit of his own nature. Chapter 44. "Now the main point of what we are saying is this: we have such a high priest, who sat down at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens, a minister of the holy places and of the true tent, which the Lord set up, not man." The old tent was erected in the wilderness by the all-wise Moses, and it was made according to the pattern shown to him on the mountain. That tent was entirely fitting for those who served as priests under the law. But the dwelling fitting and proper for Christ is the beautiful city above, that is, heaven, the divine and highest tent. It is not the invention of human skill but holy and built by God. Having come there, he brings to God the Father those who believe in him, who have clearly been sanctified through the Spirit. "For no one comes to the Father," he says, "except through me." This is the manner of what is here called his ministry. The matter is fitting for God, even if it is expressed in our words, that is, in human ones. For he is able to sanctify by his own Spirit those who believe, who have been justified by mercy and grace. He offers them to God, as it were, in priestly service, dying to the world but made alive by the Spirit and shining forth in a truly commendable life. How could this not be fitting for God? And although he is said to minister, he is not less than the Father, nor does he fall short of the glory that is his. He shows this clearly in advance by being enthroned on the divine [Textual notes: variant 'serving as priests'; or 'acting as priests'; variant 'Son'.]

seats and sitting at the right hand of the one who begot him. If it is true that every priest stands, always ministering, and could never be thought to sit beside the God he serves and share his glory, how is Christ not a priest [?], since he is on the seats of the Godhead as God and ministers in a human way? But someone may slander the truth and say: "Yes, a man in his own right sat at the right hand of the Father, joined to God merely by equality of rank." Such a person is saying that the highest throne, which befits the Holy Trinity alone, no longer belongs to the Trinity alone. Instead, some fourth one, recent and created, is now introduced to us as God after the consubstantial and Holy Trinity. Chapter 45. "But when Christ came as high priest of the good things to come, through the greater and more perfect tent, not made with hands, that is, not of this creation, he entered once for all into the holy places, not through the blood of goats and calves but through his own blood, having obtained eternal redemption." Our discussion has just shown in what way our Lord Jesus Christ became high priest for us through the greater and more perfect tent. And no one would doubt that the manner of his priestly service is incomparably better than that under the law, and far surpasses what existed in type and shadow, for he himself is the truth and the spotless victim. But notice how "our admirable high priest, who sat down at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens, entered once for all into the holy places through his own blood, having obtained eternal redemption." How, then, could the one who is at the right hand of the Father as God be said to have his own blood? Only if we believe that he who is Son by nature from God the Father was called Son of Man, and that, giving his own blood as a ransom for the life of all, he obtained this everlasting redemption for the world. For surely no one would say that it was consistent and fitting for Emmanuel to be slaughtered many times, like irrational animals, since his suffering once was enough to redeem all that is under heaven. But suppose, as some have thought, he was a man in his own right, joined to God by equality of rank and authority but divided from him in hypostasis and believed to exist separately. Then the blood given for the redemption of the world was not the own blood of the one who sits with the Father. It was rather the blood of another, who has only a relational connection with him. Consider certain rulers who do not differ from one another at all in their equal dignities: they are not thought of as one, but truly as two. In the same way, if something is joined to someone by rank while their natures, that is, their hypostases, remain divided, they would not be one but two. And the blood of one of them, say, is entirely his own and is not thought to be

another's. So it is not enough for true union to say that a man has been joined to God as if by equality of rank, that is, of authority. Chapter 46. "For Christ did not enter holy places made with hands, copies of the true ones, but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf." God says, "Heaven is my throne." So we say that the Son too rests upon the spirits above and has heaven as his holy tent. He does not enter copies of the true things as the law prescribes, like those who serve as priests bodily on earth and perform sacrifices with blood. But in what way does he now appear on our behalf in the presence of God? Was he not always manifest, even before the incarnation? It is easy to see that he is the creative Wisdom of God the Father, through whom all things were brought into existence. And indeed, as Wisdom, he says: "I was the one in whom he delighted. Daily I rejoiced in his presence at all times, when he rejoiced at having completed the world, and rejoiced among the sons of men." If the Father delighted in Wisdom, and Wisdom was in his presence daily, rejoicing and giving joy, how does he now appear in the presence of God? He appears in a new way. He is no longer the bare Word without flesh, as he certainly was in the beginning, but appears in our form and nature. For we say that he has now appeared in this way, and has, as it were, brought human nature into the sight [?] of God the Father, though it had become an object of aversion because of the transgression in Adam. He therefore presents us before the eyes of the Father as in himself, the first, insofar as he appeared as a man. He does this in order to bring us to the Father, freeing us from the ancient charges and remaking us into newness of life in the Spirit, so that from now on we may be seen as worthy of the Father's regard, having been received into the rank of sons. On the claim that our Lord Jesus Christ needed glory. Chapter 47. "Paul, an apostle, not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead." One proof is enough to show that our Lord Jesus Christ did not need glory from outside, brought in from elsewhere: together with God the Father he sends out the ministers who proclaim him. For they did not proclaim themselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord, to the glory of God the Father. But since we must follow the sacred Scriptures, never passing over the [?] [Textual notes: variant 'were brought'; [?].]

...as seems good to them, come, let us say in what way God [?], and the Father is said to crown the Son with glory. Now blessed Paul himself says somewhere about the rulers of this age: “For if they had known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.” So he knows that the one who was crucified is also Lord of glory. How then does the Lord of glory receive glory from the Father? Clearly the statement has again been made with a view to the economy. He receives it humanly, yet even so he is Lord of glory divinely. The wealth of his divine nature may be seen by us in his prerogatives that are above creation; the measure of our poverty, in his being said to receive: “And though he was rich, for our sake he became poor.” But if we govern ourselves with good thoughts toward right belief, and are eager to think what is fitting about him, we shall not fail to recognize that even in our poverty he is rich as God.

48. “The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand.” Again the Son receives as man. Yet the Father does not place himself outside of having all things under himself. For in giving them to the Son, he rules over the universe together with him, bringing the race on earth under the scepter of the Godhead through him and in him, even though it had swerved off unbridled into rebellion. For as the most wise Paul himself says somewhere: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself.” And we certainly do not mean that some other Christ, besides the one born of the holy Virgin, was reconciling the world to himself by dwelling in a man (for some of the more ignorant think so). Rather, we mean that the God and Father was reconciling the world to himself in Christ. For the Son, made man, became our mediator and, as it were, the one who reconciles us into peace, not procuring the submission of those in the world for someone else, but, as in his own person, for God the Father. For having been reconciled to Christ, we have been reconciled through him and in him to God, the Savior of us all. That is why he said: “Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest.” And that for those who come to him the reconciliation would be not with anyone else but with the one who is God by nature and truly, he gave full assurance when he said: “Whoever believes in me does not believe in me, but in him who sent me. And whoever sees me sees him who sent me.” And again at another time: “Believe in God, and believe also in me.”

49. “Father, the hour has come. Glorify your Son, so that your Son may also glorify you, just as you gave him authority over all flesh, so that he may give eternal life to all whom you have given him.” Advocate, then,

and propitiation the Son has been named. For he establishes [?] in incorruption [?], and has obtained a nature superior to corruption. And the Father himself is also glorified, as having a Son who is like him in every respect whatever, [?] and of the same working as himself. And the Son showed this by abolishing death and raising his own temple from the dead. He receives authority over all things, again in our manner and humanly, although he reigns over the universe divinely. And the Father instills eternal life in those who have been given to the Son; but this life is he himself, for he said: “I am the resurrection and the life.” So even if he is said to have received from the Father glory and authority and kingship over all things, the receiving must be ascribed to the measures of the self-emptying. But we must know that he is also Lord of glory as God, and enthroned with the Father, and in no way falls short of the preeminence and glory of the one who begot him, so far as the nature of the Godhead is concerned. For in this way we shall be pious, bringing every thought into obedience to him, and pulling down reasonings and every height raised up against the knowledge

50. “Being therefore exalted to the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this which you see and hear. For David did not ascend into heaven; but he himself says: The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.” In these words we may observe the whole mystery of the incarnation of the Only-begotten. For being in the form of the Father and in equality with him, God the Word who is from him, the all-powerful right hand and the all-working hand, is said to have been emptied because of the humanity; but he is exalted again, not passing over to a dignity foreign to him and not his by nature from of old, but returning to the glory and preeminence that is innate in him and always inherent. For he is exalted humanly, although by nature he is always most high. For he became man, and this, I think, is the measure of the nature and what is called the emptying. Yet God made man, although he was thought to be nothing other than only a man, this very thing that was seen, “was proclaimed among the nations [?],

was believed on in the world,” and has been honored as truly Son of God the Father, and has crowned himself with the glories of the highest renown of all, being believed to be God. And this is not something unaccustomed for him; rather, what we say is unaccustomed [?] is his being lowered in humanity and seeming to be exalted, although he is resplendent with unending glories. But since, for human nature and in our measures, all things are from above and from God, for this reason he is quite fittingly said to be exalted by the right hand of the Father, although he himself is the hand and the right hand that fashions the universe. Look again, I ask you, at our Lord Jesus Christ receiving the Spirit humanly, but fulfilling the promise of the Father divinely, by instilling the Spirit in those who believe, and not as something foreign but as his own. For God said somewhere through one of the holy prophets: “I will pour out of my Spirit on all flesh.” Christ fulfills this, instilling the Spirit as his own in those who have been called. And yet to be able to make anyone a partaker of the Holy Spirit would befit not a man in any way, but rather the one who is God by nature. So the Son has performed the works of God the Father, by giving the Spirit himself. The receiving, then, is human; but to pour out the gift of the Spirit from his own fullness upon others is fitting for God and beyond man. So the Word who appeared in human form is God, and for this reason sits together with God the Father.

On the statement that Christ was raised from the dead by the power of the Father.

51. The divine Paul writes about the forefather Abraham: “It was not written for his sake alone that faith was reckoned to him as righteousness, but also for our sake, to whom it is going to be reckoned, we who believe in him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead, who was handed over for our trespasses and raised for our justification.” There is one nature of the Godhead, but it is worshiped in three hypostases, both by us and by the spirits above. And since the whole Godhead is one, any of the works most befitting it would rightly be the work of it, and of it alone. For all things are done by God the Father through the Son in the Spirit. So even if the Father is said somewhere to give life, he will certainly accomplish it through the Son in the Holy Spirit. And if the Son works life in those who stand in need of life, it is not without the consubstantial Father, for he has in himself the one who begot him. Indeed he said clearly: “I do not speak on my own; but the Father who abides in me, he does the works.” And if the Spirit is said to do this, he will certainly act as the Spirit of life; and we say that the God and Father is life by nature, and so is the Son begotten from him. So the Father is said to have raised Christ from the dead; but we shall not find the

Son inactive in the resurrection of his own body. Indeed, he said to the Jews: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” And observe how, when blessed Paul says [?] “that faith will be reckoned to us as righteousness, we who have believed in him who raised Jesus Christ from the dead,” the faith has been directed not to the Father and God alone, but also to our Lord Jesus Christ. Besides (for I think we must see this too), the Only-begotten became man, and endured death in the flesh; yet he returned to life not by the power of the flesh, that is, of the humanity, but as in the might of the Godhead, “which gives life to the dead and calls things that are not as though they were.” So the giving of life must quite rightly be ascribed, not at all to the nature of the body itself, even though it became the own body of the Word born from God, but rather to the supreme power and the nature that is above creation, as in the person of God the Father, from whom the Son came forth, equal and like him in all things. And through both proceeds also the life-giving Spirit. He says that Christ was handed over for our trespasses and raised for our justification. For just as his suffering death in his own flesh took place for our sake, so that from then on the might of death would be enfeebled, so also he came back to life for our sake, inaugurating in us the return to incorruption and wiping out the charges arising from the transgression in Adam. For we have been justified in Christ, who destroyed the power of that ancient curse through his obedience in all things, and freed our nature from the ancient charges; for in it he committed no sin (rather, in him it became well-pleasing), although it had been condemned, as we might say, in Adam.

52. “Or do you not know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were buried with him, then, through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life.” Our Lord Jesus Christ, having despoiled Hades and [?] the multitude of imprisoned spirits of the souls there, came back to life on the third day. Then to the holy [?]

“...nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” So we are baptized, as it were, into the one name of the Father, and into the one name of the Son, and into his death, and into the Holy Spirit. Let those, then, who divide the one Christ and Son into two sons, saying that a man was joined to God by mere

equality of dignity, that is, of authority, with the natures divided, teach us into whose death we were baptized. If, then, into that of God the Word in particular, we shall plainly be accusing the undefiled nature of corruption, and assigning death to the one who is life by nature. But if they say: into that of the one from the woman, considered separately and apart and by himself, how are they not also saying openly that he, if he is capable of death, he into whose death we have been baptized, would surely be the one ranked together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, while the Word born from God is perhaps thrust out of true [?]? But anyone with an alert mind surely sees the absurdity of these notions. Therefore we must understand that the Word of God, having become like us, suffered willingly in the flesh. For we have been baptized into his death in this sense: as of one Son, impassible in the nature of the Godhead but passible in the flesh. And that Christ refashions us into newness of life through the resurrection, how could anyone doubt? For he presents us to himself and to the Father as alive from the dead, as it is written: “and dead to sin, but alive to righteousness.”

53. “If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus Christ dwells in you, he who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will also give life to our mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in us.” The only-begotten Word of God is life by nature. But since he clothed himself with a body subject to death, and “by the grace of God tasted death for everyone” through his own flesh, yet came back to life divinely, “because it was not possible for him to be held by it,” for this reason, according to the explanations just given, he is said to have been raised by the Father. But come now, let us consider this too, if you will. He said that the Father will give life also to our bodies through his Spirit who dwells in us; and that this is true, no one would doubt. But this very life-giving Spirit is also the Spirit of Christ himself. For it is written: “You are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him.” And again, about the holy apostles: “When they had come to Mysia, they tried to go into Bithynia, and the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them.” Since, then, the Spirit is the own Spirit also of the one who was raised, even though it is God the Father who gives us life in the Spirit, how can one doubt that the resurrection took place in respect of the humanity, but that the Word, who is God by nature from the Father, effected it together with his own Father, since the life-giving Spirit is also his own? [Variant readings:] “you”; “by death.”

54. “Since you seek proof of the Christ who speaks in me, who is not weak toward you but is powerful among you. For though he was crucified out of weakness, yet he lives by the power of God. For we too are weak in him, but we shall live with him by the power of God toward you.” Some of those who had believed in our Lord Jesus Christ were being scandalized, perhaps by words brought to them by certain people, leading to such thoughts as these: If he was truly God, and Son by nature of the all-powerful God, how did he not escape the hands [?] of his murderers? And how, having endured that most dishonorable death on the wood, would he not quite reasonably be thought to have been weak as we are, and to have been overcome by the hand of those who crucified him? To such things the divine Paul says: If you really wish to test rightly who and how great the one speaking in me is, consider your own situation, and you will find sufficient grasp of it. For he was not weak among us; rather, he made us most powerful through his own Spirit, so that we are able to master every temptation quite easily and to stand up vigorously against the onsets of the passions. What then, Paul, someone might say, do you say that enduring the cross was not a work of weakness, but that the thing was a display of power? Of divine power, then? Not at all, he says. For I confess that he was weak in the flesh, but lived again by the power of God; for he was God by nature. How, then, was he weak? By allowing his own body even to taste death for our sake, “so that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and free those who through fear of death were held in slavery all their lives.” Since, then, being weak for a short time (in the flesh, I mean) was the occasion of salvation for those everywhere under heaven, how should he not have undergone the weakness, so that through it he might abolish death? He is marveled at again for giving life to his own temple, accomplishing this not out of fleshly weakness but as by the power of God. And he himself is the power of the Father, “the resurrection and the life.” He lives, therefore, always; for he is life. And that we too shall live with him, having been weak with him in dying for the present, since we are in the hope of eternal life, how can one doubt? For he came back to life from the dead, having become a way to life for our nature. For he is called “firstborn from the dead” and “firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.”

“...even to death.” And again: “And Jesus, crying out with a loud voice, said: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit.” Those who are captivated by the opinion of Apollinaris and have chosen to think as he does, who insist and say that the temple united to the Word is without soul and without mind, what would they say, when the holy evangelists have written such things for us about Christ, the Savior of us all? For the divine and supreme nature of the Word would, reasonably, be wholly incapable of receiving terror and grief and the causes of fear. It will utterly refuse ever to be in such states, and will not endure passions like ours at all. A body without soul and mind, on the other hand, would not admit grief, nor would it conceive anything gloomy, or foresee the fear arising from things expected to come. Such things would be undergone, as everyone, I think, agrees, by a rational soul that surveys with its mind both what is already present and, besides this, what is going to happen. How then does Emmanuel say, “Now my soul is troubled”? And how did he begin to be grieved and distressed? Or what spirit at all did he commit into the hands of God the Father, if the thing is foreign to the Godhead, and does not belong to soulless flesh alone either? It is clear, then, that the Only-begotten became man, taking not a body without soul and mind, but rather one ensouled with a soul, and a rational one, complete according to the principle befitting it. And just as he makes his own everything that belongs to his own body, so also what belongs to the soul. For he had to be seen as having become man for our sake through every condition of flesh and soul. And we too are made up of a rational soul and a body. And just as, by the economy, he allowed his own flesh at times to undergo what is proper to it, so again he allowed the soul to undergo what belongs to it; and he kept the measure of the emptying everywhere, although he is God by nature and above all creation. He commits his own spirit, that is, the soul united to him, to God the Father, so that through this too he might benefit us. For of old the souls of human beings, on departing from their bodies, were sent down into the recesses beneath the earth, filling the storehouses of death. But since Christ committed his own spirit to the Father, he has inaugurated this way for us too. For we shall not go down anywhere into Hades, but rather we shall follow him; and accordingly, committing our souls to the faithful Creator himself, we are in good hopes, for Christ will raise everyone.

56. “Just as the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever eats me will also live because of me.” I would gladly ask those who divide the one into two [Variant readings:] “I commit”; “like us”; “having become.”

Christs: Who then is the one sent by God the Father, who lives because of him and is for this reason life-giving? If it is the Word who is from him, bare and by himself, how is he eaten by us, so that we may live because of him? For the divine is incorporeal by nature. But if they say that the one sent is a man, alone and by himself, how then is he life-giving because he lives because of the Father? And yet how are we not all on earth among the living, since God the Father gives us life, if indeed it is true that “In him we live and move and have our being”? Since, then, we all live because of the Father, how is it that only the body of one man does this, and the bodies of others do not rather have the same operation, if indeed, as I said, we all exist and live because of the Father? What then [?] about these things? The Word of God, having appeared in human form, has been called Apostle; for “he was sent to proclaim release to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind.” And he lives because of the Father, for he was begotten of the living Father. For it was necessary, necessary entirely and in every way, that the Son sprung from the living God and Father, who is life, should be life by nature. And since he made his own the body taken from the holy Virgin, he quite fittingly made it life-giving; for it is the body of the Life that gives life to all things. Therefore the one Son and Christ and Lord must not be divided into two sons. For the same one is life, as being from Life and from the living Father, and is also life-giving through his own body, as God who became like us and was made man.

57. “For just as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself; and he has given him authority to execute judgment as well, because he is Son of Man.” In what way might one suppose that the Father has life in himself? Is it from outside and introduced into him, given by another? Yet how would it not be nonsense to think or say this? For the statement amounts to no small disparagement of the ineffable nature. First, the God of the universe would no longer be simple in nature, but rather composite, if the life in him is other than himself. And the one who gave life to him as one who did not have it would be greater than he, and incomparably better off, if he should be found to have received it at all. But, as I said, it is among the most offensive of notions to suppose that this is how things are, and to think that the God and Father obtained life brought in from outside. He has life in himself, then, not acquired or introduced, but naturally [?], inherent in him as an essential fruit. In this way he also granted the Son to have life. Then how could the Son, having received it, have in himself essentially the

…life? For someone might say this, I suppose. He has life in himself because he exists from the Father by nature, in so far as he is understood to be God. Yet he is said rather to receive it, together with judging, although as God he is himself the judge. And he himself will teach us how he received it, when he says, "because he is the Son of Man." For it does not belong to a human being to have life of himself. But since the body united to him became the very own body of the living Word, it is quite reasonable that he is said to receive life, because that body has his life-giving power. And again he makes the matter his own, since the body that received it became his own body.

That even if Christ is called Son of Man, he is no less true God. [?]

Our Lord Jesus Christ himself says somewhere: "When the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth?" Come then, let us again examine the meaning of these words and consider this: what kind of faith will our Lord Jesus Christ look for on earth when he returns from heaven? Suppose he wants us to believe that he is not God, nor truly God, but rather a man with nothing beyond what we have. Then how could anyone doubt that he will find such a view, that is, such faith and opinion, not among us but rather among Greeks and Jews? For when the idolaters, who worship the creation rather than the Creator, hear of the cross that he endured for us, and of his death as well, they laugh, the wretches. And if anyone calls him God, they jump up at once and declare the thing to be the worship of a man. Those of the circumcision, for their part, attacked the Savior and said plainly: "We are not stoning you for a good work but for blasphemy, because you, though you are a man, make yourself God." He looks, then, not for the faith of those in error but rather for ours, who are used to thinking rightly. So those of us who have seen through to the truth must by every necessity confess that the one who became Son of Man for our sake is God by nature. Otherwise we may entangle ourselves in the charges that lie against those in error, and find without noticing that we have chosen to think as they do, holding a mean opinion of Christ just as they certainly do.

[?]

Christ says somewhere: "For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father." And again, as we were saying just now: "For as the Father has life in himself, so he has also given [variants: "should name"; "thing"]

to the Son to have life in himself, and he has given him authority to execute judgment as well, because he is the Son of Man." And the blessed David sings somewhere: "For God is judge." His disciple also wrote: "There is one lawgiver and judge." Judging, then, would befit no other being but the God over all alone. How then did he give it to the Son of Man? If he gave it as to one of us, how will he be telling the truth when he says, "My glory I will not give to another"? For being judge is the glory of God. But in giving it to the Son he did not himself cease to judge, because they are the same in substance, and the one who received it is the Son of Man. How then is it not plain to everyone that the Word is God because of his ineffable birth from God the Father, and that the same one is also Son of Man because he was united to flesh and underwent a birth like ours, from a woman? So he says to the Jews, "Why do you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth?" And again: "No one has ascended into heaven except the one who came down from heaven, the Son of Man." And again: "Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up." Or he says of himself, "For the Son of Man is going to come in the glory of his Father with the holy angels." And again: "Who do people say that I, the Son of Man, am?" Whenever he says such things, or in short whenever he is called a man in the divinely inspired Scripture, we do not say that he is a man separately and on his own, dividing off from him the Word who is from God the Father. Rather we believe that he is true God, and that for our sake, in the economy of salvation, he also became Son of Man while remaining God, and that there is one Lord Jesus Christ. It is utterly impious to divide him into two sons and two Christs after the indivisible union, which lies beyond all mind and reason and is supreme above them. Those who wished to examine everything written about Christ might perhaps find it not too difficult to set out still more ideas. But we know what is written: "Give an opportunity to the wise, and he will become wiser." For the God of all will guide your most God-loving hearing through the Holy Spirit, so that you can understand rightly. And when Christ finds your faith in this state, sound [?] and unprofaned, he will richly crown you with the good things above and declare you blessed in every way. For all our hope is in Christ, through whom and with whom be glory to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. [Variants: "to be"; "of understanding"]
